en: (The Tārābhaktitaraṅgiṇī) (No.
4930) (Title: The Tārābhaktitaraṅgiṇī)
(Author: Vimalānanda) (Number of pages: 107 pages) (Subject: Tantra)

[The Ritual of the Seven Hundred Verses, from the *Tārābhaktitaraṅgiṇī*] Oṃ Oṃ! Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa; homage to the illustrious Gurus. Having bowed to Tārā, my chosen deity, and to the illustrious Lakṣmī, the tutelary goddess of my lineage, I shall now write the manual for the Nine-Syllable Mantra, having diligently consulted the *Yāmala*, the *Ḍāmara*, the *Yoginītantra*, the *Vārāhītantra*, and other such texts.

I shall now fully proclaim the procedure for the Navacaṇḍī rite, as well as the procedure for the Śatacaṇḍī rite, the division of the Mālā-mantras of the Saptasatī, and the mantras themselves (3). I shall also state the procedures for the secret [mantras] such as Kavaca; nothing here is written without a source, and all that is presented has come down through the traditional lineage (4). Now, for the sake of devotion to Caṇḍī, I shall declare the nine-syllable mantra: Vāk (Aiṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Madana (Klīṃ), the Long One (Ā), Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), and Drīṃ.

The sages of the nine-syllable mantra are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; the meters declared by the sages are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh; the goddesses are said to be Mahākālī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; and Nandā, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā are considered its powers. It is Raktadaṃṣṭrī... [5] ...joined with the moon, the day-maker, water, two tortoises, and the lord of the Ṣiṭī. The sages of the nine-syllable mantra are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; the meters declared by the sages are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh; the goddesses are said to be Mahākālī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; and Nandā, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā are considered its powers. It is Raktadaṃṣṭrī.

The collection of seed-syllables (bījas) for Kā, Durgā, Bhramarī, and Yau; Agni, Vāyu, and Bhaga are the principles (tattvas) arising from the three Vedas. This application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing the desired objects of the devotee.

(9) One should place the Ṛṣi, Chandas, and Devatā in the mouth, heart, and [other limbs]; the Śaktis and Bījas in the [limbs], and the Tattvas again in the heart. (10) One should perform those eleven Nyāsas which bestow the desired fruits. Now...

The Mātṛkānyāsa should be performed according to the previously mentioned method (11), by which a human being attains the same form as the God. Next, one should perform the second nyāsa, named Sārasvata (12). One should place the three seed-syllables (*bījas*) at the beginning of the mantra, followed by *Tāra* (Om), extending up to the heart;

these should be placed in sequence on the fingers, specifically on the little finger as previously stated (13), in the middle of the hands, on the back, at the wrist, and at the elbow, starting from the heart.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the six limbs, conjoined with the seed-syllables (*jāti*). When this *Sārasvata-nyāsa* has been performed, dullness is destroyed. Then one should perform the third placement, accompanied by the group of Mothers (*mātṛ-gaṇa*). Brahmī, whose essence is the *Māyā-bīja*, should always be placed in the east. Likewise, Māheśvarī in the southeast; Kaumārī in the south; Indrāṇī in the southwest corner; Cāmuṇḍā in the north; and [Vārāhī] in the northeast.

Hālakṣmī, Ūrdhvavyomeśvarī, and Saptadvīpeśvarī protect the earth; Kāmeśvarī protects the waters. (18) By performing this third *nyāsa*, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. One should perform the fourth *nyāsa* accompanied by Naṃdajā and the others. (19) Naṃdajā, adorned with a lotus and a goad, is in the front limb; she who holds a sword and a vessel in her hands, Raktadaṃtikā, is in the south. (20) Pṛ...

[The practitioner] should perform the Nyāsa of the Goddess Ambikā, who is joined with the Śākaṃbharī weapon and flowers and sprouts, holding a bow and arrow in her hands, with Durgā on her left, always possessing a beautiful form, with Bhīmā at her head, and extending from her feet up to her head, bearing the luster of a swarm of bees. By performing this fourth Nyāsa, a man removes even the most grievous sins. Then, one should perform the fifth and supreme Brahmā-nyāsa, beginning from the feet.

May the eternal Brahmā protect up to the crown of my head; may Janārdana always protect from the navel down to the base of the spine. May the three-eyed Rudra protect from the base of the spine to the Brahma-randhra; may Haṃsa protect the pair of feet, and Vainateya the two hands. May Vṛṣabha protect the two eyes, and Gajānana all the limbs. Having drunk the blissful essence of the supreme and the non-supreme, may Hari [protect] all [the parts] in this performance. (24–26) May he protect all... in the Kṛta [age].

A person shall obtain [the fruit]; then one should perform the sixth Nyāsa, joined with Mahālakṣmī and the others: (27) May Mahālakṣmī, endowed with ten arms, protect the center; may Sarasvatī, powerful with eight arms, protect the upper part; (28) may Mahākālī, endowed with ten arms, protect the lower part; may Siṃha protect that pair [of feet], and Parahaṃsa the pair of eyes; [may he who is] mounted upon the divine buffalo [protect me].

May Yama protect the two feet, and Maheśa, joined with Caṇḍikā, protect all the limbs. By performing this prescribed Nyāsa on the sixth day, a man shall attain a good state. One should perform the seventh Nyāsa, which consists of the form of the root-syllables (mūlākṣara). (31) One should place the letters of the root-mantra, preceded by the Tārā (Oṃ) and joined with the Bindu (M), upon the Brahma-randhra, the pair of eyes, the two ears, the nose, and the mouth. (32) One should install [them].

By the seventh placement (*nyāsa*), the destruction of diseases occurs; one should again install [the mantra] from the mouth up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (33) When this eighth placement is performed, all suffering is cast away. One should perform the ninth placement, which consists of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the mantra in the form of a bull (*vṛṣa*). (34) From the head down to the feet, and from the feet up to the head—on the front, right, back, and left sides—one should place the bull. (35) The root...

The placement (*nyāsa*) performed with mantras brings about the attainment of the deity; thereafter, one should perform the tenth, supreme six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) placement. (36) One should place the root mantra joined [with the limbs] upon the heart and other locations; when this tenth placement is performed, the three worlds shall come under one's control.

(37) One should certainly perform the tenth [placement], which bestows the fruit described for the ten placements; having recited the five verses beginning with "Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghora... and so forth...

Having meditated upon the first *cakra* as a most excellent seed-syllable, one should place it upon all the limbs. Having recited the four verses beginning with "Protect us, O Goddess" (*pāhi naḥ devi*) by means of the root mantra, one should place the second [cakra], which resembles the sun, upon everything. Having recited the five verses beginning with "O Sovereign of All, O Ruler of All" (*sarveśa-rūpe sarveśe*), one should place the third [cakra], which has the luster of crystal, upon one's own breast. Then, one should perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) for the divided [mantra].

The wise practitioner should perform the six limb-projections (*aṅga*) with each individual syllable of the mantra, with each pair, with all four together, and with the entire mantra. He should assign [the syllables] to the crest, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, and the anus. With the entire mantra, he should perform the pervasive projection (*vyāpaka*) eight times. [He should visualize] the sword, discus, mace, arrows, bow, iron club, trident, *śakti*, *bhuśuṇḍī*, and skull-topped staff.

I worship Mahākālī, who holds a skull-bowl and a staff in her hands, who possesses three eyes and is adorned with ornaments on all her limbs; she who, pleased by the lotus-born Brahmā, raised her ten mouths and feet to destroy Madhu and Kaiṭabha,

and who wields a rosary, a sword, a shield, a trident, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, a spear, a scimitar, a shield, a conch, a bell, a wine-vessel, a blazing trident, and a sword.

I worship here Sarasvatī, who possesses a fair body born from the Great One (Mahālakṣmī), who is the support of the three worlds, and who dwells within the lotus; she is firm in her beautiful vision, has the luster of coral in her hands, and holds a bell, a trident, a plow, a conch, a mace, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her lotus-like hands; she shines with the intense brilliance of the moon and the splendor of lightning.

[She who] crushes the great Daityas—having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times and perform a fire-oblation with milk-rice (pāyasa) amounting to a tenth part of that, once the golden altar (hema-vedi) has been worshipped.

(47) Then, upon a pedestal (pīṭha) endowed with the power of recitation and other qualities, one should worship the Goddess on a seat consisting of the principles (tattva), petals, enclosures, a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus. (48) Having worshipped and meditated upon her in the center of the triangle by means of the root-mantra (mūla-mantra), [one worships] in the eastern corner...

One should worship Dhātṛ together with Svarā in the northeast; Viṣṭā and Śrī in the southwest; Umā and Śiva in the northwest; and one should worship Siṃha and Mahiṣa in the north and south respectively. (50) In the six corners, starting from the east, one should worship Nandajā, Raktadantikā, Śākambharī, Durgā, Bhīmā, and Bhrāmarī. [The mantra is: "Obeisance to Tārā, whose syllables are accompanied by the nasal bindu. (51) Obeisance.

One should worship those [Śaktis] beginning with Nandajā; I shall describe them as follows: (52) on the eight petals, one should worship Brahmāṇī, the supreme Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and then Aindrī and Cāmuṇḍā. (53) Thus it is said.

He should recite ten times what is stated in the Ḍepa Purāṇa; they should separately chant the nine-syllable Caṇḍikā mantra ten thousand times. The patron should worship a maiden who is neither too young nor too old. (76–77) One should worship a virgin girl from two years of age up to ten years of age. One should not worship one who has extra limbs, one who is deficient in limbs, one afflicted with leprosy, one whose body is scarred, or one who is blind or one-eyed. (78)

One should not worship a maiden who has an extra limb, no hands, deformed eyes, or a hairy body; nor one born of a slave-woman, or afflicted by disease. (79) For the accomplishment of all desired goals, one should worship Brāhmaṇas; for fame, one born of a Kṣatriya; for the acquisition of wealth by Vaiśyas, [Brāhmaṇas];

and for the sake of a son, one born of a Śūdra. (80) She who is two years old is joined with a tortoise; she who is three years old is joined with a boar; she who is four years old is joined with a ram; and she who is eight years old is joined with a bull.

Lakṣmī is five years old, Rohiṇī is six, Caṇḍikā is said to be eight, Śāmbhavī is eight years old, and Durgā is nine years old. Subhadrā is said to be ten years old; one should worship her with mantras. There is no lack of affection for those aged one or eight, yet they are devoid of anger and the eight [defects]. The mantras for their invocation, as taught by Śaṅkara, are now declared. Maṃ...

I invoke here the maiden who consists of the three syllables, who is Lakṣmī, who assumes the forms of the Mothers, and who is the manifest embodiment of the nine Durgās. Now I shall state the mantra for the worship of the maidens, beginning with Kumārikā: "O you who are worshipped by the world, who are praised by the world, whose nature is all powers, O Mother of the World, accept this worship; salutations to you, O Kaumārī! [She is] Tripurā, the support of the three cities, the embodiment of the knowledge of the three aims of life...

I worship the Goddess who is adored by the three worlds through the worship of the triple form; I worship Śivā, whose heart is compassion, who is both the nature of time and beyond time; I worship the auspicious Goddess, the object of worship at the beginning of the aeon. In this [state], there are qualities such as "A" and so forth.

One should worship Rohiṇī, whose nature is the non-decaying syllable *dāra* and who possesses infinite power and fortune. (89) One should worship Kālikā, who moves at will, possesses auspicious form, is the embodiment of the Wheel of Time (*Kālacakra*), bestows desires, and is noble in her compassion. (90) We worship the Great Goddess Caṇḍikā, who is fierce and heroic, who is the illusion of Caṇḍa, the destroyer of the splendor of Caṇḍamuṇḍa, and whose strides are fiercely valorous. (91) [We worship her] who always grants bliss and is peaceful.

I always worship with devotion the Goddess Śāmbhavī, who is honored by all the gods, who is the soul of all beings, who is difficult to attain, who destroys fear of worldly existence in times of insurmountable difficulty, and who removes the suffering of those in distress. (92–93) I worship the beautiful Mother Goddess Subhadrā, who possesses a golden complexion, who bestows happiness and good fortune, and who grants auspiciousness. (94) With these mantras spoken in the Purāṇas, one should perform the nyāsa upon each respective maiden.

One should mark [the ground] with fragrant scents, flowers, various kinds of food, garments, and ornaments; then, having duly placed a bell upon the beautiful Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala prepared on the altar, one should invoke and worship Śivā there. (96) In front of that, one should also worship young maidens and Brahmins with various types of ritual offerings, as well as the previously mentioned enclosures. Having performed this for four days, on the fifth day— (97)

One should perform the oblation with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), as well as with grapes, plantains, citrons, pieces of sugarcane, coconuts, *pura* fruits, sesame seeds, nutmegs, mangoes, and sweet honey-houses (*madhuvāstu*). One should offer ten oblations for each verse of the *Saptaśatī*, and ten thousand oblations with the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*), having established the fire according to the prescribed ritual. (98–100) Having performed [the rite]...

Having performed the *homa* for the deities of the enclosure with their respective name-mantras, and having properly offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and dismissed the deity from the fire, one should sprinkle the sacrificer with the waters from the jars while reciting Vedic verses. Then, one should assign as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) a gold coin, or gold, or even a cow. After that, one should feed the Brahmins with various kinds of foods and drinks, and having given them their fees, one should take [the ritual implements].

Then, by performing the *dāśīṣa* in this manner, the world is brought under control and all calamities perish. From that, one shall obtain kingdom, wealth, fame, sons, and whatever else is desired. (4) One should perform this tenfold according to the procedure for the *Caṇḍīsahasraja*. One should always choose a hundred Brahmins who are learned and of good conduct. (5) Each of them should perform ten thousand recitations of the *Caṇḍikā*; each of them should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times.

The nine-syllable mantra: (6) The previously mentioned auspicious maidens should first perform one hundred offerings with the previous mantras. Having thus completed this for ten days, one should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa) (7) according to the rules, repeating the *Saptaśatī* one hundred times, verse by verse. With the previously mentioned collection of materials, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations with the nine-syllable mantra (8). After giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests, one should feed the twice-born (Brahmins) as previously described.

Even a thousand virtuous men, intent on the propitiation of the Goddess—when men have thus performed the Caṇḍī-rite a thousand times, their every desire is fulfilled and the flood of all their miseries is destroyed. Pestilence, famine, and diseases perish, along with the abodes of mental affliction. One should not teach this ritual to the wicked, to one's own thief, to a betrayer of the Guru, or to one who has conquered his senses and is a giver of gifts; rather, one should teach this ritual to the virtuous.
Furthermore, she who is thus pleased by Caṇḍikā protects both the speaker and the listener; such is the procedure for the Thousand Caṇḍīs, beginning with the Vārāhī-tantra and Netra-vacana.

Now, one extracts the mantra according to the sequence previously stated: *Vāṃ*, *Kū*, *Aiṃ*, *Māyā* (*Hrīṃ*), *Madana* (*Klīṃ*), *Dīrghā-lakṣmī* (*Āṃ*), *Akṣaṃ* (*Drīṃ*), *Maḥ*, joined with the two ears (*Śrutīndu-yuk*) [i.e., *Mu*], the form of *Muṇḍā* (*Yai*), *Saṃvṛt* (*Jalaṃ*), the pair of *Vikūrma* (*Vikūrmadvayaṃ*), *Bhagaḥ*, *Sūryaḥ*, and *Vīja-yaḥ*. These are the mantras.

One should install the three seed-syllables of the *Dima*—beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *Namaḥ*—along with their respective *jāti*-mantras, in the nine locations starting from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) and so forth, as well as in the heart and other limbs. For example: *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ* on the little finger, and so on; likewise, *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ* is applied to the limbs. Then, *Hrīṃ* [is for] Brahmāṇī in the east, *Māyāṃ tu* [is for] Māheśvarī in the southwest, and so forth. The eighteen-armed Mahālakṣmī is worshipped with the middle fingers (*madhyamābhyām*) with the mantra *Namaḥ*.

With the root mantra beginning with "tyādi," one should place the root mantra eight times from the *brahmarandhra* (the crown of the head) down to the feet, saying "namaḥ" [at each point]. Likewise, from the feet up to the head, one should likewise place it. Thus, on the right side of the chest, on the back, and on the left side as well, one should place the root mantra eight times at each of the eight locations.

One should place the root mantra on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) starting from the heart, and the six-limbed mantra beginning with "khaḍginī. Then, meditating upon Mahākālī with the single syllable of the root mantra, he said: "kha..."

The meaning is that she holds in her right hands a *ḍginī* (a type of weapon), a sword, a discus, an arrow, a head, and an axe; and in her left hands, a noose, a conch, a rosary, a lotus, a bow, a sword, a thunderbolt, a mace, a discus, and a water-pot—thus possessing ten arms and thirty eyes. She destroys the illusion (*māyā*) of Indra, the lord of the gods. Now, the meditation on Mahālakṣmī is described:
"Holding a rosary," etc.; [she holds] a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), a water-vessel (*kamaṇḍalu*), a conch, a rosary, a lotus, a bow, a sword, a thunderbolt, a mace, a discus, and a water-pot.

On the right [hands] are a conch, a mace, and a discus; on the left, a bell, a trident, a plow, and a bow. She has the radiance of the autumn moon and resides in a golden vessel. Her mantra consists of four hundred thousand recitations, while according to the *Ḍāmaratantra*, it is nine hundred thousand. [She is] Mahiṣāsuramardinī, the crusher of the elephant [Gajāsura], born from the energy that emerged from the body of the God of gods, O Heroine. [Now follows] the meditation on Mahā-Sarasvatī: she holds a conch, a mace, a discus, a bell, a trident, a plow, and a bow in her right hands, and a noose at the end of her left; she possesses the luster of the autumn moon and dwells in a golden vessel. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of four hundred thousand [recitations], but in the *Ḍāmaratantra*, the recitation is nine hundred thousand.

One should offer oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with sesame and clarified butter for one-tenth of the total number prescribed; by this, the sage becomes perfected. This refers to the Kali age.

[The ritual site] is provided with a dot (*bindu*), a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, a twenty-four-petaled lotus, and an enclosure of earth (*bhūgṛha*). On the petals of the twenty-four-petaled lotus, starting from the petal with the dot, one should place: *Oṃ naṃ naṃdāyai*, and so forth, as well as the deities Brahmā and the others to be described later, such as *Oṃ brahmāyai namaḥ*, etc., upon those twenty-four peaceful petals located at the positions of the *tatvas*.

Reciting "Oṃ viṣṭi māyāyai enam" and so forth, one should remember the seers (ṛṣis) and others of the Caṇḍī-stava as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, and then chant the three exploits (carita-traya) encased within the root mantra (mūla-mantra). Regarding the Ḍāmara [Tantra], it says: "O King, in the case of the exploits, one should chant the nine-syllable mantra. Thus, one should chant each individual exploit encased within the root mantra; this is the procedure for the Navacaṇḍī rite, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina until the eighth day.

On the seventh day, one should recite ten thousand times; on the eighth day and subsequent days, the count is doubled. Thus, over eight days, there is a recitation of one million (ten thousand multiplied by a hundred). One should perform that recitation for ten days. In that regard, on the seventh and eighth days, the root mantra should be recited twice—either two thousand or four thousand times. Alternatively, for the root mantra, a daily recitation of ten thousand times should be performed; on the seventh day it is doubled, and on the eighth day it is doubled again. In this way, over eight days, the recitation of one million must be completed. [This applies to] Kaumārī, Brahmā...

The procedure for the worship of the Brahmins and others will be explained further on. Thus, the *homa* on the eighth day consists of ten repetitions; however, the term "Navacaṇḍī" is a name for the ritual (*karmanāmadheya*) and does not refer to a numerical count. This is the traditional recollection of the meaning of "Navacaṇḍī. Having ascertained with a steady mind that the *Aṣṭakavaca*—which is indeed the "All-Pervading Vajra Armor" (*sarvavajrakavaca*)—was formerly composed by Brahmā, one should [recite] the *Argala*, which is the destroyer of the multitude of sins.

For one who is poor, having first recited this "bolt" (*argala*), one should subsequently mutter the *Caṇḍikā*. Regarding the procedure for the loss of memory and so forth, the arrangement follows the tradition. This is the rule for the "Hundred Caṇḍīs" (*śatacaṇḍī-vidhāna*). Thus, for four days, having engaged ten Brahmins: on the first day, all [should repeat it] once; on the second, twice; on the third, thrice (twenty times); and on the fourth, thirty times.
In this manner, there are one hundred and forty repetitions (*āvṛti*). When multiplied by ten, that becomes one thousand; therein, one hundred Brahmins perform the *āvaraṇa* (circumambulation).

Each of those Brahmins should place ten stones for each of the one hundred repetitions. They should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the nine-syllable mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*) and one million times (*mayuta*). Furthermore, one hundred women should be fed. One hundred Brahmins should perform one repetition (*āvṛti*) every day. In this way, on the eleventh day, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is completed.

He states the specific rule regarding the recitation of the *Saptaśatī* and other rites: "At the beginning, the *Kavaca* (Armor) should be recited; in that regard, there are two opinions. Thus, in the *Ḍāmara-tantra*: 'The wise man should first recite the *Saptaśatī* before that jar; having first recited the *Kavaca*, he should then recite the *Caṇḍī-saptaśatī*; thereafter he should recite the excellent *Argalā*, then the *Kīlaka*, and after that the *Mūrti*, the *Rahasya*, and finally the *Paṭala*. Thus."

Thus has the procedure been described to me regarding the sequence of recitation (*japa*). At the beginning of the *Vārāhī-tantra*, one should first recite the *Argala*, the *Kīlaka*, and the *Kavaca*.

One should then recite the *Saptaśatī Caṇḍī*; this is the sequence declared by Śiva. The *Argala* destroys misfortune, the *Kīlaka* bestows fruit, and the *Kavaca* constantly provides protection; therefore, one should practice these three. One should place the *Argala* upon the heart, as well as that which bestows the *Anargala*.

Having determined that [the obstacle] will indeed be overcome, Śiva declared of old: "He in whose heart this *kīlaka* (stake) resides shall have his desires fulfilled; there is no doubt, for what Śiva has spoken cannot be otherwise. There, having consecrated the fire according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas, one should perform the *homa* by way of recitation (*japa*).
In that regard, the *homa* involves the *kavaca*, *argalā*, and *kīlaka*; as stated in the *Bhairavīya*: "In the *caṇḍī-saptaśatī-homa*, the *kavaca*..."

One should not perform the oblation with the *kavaca* (armor mantra) alone; otherwise, it becomes fruitless. The great demon Andhaka, though devoted to the oblation for Durgā, was slain by Maheśa through the mere offering of the *kavaca*. Therefore, one should never perform the oblation with the *argala* or the *kīlaka*, nor should the secret mantras (*rahasyāni*) ever be offered as an oblation, my dear.

One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with these seven hundred mantras, beginning from Mārkaṇḍeya up to Sāvarṇi, who will be the Manu; otherwise, the rite performed becomes contrary [to its purpose]. Furthermore, the *homa* should consist of one-tenth the number of recitations (*japa*) of the root mantra. Now, since the performance of the nine-fold Caṇḍī and the Seven Hundred Garland Mantra have a single objective, [the procedure for] that...

Some say that the *Saptaśatī* is so called because it is a collection (*samāhāra*) of seven hundred verses (*śloka*). Others, however, maintain that the reading "seven hundred" (*saptaśatī*) is a corruption, since the number of verses in the text beginning with "Sāvarṇi, the daughter of the Sun" and ending with "Sāvarṇi will be Manu" does not amount to seven hundred. Instead, they assert that the *Saptaśatī* is a collection of seven sets of one hundred verses (*sapta-śatī*), as there are seven groups of one hundred verses concerning Brahmā and the others. This is not [correct].

There is no deliberation regarding the meaning [of the word *śloka*] here; for it is stated in the *Harasiddhi* chapter of the *Ḍāmaratantra*: "One should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with sesame and ghee for every *śloka*," and in the *Rudrayāmala*:

"In the case of the *Saptashatī*, one should perform the oblation for each *śloka* during the ten-fold recitation. Therefore, the *homa* is performed for every *śloka*. Regarding that, when the doubt arises as to whether [the term refers to] half-verse or the whole verse, the venerable [author] said: "The word *śloka* refers to the mantra"; and others [have said]: "And other mantras in the form of *ślokas*..."
"Many [recitations] remain where the oblation (*homa*) is performed; *argha* is a synonym for *mantra*, and *mantra* is a synonym for the word *śloka*.

This is clearly stated in the Kātyāyanī-tantra. When this was established, the Jñānārṇava and the Uttaratantra were composed for the purpose of dividing the mantra into seven hundred *ślokas*. Therein, in the latter part of the Jñānārṇava, Brahmā alone, the one Lord, [spoke to] Mārkaṇḍeya...

The paths [are] the gods; the sages are five; the goddesses are thirty; likewise, the messengers are twelve. Furthermore, two by two [are assigned] according to the castes, as the King spoke. In the middle between the eastern and western [ends], there are sixteen offerings (*argha*). There are two chapters (*sasa*) and thirteen verses;
furthermore, there are five hundred and eighty-four [verses]. Thus, in the *Jñānārṇava Tantra*, seven hundred [verses] are proclaimed.

Thus, the number of verses in the *Saptaśatī* as stated in the *Jñānārṇava* has been given. Now, for the purpose of explaining the division of mantras as taught in the *Kātyāyanītantra*, the *Kātyāyanītantra* is being recited. The Lord said: "The sage Mārkaṇḍeya obtained [this] in a dream; he bestowed it upon Vyāsa and, out of affection for him, made it manifest. (1) Mārkaṇḍeya is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*) by virtue of appearing in the first verse; the second [verse] arises from the syllables beginning with 'Vyoma'."

O beloved, one should declare all the mantras joined with their respective vowels; there are eighteen verses, O lady, and five mantras beginning with the letter *vyo*. (3) The king’s speech consists of twelve syllables joined with vowels, ending with the letter *sa* conjoined with the nasal bindu, followed by letters beginning with *ya* in this manner. (4) Again, the Vaiśya spoke: "O Goddess, from the eleventh vowel [the letter *ra*], joined with the seed-syllable of fire (*raṃ*)."

For them, the five *manus* (5), the sage Mārkaṇḍeya, and the two mantras proclaimed [by him] are cited; those syllables, joined with the *svaras*, constitute the supreme *aruṇa* (6). The King spoke—these six mantras begin with *bhā* and end with *anta*; O fair-faced one! Then the Sage spoke the knowledge beginning with "O Mistress of the Gods" (7); she herself is the Sovereign of All, and at the end, the twelve mantras are manifest; "The King spoke"—thus [ends] the portion of Bhagavān.

[The mantra] known as the three mantras, neither at the beginning nor at the end; then the Ṛṣi said: "O Goddess, that [mantra] is eternal, and the mantras are desired at the end. Brahmā said: "Then from the verse, O Great Goddess, there are fifteen mantras beginning with *svāhā* at the end, O Supreme Sovereign.
Having thus praised [her], the seven mantras ending with the words of the primordial Ṛṣi, and then the words of the Blessed Lord...

"By these two [mantras] beginning with *vetādi* and *manudvaya*, the Supreme Goddess is deceived. Then, regarding the mantra beginning with *tataśca ṛṣiruvāca tathaiśakti*, there are eighty-seven verses in this chapter in their proper sequence. Among them, twelve are proclaimed as half-mantras (*ardhamantra*). All of these are to be known as oblations (*āhuti*); here there are one hundred and four [verses], with Mahākālī as the principal deity.

The seed-mantra which has been revealed for her consists of fourteen pure and variegated-limbed mantras; Mahākālī, Kālatrimūrti, Nityā, and their divisions, Sanātanī—(15)—one should certainly perform the recitation preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and worship. The seer is Brahmā, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. (16) Thus ends the first chapter in the *Kātyāyanī Tantra*, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī.

The Twenty-First Chapter, named "Traṃ. The Lord said: Now, therefore, O Lord of Gods, I shall fully proclaim the life-story of Mahālakṣmī in the form of verses, consisting of three chapters. (1) For the second [chapter], the Seer is the Speaker; the verse consists of sixty-eight syllables;
the Deity is Mahālakṣmī; the meter is declared to be Uṣṇik; Śāṅkhabharī is the Śakti, and Durgā is the Bīja. (2)

It should be known that the principle (*tattva*) is primarily Vāyu; these are the sixty-nine verses in sequence. (3) Then, O Goddess, the Seer spoke the third [section] to the Teacher: "O fair-faced one, the mantras are to be known as thirty-five verses. (4) At the end of the mantra, the Goddess spoke; one should indicate it with a single verse. The Seer spoke again: "The verses are the five eternal mantras. (5) Thus they were spoken.
Forty-four verses, joined with four [more], from the Ṛṣis, Vedas, Devas, and Devīs, up to forty-four [verses]—this is the statement of the Ṛṣis in the fourth sequence.

Furthermore, twenty-six verses are the statement of the Sumantu-Ṛṣis; two [verses] are in the form of mantras. Thus, this hymn and mantra is extremely secret and very purifying. The Goddess said: "Let this sixteen-syllable mantra be chosen. Thus, O gods.

Then the Blessed Lady spoke this verse: "This mantra consists of one hundred syllables; again, there are twelve and three more" (9). The Sage said: "Thus propitiated, he [is pleased]; these are four verses, and the forms and measures are fourfold" (10).
"In the middle of each single verse, O Supreme Goddess, there are thirty-six; by means of two half-mantras, there are forty again" (11). Thus the oblations are to be known on another day.

O fair-faced Lakṣmī, the middle narrative of Mahālakṣmī, the deity of the three worlds, should be known [as follows]: thus, the fifty verses of the middle narrative, as well as one hundred mantras, should be understood according to the divisions of Lakṣmī. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Middle Narrative," in the Kātyāyanī Tantra. The Lord said: Listen with single-minded attention; I shall proclaim its extraction.

The sage Gramānasā said: "In ancient times, the gods, who are the very form of verses (śloka), praised the Māyā that had entered [the world]. Thereafter, those gods spoke the thirty-two verses beginning with 'Obeisance to the Goddess' (namo devyai). Then, through their forms, they uttered sixty-three mantras for the various incarnations of that Māyā, whose nature is delusion (bhrānti). These are the sixty-three oblations (āhuti) consisting of the essence of those mantras."

One should offer three oblations with the *petī* mantra. Thus, there are eighty mantras; "the seer said" (*ṛṣir uvāca*) occurs here. (4) Likewise, in the section beginning with "why do you not accept these seventeen mantras joined by you? (*evaṃ stāvad iyuktān tvayā kasmān na gṛhṇāsi maṃtrān saptadaśa uta te ṛṣyuktiś ca niṣampati*), there are nine mantras, and again "the seer said" (*ṛṣir uvāca ha*) occurs. (7) With the single mantra beginning "he moves through the year" (*saraś carati*) and the triad of mantras beginning with [the next], he performs the purification (*śuci*).

The divisions of the mantras have been proclaimed. Now, "The Goddess said" (*devy uvāca*) occurs four times; "The Lord of the Daityas said" (*daityeśvara uvāca*) occurs once; and "The messenger said" (*dūta uvāca*) occurs four times according to the distinction of the mantras. Furthermore, "O Bali, you are [a messenger]" (*bali kṣāsīti*)—these four mantras are to be understood as "The Goddess said" (*devy uvāca*). Following that, "Thus it is; let Śumbha, the lord of power, do what is appropriate"—these two mantras are the *maṅga-mantra* (auspicious mantra).

Or else, O Maheśānī, there are twenty-nine verses in addition to one hundred; listen now from this ocean of devotion to the supreme mantra of Dhūmrākṣī, which reveals the distinctions of the extraction of mantras (11).

Having heard the four verses beginning with "The seer has spoken" (*ṛṣyuktaśca*), and after that being instructed with the words "The seer spoke again" (*ṛṣiruvāca*), the Goddess then spoke the threefold mantra (12).

"Then, having been addressed by the Lord of the Daityas with these mantras, who is proclaimed as 'Purī'? (13) Thereafter, the Sage spoke thus; being so addressed, he rushed forward—thus, in twelve verses beginning with this, Dhumrākṣī is described. (14) Twenty-four principal deities are to be offered oblations in sequence.
(15) Now, therefore, follow the various forms of Caṇḍikā, the mantras in the form of oblations, and the declaration of the Seer, O Queen."
From the twenty-third name onwards, R̥ṣi said: "These two divisions of Mothers [are recited] in sequence;

thus, in this chapter, O Goddess, there are twenty-seven [verses] including Dhūmrākṣa. (17) "The oblations consist of the various mantras; O Pārvatī, hear [the mantra] of Tāraktākṣī. (18) "And when Caṇḍa was slain... and so forth, until the end of the chapter—these sixty-three mantras constitute the oblations in their respective order. (19)
There, the eight great Śaktis are beautiful and possess moving limbs; then, O fair-faced one, hear from me those secret Bhairavīs and Tārās.

(20) The two verses beginning with "Oṃ jaya vicitrām" were composed by the Sage as an ornament; the verse beginning with "ṛṣiścakāra kopaṃ hi" [and so forth] constitutes the form [of the mantra]. (21) Twenty-seven are to be known as the forms of the deities and mantras; there, O auspicious one, forty-one oblations are to be performed. (22) This is in the tenth [chapter].
Seated upon a lotus, holding a trident and a noose, the principal [form] has four arms with arrows and a bow in her hands and auspicious eyes.

(23) The seer [recites] the two mantras beginning with "Ṛṣir niśumbhānihitām" and so forth; then, by the mantra "Devī," he is followed by one [mantra]. (24) Again, by the mantra "Devī," the distinct divisions are proclaimed. Then the seer himself concludes with twenty-two and a half [verses]. (25) Dvā.

O fair-faced one, all these thirteen varieties of the Mothers of the Three Ages, as well as those born of the mountains, are described in verses for the rites of *homa* and libation. O Pārvatī, all these mandalas and desires are accompanied by mantras and meditations, preceded by the [thirteen] cities. O beloved, there is a group of ten deities according to the distinction of their conduct; they are indeed difficult to overcome and most terrible in the midst of perilous and fearsome battles. (26–28)
During a journey, in times of dispute, during all auspicious rites, when there is agitation of the mind, or for the sake of clarity regarding poison, one should recite this [hymn].

(29) Whether one is free from desire or possessed of desire, it truly bestows the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). Whatever desire one shall remember while meditating upon her form, one certainly attains that. (30) What more need be said here? What else do you wish to hear? (31) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Kātyāyanītantra*. Pārva.

He said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, bestower of grace upon devotees, I now desire to hear this mantra consisting of Hari and Hara. (1) [Tell me] of Navadurgā, Rathānadurgā, Nārāyaṇī, Kumārikā, Bālā, Tripurasundarī, and the secret of your own form; O highly fortunate one, tell us all about their manifestations, their locations, and their movements."

Maheśvara said: O fair-faced one, just as the Goddess was born on the Himālaya from the Daitya Śumbha, and how she accomplished her purpose through the gods and the breaking of their mantras—likewise, O Lord of Gods, I shall proclaim this secret which grants all goals; it consists of three chapters concerning the form of her life-story. Thus, the thirteenth chapter has been declared by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya; I shall now proclaim its extraction.

O beautiful lady, the sage Sumantu, born of Vyāsa, has proclaimed this auspicious [text] for the oblation to the Goddess; it consists of thirty-four verses and is considered to have eight principal divisions. Then, O Queen of the Gods, the Goddess granted a boon with a single mantra.
The gods likewise requested the pacification of all afflictions. Thereafter, O Mistress of the Gods, the Goddess spoke one verse regarding the Vaivasvata [Manvantara].

The fourteen verses beginning with "reprā" [and so forth] describe the fifty-five offerings (*sarvāhuti*) to the Goddess, which are remembered as being fivefold. Therein, the distinctions of the forms of the descent (*avanāra*) are each separate. Jālā is the eleventh chapter-distinction; she herself is Nārāyaṇī, the Vaiṣṇavī power (*vī-śakti*), proclaimed as the Goddess whose vehicle is Garuḍa. One should meditate upon her thus: holding in her hands the conch, discus, mace, and the Śārṅga bow. She is indeed such.
O you who are firm in your vows, the Vaiṣṇavī-śakti has been described to you; now, O Goddess, I shall tell you what I have learned from the mouth of the Goddess.
The Goddess said: "Thus, with the half-verse *sāpayenamiṣvañcamāsadā* (13), together with that [previous] half-verse, there are twenty-eight *rūpaka*s.

Then the Seer (*ṛṣi*) said: 'Having spoken the verse from the beginning' (14); the tradition is established by nine verses including that half-verse. Thus, in the twelfth chapter, there are forty-one oblations (*āhuti*s). Then, in the thirteenth [chapter], O Goddess, the Seer said: 'Now...'"

"Enatekatthitthaṃbhūya" and so forth—these three and a half verses; then again, "Mārkaṇḍeya uvāca"—these six verses; then the Lord spoke, O Supreme Goddess: "Whatever is requested by you, O King, I shall grant satisfaction with a single verse"; then again "Mārkaṇḍeya uvāca"—these two verses; and then again the Lord himself spoke.

Thus, having spoken these two mantras—the *Śloka-trapaṇa*, *Vaitasta*, *Mārkaṇḍeya-cukti*, and *Ītyātapa-śiva*—he said: "He shall become a Sāvarṇi Manu; may those mantras grant you the desired success. (19–20) In the twenty-ninth chapter, the offering (*āhuti*) is prescribed here;
thus, through thirteen chapters, the rites of fire-oblation (*homa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*) [number] one hundred and sixty-four. (21)
O Daughter of the Mountain, I have told you that the mantra beginning with *Sa* and ending with *Na* is extremely difficult to obtain;
it must be known through the method of the authentic lineage (*satsampradāya*), for otherwise the mantra is fruitless—this is the truth declared by me in the observance (*samaya*).
(23) In rites of libation (*tarpaṇa*) and offerings, one should utter the mantra as *tena maṃtreṇa*, or else say "I offer libations" (*tarpayāmi ca*). (24) vi.

O wise one, I have now declared this which pertains to the supreme secret; it must be guarded, it must be guarded, as if from one's own womb. There is no mantra higher than this, no path higher than this, and no knowledge higher than this. This entire portion of the ritual is the most secret of secrets, the supreme state, difficult even for the gods to attain. That which [I have told you] is the mind... (Note: The final fragment "yanmanoyā" appears to be incomplete or corrupted.)
"Know for certain that there is no other mantra like it, which grants the perfection of the eight siddhis such as *aṇimā* and bestows immortality. (28)
In the *Kātyāyanī Tantra*, within the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī, this is the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Mantra Garland of the Saptashatī. [It states:
"The wise Vindu, son of Tāṃyu, residing in Padaghnā, having bowed down, [composed] the Saptashatī mantra without [repetition].
This hymn known as the Saptashatī consists of five hundred and seventy-eight verses; it is called 'Saptashatī' because of its numerical count [of seven hundred]."
(2) One should offer oblations while reciting the mantras in their various divisions; according to the *Jñānārṇava*, I shall clearly explain this one [mantra] dedicated to Agni.

(3) According to the system of Kātyāyanī alone, I have declared the division: Mārkaṇḍeya said, "First there is one [verse], then another, followed by seventeen verses and half a verse; thus, it shall indeed consist of twenty-one. (4) Thus it is.

The Śyokti consists of twenty verses; likewise, there is another three-verse hymn, and then again half a verse, making twenty-five in total. Thus, the *rājā* and *ṣaḍiti* hymns consist of [these]. From the *dya* and *vaiśya* sections, the mantra consists of half-verses. Furthermore, in the *mārkaṇḍeya*, there is both a half-verse and a full verse. Again, the mantra consists of half-verses; for the *rājā*, the mantra consists of half-verses. And these are the mantras.

Thus, forty verses, four *ṛṣis*, and half-verses as mantras; again ten, nine, and a half; then the king himself, one less than fifty, is called *puṣṭi*. Again a half, again a verse, again a half, again an *ṛṣi*, again a half, and again verses—these are the six mantras.
Then follows a half-verse: "The Lord of Splendor [placed] the Goddess Nidrā in the scales of Viṣṇu."

Thus, the total number of mantras in this reading is said to be seventy-one: (12) one mantra consisting of half a verse of the *Brahma* hymn, and thirteen mantras consisting of full verses; five mantras consisting of half-verses of the *Ṛṣi* hymn, and five mantras consisting of both half-verses and full verses;
(14) two half-mantras of the *Bhāgavat* hymn, and again one half-verse of the *Ṛṣi* hymn; and finally, one full verse of the *Ṛṣi* hymn.
There are two pairs of mantras, sixty-four verses, and twenty-four half-verses; thus [the Lord] spoke. (15) uvāca.

The *Mānavamantra* consists of one hundred and four verses; it was spoken by Kaśyapa. Within the twelve verses concerning the meditation on the *pada*, there are two verses for Mārkaṇḍeya and three for Vaiśravaṇa; thereafter, the five sages (*ṛṣipañcaka*) are indicated, followed by the Lord alone. Then, the unity with Brahman (*brahmāikya*) is proclaimed in one hundred and four verses. Thus, the first chapter is said to consist of the *Kātyāyanī-mantra*. (16–18)
Thus ends the first chapter, the section on the division of mantras, in the *Itikātyāyanīya-matra*. From the chapter itself, the sage spoke once:

"Manu [spoke] sixty-eight verses; as many are considered the beautiful ones. (1) All the mantras in the second chapter are sixty-nine. Thus [ends the section]. (11) At the beginning, the sage spoke one [verse]; after that, twenty-five [verses] follow. Nihamā...
There are no half-verses; furthermore, [the sequence] ending with "ogākulākṣaram" (120) is as follows: the Goddess spoke once, another [spoke] "garja garja," the Seer spoke, and again a verse;
five verses [were spoken by] two Seers, and one by the Goddess—thus there are forty-one verses.
All the mantras in the third [chapter] amount to four hundred and forty-two (342). Thus is the doctrine of Kātyāyanī. Ādhoṛ.

The verses beginning with "Śiruvāco" and "atiśakrādyāḥ" are thirty-six mantra-ślokas; then there are two Ṛṣi-ślokas, followed by the Goddess’s verse. Then the half-verse mantra "vriyaṃtāṃ tridaśāḥ sarve yadasmato 'bhivāñchitam" was spoken by the gods. Thereafter, the half-verse mantra "bhagavatyā kṛtaṃ sarvam" [expresses] the meaning that everything has been accomplished by the Blessed Lady. Then the half-verse mantra "yadambāṃ nihatvārdham... [and so on].
There may be three *kāma-mantras* (3). Four verses (*śloka*) are proclaimed as the *ṛṣis*, while the *mantras* are said to be four.
Three *ṛṣis* were spoken by the Goddess, one by the Gods, and five by the [Gods] with [their] words (4). There are twenty-five verses (*śloka*) as *mantras*.
Here, there are exactly two *mantras* consisting of half-verses (*ardha-śloka*). In this chapter of thirty-six verses, there are forty [syllables].
"In the case of mantras used for the *āhavanīya* fire and other rites, the division and counting should be performed by adding two," so says Kātyāyana.
In the fifth chapter, consisting of seventy-six verses, there are one hundred and twenty-nine mantras according to the *Kātyāyanīmata*.

(1) One seer (*ṛṣi*) spoke thus: "In ancient times, [there were] six auspicious and glorious mantra-verses"; then the gods spoke: "Eight [verses], O Manu. (2) The five mantra-verses beginning with "Salutation to the Goddess" (*namo devyai*) are proclaimed; thus, there are thirteen mantras in total.
From "yā devī" up to "pādayoḥ," there are twenty-one verses ending with "bhrāntyantāḥ.

Among them, there are three mantras per verse; thus, there are sixty-three here. (4) (63) The mantra "yā devī sarvabhūteṣu viṣṭum āyeti śabditā | namaḥ tasyai" is declared to consist of twenty syllables. (5) "namaḥ tasyāḥ" is declared as the second [mantra]. It is called "Cakṣu."

"O Rakṣas, the eight-syllabled third [verse] is also named; salutations to him, salutations again and again. (6) Thus, the wise should know that there are twenty-two verses; with the thirteen preceding mantras, the section beginning with "Aṃsīti" is proclaimed. (7) There are two verses beginning with "Stutāsurā," and then "Oṃ yaccaiva"; furthermore, there are seventeen verses of the Ṛṣi, followed by three verses of the Ṛṣi. (8) And the section beginning with "Dūta" consists of nine verses. Ṛ.

From the *Ṣirekovikātata* [there are] four verses; then again the *Catuśloki*, then again the *Dūtacatuślokī*; and finally, including the two verses of the *Śirvaśloka*, there are forty-one verses in total. When combined with the eighty [verses], it should be understood that there are one hundred and twenty-nine verses, and furthermore, there are three hundred and five oblations (*āhuti*).

The sages declared four [offerings], the gods spoke once, the messenger spoke twice, and likewise the Goddess spoke a second time. (12) Twenty-two oblations are prescribed for the verses, and sixty oblations are considered [for the rest]; thus, one hundred and twenty-nine oblations are held to be required.
(13) Thus ends the division of mantras in the *Kātyāyanītantra*, in the sixth chapter consisting of twenty-five verses.

All the verses have been proclaimed as mantras; [there are] one goddess and three ṛṣis (1). Thus, twenty-four mantras have been fully proclaimed (2). [Thus ends the section by] Kātyāyana (0). In the seventh chapter, which consists of twenty-five verses, there are seven mantras. All the mantras are in the form of verses; the Ṛṣi said: "Then there are two" (1). Thus, the number of mantras is proclaimed to be twenty-seven (2).
Thus, in the eighth chapter known as the "Sixty-one Verses" (Ekapaṣṭiśloka) of the Kātyāyana [Tantra], sixty-one mantra-verses have been proclaimed;

at the end of these, there is one half-verse, and at the beginning, there is one verse for the seer—thus, there is a continuous sequence of sixty mantras. Furthermore, in the [chapter] associated with Kātyāyanī, which consists of thirty-nine verses, two mantras are declared to be contained within that same number of chapters.
(1) "Rājārṣiśca" and so forth—this is the ninth chapter-section of the *Muni* [text] by Kātyāyana.

In the tenth [chapter], there are twenty-seven mantras in the form of verses, consisting of twenty ślokas along with their halves; of these, the final one consists of half a śloka. Furthermore, there are two mantras spoken by the Ṛṣis and likewise two spoken by the Devas; such is the collection of thirty-two mantras.

Oṃ. Thus ends the tenth chapter, the division of mantras for Kātyāyanī, which should be known to consist of fifty and a half verses. In the eleventh [chapter], fifty verses and mantras are clear; at the end, there is one mantra of half a verse. It is stated that there are two goddesses and one seer (ṛṣi), and the gods are one. Having counted fifty-five [verses], in the thirty-fifth subsequent verse, it should be known that "the gods said" is indeed one [unit].

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the *Mantravibhāga*, according to Kātyāyana. In this twelfth chapter, which consists of thirty-eight verses, there are forty-one mantras; among them, there are two oblations (*āhuti*). The verses consist of half-verses and full verses, totaling thirty mantras.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) is [the same], and the phrases "The Goddess said" (*devy uvāca*) occur one by one. Thus the number has been clearly stated. Thus ends [the section] of Kātyāyana. Chapter twelve.

The division of the mantras for purification is proclaimed in the thirteenth [chapter] as one hundred and fifty verses. There are eleven and a half oblations consisting of twelve-verse mantras (1). With six utterances, there are twenty-nine oblations; Mārkaṇḍeya is three [verses], the Goddess is two, and there is one Ṛṣi (2). Thus is this division of mantras pertaining to the *Devīmāhātmya* by Kātyāyanī.
This [text] has been clearly elucidated according to the system of the *Nīta-tantra* by Anantaśarman, a resident of Padagrāma belonging to the Kaśyapa lineage.
By him, this mantra should be understood as divided up to seven hundred [verses]. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the "Division of Mantras," in the *Kātyāyanī-tantra*.
Now, the division of the mantras is stated according to the *Jñānārṇava-mata*, beginning from the first chapter.

Then follows the sequence up to thirteen (7). This number is to be understood as non-sequential; it should be known by the wise according to the following order: five, two, two, three, four, three, two, two, one, three (2). Thus, each one by one, the determination of thirty-eight [verses] is reached. Likewise, the gods are in the fourth [section], above in the fifth, in the pair of Meru and Rudra. The number of gods is five, while the introductory verses are thirteen. The *ślokas* are four.
And likewise five hundred [verses] for the *Śīrṣastuti*. Thus, the doctrine of the *Jñānārṇava* is another [text] equal to the *Kātyāyanī*.

This is the division of the mantras of the *Saptaśatī*. Having understood this division, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the nine-verse mantra of the seven hundred verses, and then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in sequence with a tenth part of that [recitation].
This refers to the procedure for the *Śatacaṇḍī*, meaning the procedure for the *Sahasracaṇḍī* is ten times that. In that [rite], there is the selection of one hundred Brahmins.

Those hundred Brahmins should each perform recitations of the *Saptashatī* ten times; they should perform the *japa* of the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa*) ten thousand times each. For one born of a Kṣatriya lineage, there is a tenfold increase. Having thus completed it over ten days, on the eleventh day, a fire sacrifice (*homa*) should be performed with the *Saptashatī* repeated a hundred times, with each mantra counted by the target number and the nine-syllable mantra. To each officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), he should give gold measured at ten *niṣkas*. This is the remainder.

As before, three *viṣṭus* constitute a *niṣkala*; five of those make a *kṛṣṇala*; five of those make a *māṣaka*; twelve of those make half an *akṣa*; four *māsakas* make a *suvarṇa*; four *suvarṇas* make a *niṣka*; the remainder is as before. This is the procedure for the *mahācaṇḍī*. Ten times that is the procedure for the *yutacaṇḍī*; ten times that is the procedure for the *lakṣacaṇḍī*. In the feeding of Brahmins during the *nyāsa* ceremony, one should know that there is a tenfold increase for each successive stage; the rest is easy to understand. Furthermore, regarding the specific seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the recitation (*japa*) on the lunar day (*tithi*), the *Ḍāmaratantra* states: "One should recite the *vāgbhava*, *hau*, *hṛ*, *sū*, *klīṃ*, *śrī*, *kūrca*, then *kṣauṃ*, *līṃ*, and *phrauṃ*; these are the seed-syllables ending in *kavaca* and *astra*. One should recite them in direct order (*anuloma*) and reverse order (*viloma*) for each verse, O King, in the *Navārṇa-tārgalā*."
The ritual procedure is thus remembered: one should recite the Vāgbhava, the Mountain-born (Māheśvarī), and Kāma in the *kīlaka*; the state of being established in splendor occurs at midday.
That which is beyond the supreme (*parāt para*) by which one attains perfection—therefore, one should recite the King (Nṛpa), the Tārā, and the Heart as before at the beginning of the verse.
One should recite the Heart, the end of the Supreme (*parānta*), and the Tārā from the verse; O King, [one should recite] the Praṇava and the Kāmarāja ending with the Heart in the third [part].

One should conquer the heart, the *kāmatāra*, and the verses as before; by this, O King, the defects of curses, nails, and bolts perish, and Caṇḍikā becomes well-pleased through the mere utterance of the syllable *ṭha*. *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *Bhairavī* (Hūṃ), *Vāk* (Aiṃ), the *tāra* (Oṃ), *Laṃ Raṃ Yaṃ Kṣaṃ Vaṃ Maṃ Kuṃ Oṃ Hauṃ Ahaṃ*—this is declared to be the secret. O King, one should recite it in both direct and reverse order for each verse. It is the *māyā-puṭi*.
O King, one should recite the *Mātṛkā-ghoṣa-kūrca-mantra*—namely *laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ ku hauṃ mā*—in the middle of the secret [mantra] of the *Pañcabhairavī*.

One should recite the *Vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], followed by *laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ ku hauṃ mā*, the *Mātṛkā-ghoṣa*, and the *Kūrca-mantra* at the end. O King, one should recite this triad of secrets in both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order. Having thus recited, even by the mere reading of the *Caṇḍikā*, she becomes the bestower of success (*siddhi*). The mantra is: *Laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ ku hauṃ mā laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ ku hauṃ mā a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣa laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ ku hauṃ mā.* Thus, by merely reciting this, *Caṇḍikā* grants the desired accomplishment.

O King, in the Kali age, one shall obtain the fulfillment of all desires by performing the *Rasakṛtya*; in the Kali age, Caṇḍī is easily perfected, and in the Kali age, Caṇḍī is the bestower of boons. O King, there is no other lore (*vidyā*) [like this] in the Kali age; it must be kept secret, kept secret, and kept secret with great effort. It is a secret, a supreme secret, and a most supreme secret. Thus: *Ihaiḥ hrūṃ śrīṃ huṃ huṃ ślaulīṃ prau iti*. From this seed-syllable (*bīja*), [the mantra] extends from the beginning to the end, *vakaca-caprati*.
One should recite the nine-syllable mantra in forward and reverse order in each verse; in the *ārgala* verses, one should proceed as before.
One should recite *pet aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ* and so forth at the beginning and end upon the *kīlaka*, as before. (3) *Oṃ hraṃ sauḥ namaḥ*; thus one should recite in the first chapter (*caritra*) as before.

(4) *Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ*; thus one should recite in the middle as before. (5) *Oṃ klīṃ namaḥ*; thus one should recite at the end. (6) *Hrīṃ hrasraiṃ eauṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ kuhauṃ aṃ haṃ*; this is the first secret (*prathamarahasya*). (7) *Hrīṃ heṃ hroṃ hrauṃ*.

*Aṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ kṣaṃ paṃ yaṃ ku hauṃ aṃ haṃ*—thus in the *Madhyamarahasya*. *Hrīṃ hasrauṃ klīṃ aiṃ raṃ laṃ pha kṣa vaṃ yaṃ kaṃ hauṃ aṃ haṃ*—thus in the *Aṃrarahasya*. One should recite [these] in forward and reverse order at every verse (*pratiśloka*) as before. This is the procedure for total victory (*sarvājaya*). *Oṃ hastrauṃ hrīṃ hasrauṃ kṣa ma la va mī ḍa ma la va phreṃ ī kṣā (6) utkīla (2) svāhā*. *Oṃ aiṃ huṃ (2)*.

*Hrīṃ klīṃ (8) hrīṃ hrauṃ (2) cāmuṇḍeśāya vimocaya cāmuṇḍāyai vicce ce viyai ḍāmuñca hrauṃ (2) hrīṃ krīṃ hrīṃ huṃ (2) aiṃ oṃ phaṭ svāhā.* This is the *pāṅga-pavimocana*. *Eṃ ī raṃ laṃ haṃ hrīṃ ṭhaṃ klīṃ utkīlinyai namaḥ. Oṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce ce viṃ pai ḍāmuñca klīṃ ṭhaṃ hrīṃ hraṃ la raṃ iṃ aiṃ svāhā.* This is the *navārṇa-utkīlana*. (1) Thus [ends] the nine.
The *Utkīlana* of the thirteenth chapter: *Oṃ hraḥ trauṃ utkīlaya svāhā*. [Recite this] three times. Then:

*Hrīṃ ma utkīlaya utkīlaya niṣkīlaya niṣkīlaya hrīṃ svāhā*. Submerge [the object] in ordinary water while reciting [this] until twenty breaths have passed. By reciting *Hrīṃ*—the root mantra—over each syllable twenty-one times, there is liberation from the curse (*śāpa-vimocana*). Now, the *Saptaśatī-mālā*.

Regarding a mantra obtained in a dream, because it is a "perfected" (siddha) mantra, there is no requirement for preliminary ritual service (*puraścaraṇa*), as only *japa* and *homa* are prescribed. Therefore, through the lineage of oral tradition, the fulfillment of various desires is achieved simply by reciting the root mantra conjoined with the *mūla-mantra*. For this very reason, the authors of the Tantras have provided only the description of specific applications (*prayoga*). They state the application in every verse: one should recite the *praṇava* (OM) at the beginning and end [of the mantra] for the attainment of mantra-perfection (*mantra-siddhi*).

One should recite this great hymn, preceded by the *praṇava* and the three *vyāhṛtis* at the beginning and in reverse order at the end, as well as the *Āditya-hṛdaya*. Thus, having obtained the boon of the Goddess, one should recite it verse by verse for the attainment of one's own desired goal. For the warding off of all evils, one should recite it twice in the middle; others say it should be recited once when complete. At every chapter (*carita*), one should mutter the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) one hundred and eight times. By reciting [the hymn] in this manner, there is the attainment of the mantra.

The first [method] is: one should recite "Dhṛtiḥ" at the end of every twenty-one verses. The third is: one should recite "Sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye" at the beginning and end of every verse. The fourth is: one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at the beginning and end of each chapter. Then, having worshipped the deity of the first chapter with sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*)—beginning with "Salutation to the Deity"—one should [proceed] with water upon the ground.

Having drawn a triangle with sandalwood paste and having written the two mantras "yadvāgvadantī" and "iti ruk" in the directions starting from the east, one should place one's hand over it and recite the nine-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, having smeared the *mārjya* on the forehead, one should wash and drink the waters contained in thirteen vessels. Having performed this once during the day, one should go home. This results in the perfection of speech, such as the power of poetic composition. Thus ends the fifth [chapter].

(5) One who desires the attainment of knowledge should recite [the mantra] encased by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the beginning and end of each verse; this is the sixth [method]. (6) One who desires the removal of obstacles should recite it with the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively at the beginning and end of each verse for six months; likewise, in eleven months, two [results] arise as previously described. (49) (7) When this is done, there is the attainment of all desires; this is the seventh [method]. Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should worship with the eight fragrances (*aṣṭagandha*).
Having drawn an image of Mṛḍānī with eighteen arms and worshipped it with the sixteen types of offerings, one should stand behind it facing westward.
Having drawn a square measuring three finger-breadths on the ground, placed three blades of *kuśa* grass upon it, and scattered sesame seeds, one should sit in a comfortable posture.
Reciting the verse beginning with "Kālī karālavadanā," one should chant each chapter once at the beginning and end, and [the mantra] following the chapters.

The practice of *lomavilomānuloma* (forward and reverse order): one should complete [the recitation] within ten *ghaṭīs*. In this manner, the second round should be performed before midday, and its completion should occur after the afternoon. The third round follows closely after the afternoon; it involves drinking cow's milk, which destroys all enemies. On the eighth day, having bathed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and having bathed with fine powder, one should remain with wet clothes and the topknot (*śikhā*) tied.
From sunrise until sunrise, one should recite the *mālā-mantra* joined with the *sampuṭa*. Within a day and night, Caṇḍikā becomes manifest.

Thus ends the ninth [chapter]. Having recited the verse beginning with the *praṇava*, and having recited the well-known verse, one should recite a quarter-verse (*caraṇa*) of the *Gāyatrī* for each verse: the first quarter in the first chapter, the second in the second, and the third in the third.

One should recite the three feet [of the Gāyatrī] within the three cycles of *vaṃcarita*. The remaining *siddhas* beginning with the *kavaca* are to be recited; all sins are destroyed. Thus ends the tenth [chapter]. [In the mantra] "I offer this *arghya* to Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī," and so forth, the *arghya* [is offered]; thereafter, the fifty verses [are recited], followed by the recitation of the third foot of the Gāyatrī. Having thus completed the worship...
One should recite "ṛṇā jayet" (11); one should recite the complete eleven-syllable Gāyatrī at the beginning and end of each verse for the attainment of knowledge (12);
and at the end of the verse "namo devyāḥ" (13). Having stood thus, one should recite the first *caritra* in the first triangle of the first maṇḍala;
having turned, one should recite the second *caritra* in the second sixteen-sided figure; and having turned again, one should recite the third [caritra] in the third eight-sided figure.
One should recite "Namo Devyai" at the end of every verse; furthermore, one should recite it after all the verses in reverse order of what was performed [previously], and then again in direct order.

Thus, the thirteenth offering (*bali*) is accomplished at that time, and everything becomes perfected. Furthermore, regarding the eight quarters of the two *ṛc*s beginning with "Pravādi," one should recite them at the beginning and end of each verse.

One should recite eight verses; then one should recite four half-verses (*ardharca*); then two verses; then again three verses beginning with the first, ending with the thirteenth; then two verses; then four half-verses; then eight quarters (*pāda*); thus one should sacrifice with each *śloka*.
Again, from the first verse, eight quarters in eight verses; then four half-verses; then one [verse] in one [verse].

In the first four [verses] consisting of two lines each, there are eight quarters (*pādas*) in the fifth and sixth verses; when arranged in this manner, the *vāku* (the desired arrangement) is accomplished. Thus ends the fourteenth [section]. (14) "May the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled"—this [mantra] of nineteen syllables should be recited at the end of every verse. (21) [The number zero. (17) Thus ends the fifteenth [section]. For the sake of others, [recite] the best [verses] for Indra.
At the beginning of each verse, one should recite: "Place the treasures here. This is the sixteenth [verse] regarding the attainment of wealth.
"Place them here" is for the sake of the sacrificial oblation; this is the seventeenth. In the third verse:

"Free from debt in this world, free from debt in the next, and free from debt in the third—may we, free from debt, enjoy all paths, drinking the soma-juice of the gods and the offerings of the ancestors, in our own hands."

Having spread out a layer of earth mixed with clay and remained [seated], one should recite "apasarpatu" and "āpo hi ṣṭhā" while sprinkling water on the head; then, placing the hand upon the heart, one should mutter "anṛṇā" one hundred and eight times. Having sprinkled water on the *arghya* vessel and consecrated it with the *gāyatrī* mantra and "oṃ tryambakaṃ" one hundred and eight times, one should drink [the water]. First, having muttered the "anṛṇā" mantra and having muttered the *adhyāya*, one should likewise [mutter] that mantra one hundred and eight times.

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times. Then, having prepared curd, honey, and ghee together in one place; sesame, grapes, and sugar-candy together in another; and *yāvakamala* (barley-meal) in yet another—having recited over each of these substances one hundred and eight times, one should offer oblations (*homa*) into the fire. First, having offered with the verse of the chapter, one should then offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *āyuḥ-mantra*. The fire [is then] released.
Having performed the *rjanānta* (the concluding rite), one should begin the recitation of the next chapter. The entire procedure is exactly as before;

thus, by performing the *rjanānta* for thirteen chapters, there is liberation from debt. This is the eighteenth [chapter]. Having spread milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in a copper vessel and covered it with ghee and sugar, one should write out the mantra "Namaḥ devyai" in its entirety using the method of *praveśagati* (entry-movement); this is the sixteenth [chapter].

Having worshipped with ritual services using the mantra "Namaḥ Devyai" and recited it three times, one should consume it; within twenty-one days, the vision of the Goddess becomes manifest. Taking a flawless copper pitcher—measuring nineteen, twelve, or seven *śers* and capable of holding water—one should go to a confluence (*saṅgama*), invoke the Goddess with these mantras, pray, and bestow knowledge while standing in the water.

Having recited the thirteenth chapter [of the Ṛgveda] once, having filled the water-pot, and having recited the hymn beginning with "udyaṃ tamasaspari," one should turn around, face the village, and upon reaching the bank, face the house and recite the two verses beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ.

Then, standing on the path behind, one should proceed while reciting the Śrīsūkta; and for the chariot, horse, and so forth, as well as for the cow, one should enter the house while reciting the verse beginning with "amita."

One should enter [the mandala] with concentration; thus, in the center of that single mandala, the attainment of fortune (lakṣmī) through horses and other means occurs. Then, on level ground, having performed the meditation measured by a *droṇa*, and having placed a jar according to the Vedic rite upon a heap [of grain], and having clothed [the deity] and sipped water (*ācamana*), one should place a square vessel made of gold or silver upon the jar, and then that—

Oṃ: Having fashioned an upward-facing triangle with a golden needle weighing three-quarters of a suvarṇa, and having placed within its center a drop (bindu) of one's own color, one should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the Bhaga-mantra: "O Goddess, grant me form; O Goddess, grant me fortune; grant me sons; grant me dharma; and grant me all desires.
Then, having worshipped it with the sixteen offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra) while reciting the mantra "Śaktuveti," one should remember that very tantra with this same mantra.

One should recite the Bhaga-mantra one thousand and eight times. Then, having tied a thread around the mouth of the water-pot and holding it, one should recite the Bhaga-mantra twenty-one times. Whoever drinks the water from the pot will attain the arising of great fortune. This practice is to be performed immediately after entering the mandala. Thus ends the twentieth [section]. Having prepared a seat with clay from the root of a horse and the heartwood of a Śamī tree—

Having prepared a seat there and recited the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one should read the thirteenth chapter; within ten days, all sins will be destroyed and the deity will become pleased. This is the twenty-first [chapter]. Having brought a young woman of sixteen years, one should consecrate flower-oil one hundred and eight times with the mantra "devīṃ vācā ca" and perform an oil massage on her head; then, with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," one should pour water over her once.
Having established the fire with the mantra, "O Agni, you who know the way of Varuṇa, protect us," and having kindled it,
one should bathe her there with that heated water. Then, having given a pair of garments with the mantra, "Give us [clothing] that is soft," and having adorned her with flowers using the mantra,

"This flower is for splendor," one should apply white sandalwood paste from the navel to the neck, yellow paste on the face, and red sindūra at the center of the forehead, while reciting the sixteen [syllables] beginning with "Vācā devi."

Touching the head, the heart, and the *yoni* while being honored by the attendants (*cāras*), one should recite the *mālā-mantra* three times; until the end of the *maṇḍala*, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) come to pass.

Thus ends the twenty-second [chapter]. (22) One should recite the verse beginning with "indra śreṣṭhān" at the beginning and the end of each stanza; the attainment of the best of substances occurs. Thus ends the twenty-third [chapter]. (23) In the seventh section of that very [work], at the beginning of any one of the divisions, for every stanza...
One should recite thus: twenty-four [verses]. Of these very four quarters, there are four recitations at the beginning and end.
*Oṃ* is the first syllable; in the first chapter, the first quarter is at the beginning and end; in the second, the second; in the third, the third; and in the fourth, the fourth.
Thus, from the fifth to the twelfth sūtra, thirteen [verses] are pure. It is complete. Thus, in the center of the maṇḍala, all desires [are fulfilled].

(25) One does not fail to attain [the goal]; thus ends the twenty-fifth [chapter]. One should recite the nine-syllable Durgā mantra at the beginning and end of each verse until the end of the mandala; whatever desire shines forth in the mind, one attains that very thing—thus ends the twenty-sixth [chapter]. (27) One should first take up the Durgā mantra and recite it a hundred times; there is success in all things—thus ends the twenty-seventh [chapter]. In a house smeared with sandalwood paste, there are eight-petaled lotuses in the directions.

Having drawn a triangle with its center marked by a jar and a bolt, or an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the eight groups of eight [syllables] of Suvr̥hmanyā starting from the east in sequence.
In the center, within the eight petals upon the ground, having written the nine-syllable mantra, one should worship it with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Having established a water-pot (kalaśa) upon that, and having first written the mantra in the water with chalk, as before...

Having worshipped [the manuscript], one should write the letters with gold-leaf and sandalwood paste upon it; then, preceded by the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the vital breath), one should worship it with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). While performing circumambulations, one should repeat the *mālā-mantra* and offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) into the previously mentioned water-pot (*kalaśa*). This should be done nine times. At the end, there is the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). However, for that which is inscribed on the ground, there is no dismissal as long as one lives. [This applies] to the invocation (*āvāhana*).
The mantras for the eight Durgās are as follows: (1) *daivīrāpaḥ* for Vajrayajñānavatī; (2) *asme somāḥ* for Maheśvarī; (3) *kumāraṃ mātā* for Kumārī;
(4) *viṣṇuryoniṃ kalpayatu* for Vaiṣṇavī; (5) *uddhṛtāsi varāheṇa* for Vārāhī; (6) *garbhaṃ dhehi sinīvāli* for Nārasiṃhī; (7) *indrāṇīmāsu nāriṣu* for Indrāṇī; and (8) *gaurīrmimāya* for Gaurī.

Having thus completed the *maṇḍala* with the *śāntyāḥ*, one should recite at the end of each verse of the hymn beginning with "adya mannāṃ vindate" (RV 1.82)—which consists of twenty-eight verses—the mantra "mā hi ṣṭhāḥ pitaraḥ" (RV 7.46.3), which is the first and last half-verse of the eighth chapter. One should recite this one hundred and eight times. At the conclusion of the *maṇḍala*, it is said that one obtains the desired food. Thus ends the twenty-ninth [section]. (291) Oṃ.
