One should recite up to the thirteenth [chapter]. In the second round, having chanted one hundred and eight times within the middle of the eighth chapter, one should conclude. Likewise, in the third round, one should conclude by chanting at the beginning of each verse of the eighth chapter. By performing this for forty-nine days, all defects caused by enemies such as *parikṛtya* and *kṛtyā* will surely perish. Having thus chanted, one should chant again in the reverse order (*anuloma*).

Having recited the remaining chapters, one should recite them again; at the beginning and the end, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times in reverse order. The destruction of enemies is certain, and one becomes liberated from death. This is the thirty-first [chapter]. Having consecrated sugar with the recitation of the *mālā-mantra*, one should have a well-dressed woman bring water mixed with that sugar into the midst of the people; this is an extremely secret [practice]. This is the thirty-second [chapter].

On the fourteenth day and on the new moon, at the junction [of the days], when the *sugandhālaka* has arisen, one should prepare two figures made of fragrant substances, dressed in red garments, with their bodies smeared and equipped with weapons; one should recite the names of those [deities] in place of the names of those respective weapons. At the time of the curd-offering, one should strike the *kūṣmāṇḍas* with those very weapons. Then, one should conceal them. Whichever one among them is given to someone, that person will be victorious in battle; one should fumigate it with incense while it is in the midst [of the rite].
Furthermore, one should understand that yoga is to be practiced in that very same way and the science of ethics (*nīti*) is likewise attained; thus ends the thirty-third [chapter].

Having brought a pitcher filled with flowing water, one should worship it with sixteen services (*upacāras*) using the *Puruṣasūkta* consisting of sixteen verses, and consecrate it by reciting the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇava*) one thousand and eight times. If it becomes empty, it must be refilled; thus the world becomes prosperous. Thus ends the thirty-fourth [chapter].

(34) Alternatively, on the twelfth day, an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) should be performed with the previous mantra; by the end of the year, all people become submissive. Thus ends the thirty-fifth [chapter]. (35) Regarding the mantra "ayaṃ te yoniṛtviya..."—one should recite this mantra at the beginning and end of each verse ten times; thus one obtains a virtuous son. Thus ends the thirty-sixth [chapter]. (36) Regarding the verse "udyaṃs tvaṃ..."—facing east, [one should recite] the verse at the beginning and end... [first]...

Oṃ. One should recite [the mantra] during the first circuit facing east; during the second circuit facing south; and during the third circuit facing west. Having performed this on the first day in this manner until the end of the maṇḍala, at the conclusion, one should perform a single circuit of the homa offering upon a copper plate. All diseases, such as fever and others, are destroyed.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh [chapter]. [One should perform it] while pouring streams of milk from a pot onto the head and streams of water from a pot in the right hand simultaneously, like a horse.

One should circumambulate in that manner while reciting the *mālā-mantra*; by this, the three worlds become subjugated. Thus, [the thirty-eighth: taking water in the left hand from a copper vessel, one should recite the nine-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times facing the west for the ancestors. Having consecrated the water and performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. In this way, [one completes the rite] up to the end of the mandala.

Because of this, for as long as one lives, all desires are fulfilled; together with one's family, there is the attainment of desired food; one does not suffer from the consequences of actions performed by others; and no one attains superiority over him—this is the thirty-ninth [chapter]. On the first day, one should mutter eight thousand [recitations] at midnight while naked. On the second day, anointed with flower-oil, one should mutter the nine-syllable mantra as before. On the third... [text ends]

With *yepuṣpa* oil, one whose body is white, surrounded by fire in the direction of Puṣpa, should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and perform recitation (*japa*). On the fourth day, however, one should again perform the *tūkṣṇī* recitation, surrounded by the ritual materials such as pumpkins and coconuts. After establishing the deity in the place of practice, the vision of the Goddess shall become manifest. Thus says Tvaritarāma; having recited the *Navārṇava*, [one attains] ten thousand plus fifty.

Having come to the house, one should recite the *Ghamarṣaṇa* mantras; all successes will be attained—this is the forty-first [chapter]. One should mutter the *Saṃgamṛṣṭi* mantra ten times for each verse; there is the accomplishment of all rites—this is the forty-second [chapter]. By performing ten thousand oblations (*homa*) with two blades of *dūrvā*, *guḍūcī*, and *khaḍga* smeared with honey and clarified butter while reciting the verse beginning with "May you live a hundred years" for each verse, [one attains] iron-strength.

The forty-third [chapter] is "Ranivṛtiḥ" (43). By reciting the *Mālā-mantra* with the reversal of the first and last verses of each *Śloka*—beginning with "Ākṛṣṭena," "Ambaka," and "Jātavedase"—one does not incur the effects of another's ritual magic (*parakṛtyā*) and so forth; this is the result. The forty-fourth [chapter] (44): Having recited the verse beginning with "Ākṛṣṭena" at the start of each *Śloka*, and then performing the purification (*mārjana*) with the three verses beginning with "Pohiṣṭhā," one attains wealth. *Mā*.

The removal of the sins of the wicked and the removal of old age; this is the forty-fifth [chapter], the Citipañcātvāriṃśa. Standing upon kuśa grass, holding water in a copper vessel upon kuśa grass, placing kuśa grass over it, and covering it with his right hand, one should drink the water after consecrating it twenty-one times with the nine-syllable mantra. By reciting it twenty-one times within the maṇḍala, speech becomes divine. Thus ends the sixth [section].
(46) For the desire for a son: three repetitions encased by the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) for up to forty-one days.

(47) For subjugation (*vaśya*): ten repetitions encased by the *kāmabīja* for up to three days. (48) For eradication (*uccāṭana*): thirteen repetitions with the syllable *phaṭ* as a suffix, encased by the *māyāvīja* (the seed-syllable of illusion) for up to seven days. (49) For one desiring wealth: the *ramāvīja*.

The fifteen-fold repetition for one who is intoxicated [with pride] must be performed until the end of fifteen days. Now, the procedure for the *Navaślokī*: having become pure by consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other substances, and having first recited the *Gāyatrī* ten thousand times, one should then recite it another ten thousand times while seated upon a vessel of milk. At an auspicious moment at night, having hung a bell in each of the directions starting from the east, one should invoke the respective deities in the order beginning with the east and worship them with the sixteen offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).

Then, having stood in the center and laid down eight lines, one should bind [the cord] with the east-west line at the two big toes; then below that, at the two little toes in the northeast and northwest; then to the south and north below that; and finally in the southwest and northeast below that. Having bound it thus, one should rise and recite: "O Viśveśvarī, O Jagaddhātrī, you who were praised before (1), you who were praised in the past (2), you who have been praised from the beginning (3)—to you, obeisance! (4).

HA (4) SAṂRVĀVĀDHĀPRA(0) (5) SARVAMAṄGALAṂ (6) SṚṢṬISTHI(7) ŚARUṆĀGATADĪ(8) SARVASVARŪPE(9). Reciting these nine verses, having heard the sound of the mṛdaṅga drum in the midst of the assembly, he should remove his lower garment and bind it around his head with "OṂ. Then, upon hearing the sound of the vīṇā lute, he should again stand as before and recite [the verses] as previously described. Then, upon hearing both sounds...

At the time of the ritual bath (*vaṇāvasara*), one should stand while holding in both hands the materials for the fragrant substances and the offerings (*naivedya*), and perform the recitation (*japa*).

Then, one should begin the prostrations (*namaskāra*) until the conclusion. Following the one thousand and eight prostrations, one should have both young women perform an ablution (*abhiṣeka*) upon one's own head. Afterwards, outside, the Brahmins should recite the *Rātrisūkta*, the *Śāntisūkta*, and the *Śrīsūkta*.

Then one should give food as desired to the young women who perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). After that, having drunk [the liquor] comfortably, [one should say]: "The hunger of the Blessed Lady has been allayed.

Thus ends the forty-seventh [chapter]. With the twenty-five verses beginning with *agnirna dīdhitibhir*, by which he always honors all beings, one should study this hymn (*sūkta*) and recite it. When [the hymn] begins with the verse starting with *yadā ṛcaṃ* and ends with *ekaṃ saṃpūrṇā*.
One should recite the remainder [of the hymn], thinking "may I not incur contempt"—this is the forty-eighth [method]. Now, regarding the method for the Śrīsūkta:

having recited the first verse in its entirety at the beginning, one should then recite the remaining verses. Starting thus from the second verse up to the fifteenth verse, and reciting fifteen times, this constitutes the fifteenth method. Having recited the Sūkta sixteen times in this manner, one should recite the Sūkta at the end of the verses.

Having recited [the hymn] in its entirety in sequential order, one should then recite it sixteen times at the end. In this way, sixteen repetitions bring about the fulfillment of all desires. Thus, forty-nine [verses]. One should worship yellow *akṣata* grains according to the path instructed by the Guru. Having invoked [the deities] within the individual verses arranged [therein], one should worship them with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Alternatively, having invoked [them] with a verse, one should worship with the [individual] verses; [this constitutes] sixteen [times] five.

There are one hundred *śloka*-offerings, resulting in the attainment of great prosperity; thus, having worshipped the thirteen maidens with sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) verse by verse, one should recite the chapter. In this manner, the first cycle consists of thirteen chapters; in the second, twenty-one; then in the third, three hundred and twelve; and then in the fourth, and so on in sequence, until the completion of the sixteen cycles, which is the Great [Accomplishment].

"Oṃ, the fruit of success arises"—thus, after reciting fifty-one verses, one should offer a single garment; at the end of each chapter and at the end of each verse, one should likewise offer a garment.

In this manner, sixteen garments of different colors are to be offered. One should meditate on Kālī with her terrifying face as dark blue. By this, within a few days, there is the attainment of fruits such as a royal throne and many garments according to one's desire.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) twice with *hrīṃ klīṃ* on the hands and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and having meditated [on the Goddess] as "residing in a red ocean" (*raktāmbhodhisthitā*), one performs the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) three thousand times with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ svalpair ahobhiḥ śrīṃ*. Desired success (*iṣṭasiddhi*) is attained. (1) For the Durgā-mantra, the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Īśvara, the Deity (*devatā*) is Mahākālī, the Seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *klīṃ*, the Power (*śakti*) is *hrīṃ*, and the Nail (*kīlaka*) is *hroṃ*; the rule for victory is: *oṃ aiṃ durge smṛtāḥ*.

For one who has fallen into poverty, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the attainment of wealth is as follows: first, for the purpose of purifying the body, one should recite the Gāyatrī twelve thousand times. Then, [the mantra is]: *Oṃ rodurge śrīṃ yatindra dhi oṃ dāridrya citāḥ oṃ maghava jahī oṃ hrīṃ*. At the beginning, for the sake of bodily purification, the Gāyatrī is recited twelve thousand times.

Having fashioned three images of Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī out of silver, gold, and copper respectively—measuring one *droṇa* each according to the sequence of the three *parārdhas*—one should cross over [the ocean of existence].
Among them, Mahākālī is made of silver and seated upon a cock;
in the middle is Mahālakṣmī, made of gold, possessing eighteen arms and seated upon a lion-throne; and on the right is Mahāsarasvatī, made of copper.

Having meditated upon [the goddess] seated on a peacock throne made of gold, and having worshipped her with the *Śrīsūkta* and the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should offer the *mantra-puṣpa* (flower-offering) to Mahākālī, who is to be worshipped first. Then, taking priyaṅgu seeds, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and turmeric, one should worship her with each verse of the first chapter (*carita*) and with the *samasta-vyāhṛtis*. In this same manner, one should worship her with the middle and final chapters. Through this, in six months, [one attains] knowledge (*vidyā*).
Thus ends the fifty-third [chapter].

Thus concludes the twelfth section on the rites for specific desires (*kāmyaprayoga*) within the *Tārābhaktitaraṅgiṇī*, a commentary on the *Saptaśatī* composed by Vimalānandanātha. The Lord said: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim out of a desire for the welfare of my devotees the procedure for the offering of lamps (*dīpadānavidhi*) to Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and likewise to Sāvitrī."

O Dear One, this is more secret than the most secret; having performed an oil massage, wearing red garments and being pure, one should—adorned with the eight self-mantras on the eight petals to the east—the wise man place a copper pitcher weighing sixteen *palas*.
It should be endowed with the five gems, accompanied by five blades of *dūrvā* grass, mixed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and saffron, and provided with a pair of cloths and fruits.

Upon that, one should place a copper vessel fashioned with eight petals; there, the Great Lakṣmī should be installed, accompanied by a pair of lotus feet. Whether she is made from one *pala*, half of that, or even half of that again, that eight-armed goddess is to be worshipped with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood. To the southeast of that, one should construct a square measuring sixteen finger-breadths, equal on all sides, with a height of four finger-breadths for prosperity.

(7) There, one should place a vessel made of leaves; one should not burn it with cow-ghee for thirteen days. (8) One should invoke the Goddess there, the deity of the first chapter, reciting the mantra of Bagalā adorned with a thousand arms:
(9) Oṃ hrīṃ bagalāmukhi, paralyze the speech and mouths of all the wicked, nail down their tongues, and destroy their intellect! Yaṃ.

"Hrīṃ Oṃ Svāhā! Worship her with garments of red cloth and ornaments that adorn her limbs. Then, at the beginning of each chapter, one should worship her with pure bilva leaves using these ten mantras; listen now as they are declared here. [She who is] the Sovereign of the Universe, the Sustainer of the World—may she grant the three aims of life (dharma, artha, kama). The suffix 'anuṣaṅga' is proclaimed to apply to all three purposes. [She who is] the pacifier of all afflictions..."

[Reciting] "ranaṇāgati," "api," "sarvasvarūpi," and "ete sarvābhyudayakārakāḥ," which are intent upon subduing enemies and pacifying all afflictions, one should worship with truthful mantras. Then one should meditate; for every verse and every utterance, one should worship again, performing sacrifice with the previously mentioned mantras encapsulated by Bagalā, as well as with incense and lamps.

Oṃ, having offered the milk-rice (pāyasa) and the primary sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the Supreme Goddess. Having thus worshipped the deity of the chapter following the second chapter (Chapter 15), one should perform the Great Worship (*mahāpūjā*) at the conclusion of the worship of the Goddess.
To her right, one should install and worship Mahākālī in a jar; likewise, one should perform worship before the lamps, and to the north, Sarasvatī. Thus...
One should perform [the rites] every day for forty-nine days; one should indeed offer twenty-four [oblations], or even twelve.

Every day, one should feed the *bhāvyās* (virgins), and a young woman (*suvāsinī*) should perform [the rite]. One should give them thirteen items, such as bodices and garments. Or, having worshipped each one individually, at the conclusion of that, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). Inside the pavilion, in a lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should offer] milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One who is not skilled [in this] should, having prepared a square [altar] with bilva leaves and sesame seeds—or even a square [pit]—perform the ritual bath with water from a jar.

Thereafter, one should worship the preceptor and give a dakṣiṇā of one hundred rupees. Three palas of gold, a necklace, a white garment, an umbrella, and two chowries [are to be given]; for Mahālakṣmī, one pala, and half of that elsewhere. Furthermore, more should be given to the Guru.
The gift of water, likewise the gift of land, the gift of earth, the gift of white cloth, and that which is charming; (24) all were devoted to fasting and always delighted in honoring the gods.

They were free from the touch of Śūdras and were always adorned with betel. (25) The entire procedure beginning with Navarātra is proclaimed here; if one so desires, O Goddess, one may worship the Goddess at will in a single water-pot. (26) Wealth...
One who desires sons and a wife should complete [the rite] in the forenoon; one who desires the destruction of enemies should do so diligently in the afternoon.

One should feed a thousand or even a hundred Brahmins; thus one attains all desires—there is no doubt to be made here. (29) Thus ends the procedure for the offering of lamps during the *Saptaśatī* in the *Vaihāyasī-paṭala* of the *Yoginī-tantra*. Now, the practice...

On a day favorable for the task and when the Moon is auspicious, having performed an oil-bath (*abhyaṅga-snāna*) in the morning and wearing red garments, one should pay homage to the Goddess, the Guru, and others. Then, having declared the place and time, [one should recite]: "For the sake of pacifying the obstacles to my auspicious marriage—whether occurring in this birth or in another—and for the removal of the mental afflictions and the fruits of past sinful actions that obstruct the attainment of a long-lived son, [I shall perform] the *govatsa-pūjā*..."

Whether by the separation of mother and child for a *yojana*, or by hatred toward others, hatred toward one's guru, or by devouring a fawn, or by injury; likewise, by knowing the defects in another’s womb, or by the fault arising from touching the hem of a wicked woman’s garment, or by sitting upon a pond— [one may perform this rite] for the sake of removing all such obstacles to progeny, and for the sake of long life and virtuous sons for the performer.

"I shall perform the rite for the offering of lamps for the *Vātsyāyanasaptaśatī*. First, for the sake of removing obstacles and ensuring success, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the *svasti-puṇyāha-vācana*, the worship of the *Amṛtakā* [deities], and the *Nāndī-śrāddha*. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should describe the aforementioned procedures and the fruit of those procedures within the resolve. Then, [one prepares] a square measuring sixteen *aṅgulas* on each side and four *aṅgulas* in height.

Having prepared four pure and leveled altars made of clay, one should install there the famous *ghaṭārgala* machine. Having duly established it with three measures of sixteen *palas* each of lac, one should worship the eight powers (*śaktis*) upon the eight petals starting from the east: to Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityavilāsinī, Aghorā, Maṅgalā, [and the remaining two]. Then, one should place five jewels in the jar.

Having placed dūrvā grass with its tips intact, *rocanā*, saffron, oblation materials, and a pair of garments there, one should fashion an eight-armed golden image weighing one *pala* or half of that. After performing the ritual of invocation (*nyāsa*) and the consecration of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should install it in the water-pot (*kalaśa*) with the mantra "I take you into my house" (*gṛhāva*).

Then, having worshipped it with the mantra "O Form, grant me sons, grant me wealth" (*rūpaṃ dehi putrān dehi dhanaṃ dehi*), one should offer a handful of flowers with the mantra beginning "With joined palms" (*karānvitena*).

Having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to this rite, one should worship Mahākālī on the south and Mahā-Sarasvatī on the north with substances such as camphor, agallochum (*agaru*), and parimala; having worshipped them with turmeric, vermilion (*sindūra*), collyrium (*añjana*), flowers, oil, and the like, and having cleansed the hair and performed worship with mirrors and other items,

[one should place] before them a copper vessel thirty-two *palas* in weight, sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) in length, four finger-breadths in width, and four finger-breadths in height, placed upon a base.

Having placed the prepared [materials] there— namely, cow's ghee or other ghee, and having lit thirteen lamps made with wicks fashioned from red and other colored threads by auspicious young women and others— one should offer a handful of flowers while reciting "rūpaṃ dehi," "stutāsuraiḥ karotyādi," "vartibhiḥ sarvabādhāpra," "kādyami smaryatrapradāṣakaṃ," and "sarvamaṅgalaviṣṭumāya."

Having thus worshipped You as the first lamp, beginning from the first chapter up to the flower-offering (*puṣpāñjali*) for the deity, and likewise having offered flowers with each verse up to the end of the twelfth chapter, Viśveśvarī was praised with nine verses, Jayā was praised [with nine], Pūṣkarasā was praised [with nine],
Sarvābādhā was praised [with nine], Sarvamaṅgalā was praised [with nine], Sṛṣṭi was praised [with nine], and Sthiti was praised [with nine].

Having offered flower-offerings (*mantrapuṣpa*) with these mantras for each chapter to the one who has come to the battle (*raṇāgata*) in his entire form, and likewise in the flower-chapters (*puṣpādhyāyeṣu*), an oblation (*naivedya*) of milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), sugar, and fresh ghee should be presented. In the verses beginning with "remover of all afflictions" (*sarvabādhādiślokeṣu*), the specific desire (*kāmanollekha*) should be stated as: "grant me a son" (*mama putrapradānakaḥ*) and "destruction of my disease" (*mama rogavināśanam*). At the end, the great worship (*mahāpūjā*) [should be performed] for Brahmā in each chapter.

Three *na* syllables, three *suvāsinīs*, and *bhobhujayat*. Thus, in fifty-one days, for a great rite, twenty-four days are prescribed for the middle application; thirteen days for the inferior; and at the conclusion of the ritual, one hundred *brahmans* and one hundred *suvāsinīs* should be honored. Having given the teacher (*ācārya*) a gift consisting of three *la*s, and having given that seat (*pīṭha*) to the teacher, [one should act] with certainty.

For the attainment of a son and for subjugation (*vaśya*): *oṃ hrīṃ raktacāmuṇḍe turu ānaya amukaṃ me vaśyam ānaya svāhā*. With this mantra, one should worship at the beginning and end of every recitation. At the conclusion of all [recitations], one should perform ten thousand oblations (*āhuti*) with *kuṭa*-oil; by performing a thousand oblations with this mantra using red sandalwood and black mustard seeds, one shall bring even a king under one's control. Furthermore, having offered honey and *aśoka* flowers for three nights, one should proceed as previously described.

Oṃ, by the power of the Caṇḍī mantra, one shall certainly become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); the meaning is that [the recitation] should be performed one thousand times as before. For the purpose of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), however, [the mantra is]: "Summon so-and-so, svāhā! All else is as in the previous pillar-rite (*stambhana*). Oṃ hrīṃ bagalāmukhi, paralyze the speech, the feet, and the mouth of all evil ones; pin their tongues, destroy their intellect! Hrīṃ svāhā! The worship, fire-offering (*homa*), and other rites for this mantra are to be performed as before.
Thus, [the section] beginning with "the eradication of delusion," "subjugation," and "the pacification of all afflictions" should be recited exactly as it stands.

For the sake of wealth, worship is performed with *bilva* leaves; for subjugation (*vaśya*), with *karavīra* or *japā* flowers; and for the sake of a son, with *tulasī* leaves. Two or one of the best among the four castes should perform the *homa* at its conclusion, either in a *yama-kuṇḍa* or on a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). One should complete the *homa*.

Having worshipped the preceptor today, having given a hundred cows as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and having presented various other offerings, one should complete the rite according to the sequence of the ritual manual and offer it to the Goddess. Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the lamp in the *Saptaśatī* within the *Tārābhaktitaraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Vimalānandanātha. Furthermore, in the *Vārāhītantra*, listen to the fruit of reciting the *Devī* [text], O Goddess; I shall declare it.
Having first worshipped it with mental resolve (nāmamaya-saṃkalpa), the practitioner attains success by reciting its limbs in sequence, through the offering of oblations (bali), and so forth.
For the sake of pacifying calamities (upasarga), a person should recite it three times; for the pacification of planetary influences (graha), O Varānanā, one should perform five recitations.
When great fear has arisen, one should increase it to seven recitations; through nine recitations, there shall be peace, yielding the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

One should recite the Rudra-āvṛti for the sake of prosperity, such as bringing a king under one's control; through this Āvṛti, the fulfillment of desires occurs and the destruction of enemies is certain. By performing the Manu-āvṛti, there is the destruction of enmity, and likewise, the enemy comes under one's influence. A person surrounded by the Pañcadaśa-āvṛti attains happiness and fortune. They know that in the Kalā-āvṛti, there is the acquisition of sons, grandsons, wealth, and grain, as well as the destruction of the fear of kingship.

O Dear One, for the purpose of driving away [enemies] from one's house, one should perform seventeen or eighteen recitations; likewise, for the liberation from the great Brahma [bondage], the wise person should recite "Oṃ Viśāvarta. Through twenty-five recitations, there shall be release from bondage. When one has encountered danger, or when afflicted by an incurable disease, or when facing the destruction of progeny, the extinction of the lineage, or the arrival of misfortune, or when enemies increase and diseases proliferate—[in these times, one should recite].

In the event of loss of wealth, exhaustion, as well as the occurrence of the three kinds of portents, and likewise in the case of a great transgression, one should diligently perform the *Śatāvarta* rite;

from that, happiness, prosperity, and growth are attained, as well as royal advancement through another hundredfold repetition. O Goddess, whatever is meditated upon by my mind shall be accomplished after one hundred and eight [recitations]. Through the joyful performance of this rite, the goddess Lakṣmī herself becomes steadfast and grants the fulfillment of all desires.

By reciting the *Caṇḍī* one hundred times, one shall attain the higher realms beyond desire; all perfections (*siddhis*) are accomplished for the sake of success. Having received the water offering (*arghya*), one should cease; one should not study [the text] when it is not the time for recitation. If one ceases in the middle of a section, one should recite the beginning of that chapter again.
Furthermore, having placed the deity before oneself according to the commentary, and especially having honored the Brahmins, the reciter should loosen the knot, O descendant of Kuru.

"I shall perform [the rite of] Śatacaṇḍī, Sahasracaṇḍī, Ayutacaṇḍī, or Lakṣacaṇḍī through the medium of a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of dispelling fear" (or, "I shall perform such-and-such Caṇḍī for the sake of accomplishing such-and-such a task, as prescribed in the Arthavāya"—thus is the brief statement). One should request the officiating priest (*ācārya*) as follows: "I choose you, the Brahmin named So-and-so Śarman, who is absorbed in meditation, to be the *ācārya* in this rite; I am your devotee. "You are my refuge, you are my ultimate resort; by your grace, O Brahmin-sage, may everything that is in my heart be accomplished. Then, for the purpose of chanting the mantras of the gatekeepers, Brahmins should be chosen as before; all [other duties] should be performed as before, and the prayer for the completion of this sacrifice should be offered to all.

O you who are present here, being entreated by me, please perform the rite for peace (*śāntika*) according to the prescribed rules. In that regard, for one *Navacaṇḍī* there shall be one Brāhmaṇa; for ten *Śatacaṇḍīs*, ten Brāhmaṇas; for a hundred *Sahasracaṇḍīs*, a hundred; for ten thousand *Ayutacaṇḍīs*, a thousand; and for a million *Lakṣacaṇḍīs*, ten thousand Brāhmaṇas. All those Brāhmaṇas are devotees of Caṇḍī. Thus, let the worship with *madhuparka* be performed for all of them.
One should give you a ring, an ear-ornament, two garments, a water-vessel, a seat, and water for the *arghya* offering in one's hand.

(3) For the preceptor (*ācārya*), [the fee] should be double. Then, having performed the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the duties of the sacrifice, and having remembered the time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) from the sacrificer: "I shall perform the work of the preceptor. Having scattered white mustard seeds with the mantra "yad atra... and having [purified] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having sprinkled the pavilion with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and the six verses beginning with *śucī vo havyā*, and having joined his palms in reverence (*añjali*),

he should mutter the two mantras beginning with *svasti anantārkṣyām*. Then, having worshipped the deity Vāstu in the southwest (Nairṛta) corner of the pavilion up to the offering of the bali-oblation, and having encircled the pavilion with a triple-thread cord sown with barley, he should proceed.

Then, in the eastern direction, outside the door of the pavilion, at a distance of one cubit, having invoked a very firm archway with the mantra *agnim īle purohitam*, and having placed Rāhu and Bṛhaspati there, he should worship them with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*),
duly install the water-pot (*kalaśa*), and worship Dhruva. Then, on the right side, having invoked a beautiful archway with the mantra *iṣetvorjetvā*, [he should worship] Sūrya...

Oṃ. Having worshipped Gārutatra and established the water-pot (kalaśa), one should worship the Earth. In the west, having invoked the Sukarma-gate with the mantra "agnayāpāhi," and having worshipped Śukra and Śuci there, one should establish the water-pot and worship Vāk there. In the north, having invoked the Suhotra-gate with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," and having worshipped Soma, Ketu, and Śani, one should establish the water-pot and worship Vighna.

Then, having placed two water-pots (kalaśas) to the south and north at the eastern gate, and having established Airāvata there and worshipped him with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should choose two Ṛgvedic priests (ṛtvij) with the words: "O best of Brahmins, the Ṛgveda, the Paippalāda recension, the bull, Gāyatrī, and Soma as the deity; you belong to the Atri lineage; O eminent priest, be my officiant in this sacrifice. Having chosen the two Ṛgvedic priests and worshipped them with the mantra "Agnim īle," one should meditate upon Indra and say, "Come hither..."

The Lord of the Gods, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, is praised by all the gods, Siddhas, and Sādhyas; being fanned by a host of celestial nymphs, he protects our sacrifice—O Blessed One, salutations to you!
"O Indra, come here! Having thus invoked him and worshipped the door-vase, he should raise the yellow banner with the mantra *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*.
Then, having worshipped Indra, the Lord of the Gods, the most excellent one with the thunderbolt in hand, with the mantra *trātāram indram*.

"Obeisance again and again to the gods of great strength and intent upon a hundred sacrifices, who are ever devoted to their own [nature]. Having thus bowed and sprinkled [the area] with *arghya* and nectar, one should offer at the eastern door on the upper branch: "Oṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. To his right: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vighnanāśana. To his left:
"Obeisance to Kṣetrapā-Bhairava. To the right and left of Kṣetrapāla, in the southeast, [one should worship] Māṃmā Mahālakṣmī.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ namo saṃsarasvatyai" and "Oṃ namo madhyedvāraśriye," then, below the right and left door-frames, [one should worship] with "Oṃ śaṃ, obeisance to the Śaṅkha-nidhi and Vasudhārā deities; obeisance to the Padma-nidhi and Vasumatī deities. Above those two, on the right, "Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa"; on the left, "Oṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. Then, above those two, on the right, "Oṃ gaṃ..."

*Oṃ*, salutation to the Goddess Vāmā Yamunā. Then, above those two, on the right, *oṃ*, salutation to Dhātrī; on the left, *oṃ*, salutation to the various [goddesses]. *Oṃ*, salutation to Dehalī at the threshold. Then, having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra: *Oṃ lāṃ, to Indra, together with his limbs (retinue), together with his entourage, armed with the thunderbolt, whose vehicle is Airāvata*, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Thus ends the worship of the eastern door. Then, having established the water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the southeast, there [is] Puṇḍarīka.

Having meditated upon the sacrificial fire as the deceased, one should invoke him with the mantra: "O Rāhu, come! O bearer of the great oblation, you who are honored on all sides by the best of sages; protect me along with this living world and my sacrifice; salutations to you. Having thus invoked the fire with the mantra "agnidūtam," and having raised a red banner and flag, one should worship the Fire with the mantra: "The Puruṣa of the southeast is red, the imperishable embodiment of all gods, the smoke-bannered lord of the quarters."

Having thus bowed with "Obeisance, obeisance to Him who is eternally present," and having offered the bali-oblation with "Oṃ Śaṃ, obeisance to Agni, whose weapon is the Śakti and whose vehicle is the ram," one should then place a water-pot (kalaśa) to its right. There, having worshipped the elephant of the quarter, Vāmana, one should [worship] the Yajurveda:

"O best of Brahmins, you are the Yajurveda, born of the Vṛddhi-jāta; you have Kātarākṣa as your seer, the *aiṣu* as your weapon, Viṣṇu as your deity, and you are a descendant of Kaśyapa; O eminent priest, be my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in this sacrifice."

Having chosen two officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having worshipped them with the mantra "Īṣe tvā," and having meditated upon Him, he should invoke [Yama] with the mantra: "Come, come, O Vaivasvata, King of the Dead, honored by all the gods, embodiment of Dharma! In the midst of the joy and sorrow of the auspicious and inauspicious, O Lord, protect me; salutations to You.

Having thus invoked Him, and having raised the banner and flag with the mantra "Ayaṃ gaurī" (This is Gaurī), he should worship the shoulder [of the sacrificial post] with the mantra "upanāyasomaṃ" (Bring forth the Soma). Then, he should worship the Great Goddess (*Mahāmahi*).
"I invoke the one of great strength, mounted upon a bull and holding a staff; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice.
Then, having sprinkled the southern door with the nectar of the *arghya* water, [one should offer] above it: "Oṃ glaḥ, obeisance to Gaṇanātha. Then: "Obeisance to Dvāraśrī.
Then, on the right and left door-frames as before: "Oṃ kāṃ, obeisance to Kāmadeva"; "Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Vasanta. Then...
Salutation to the goddesses Padmanidhi and Vasumatī in the upward and downward sequence; Oṃ Paṃ, salutation to Padmanidhi and Vasumati;
Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa; Oṃ Kṣaṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla; salutation to Gaṇadevī; salutation to Yamunā; Oṃ Dhāṃ. (The page numbers from this point are incorrect.)

Oṃ *dhātre* adhām *dehalyai* in front of this [threshold]. Oṃ *vaṃ*, having offered the *bali* to Varuṇa, who rides upon the makara and holds the noose, and having performed the *ācamana*—thus is the worship of the western door. Then, having established the water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the northwest (*vāyavyā*), having invoked the flower-offering and white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) therein, and having meditated upon Vāyu: "Come, come! For the protection of this sacrifice, you who ride upon the deer, accompanied by hosts of lions and perfected ones (*siddhas*)."
"O Lord, salutations to you, the lord of life, the observer of time, the one who bestows gifts, and the one who receives offerings.

Having thus invoked him and raised the smoke-bannered flag and the banner, he worships Vāyu with the mantra: "I invoke Vāyu, who moves through the sky and possesses the speed of a fresh lotus; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice. [He worships] Ananta, the one of great splendor...

Having bowed with the mantra: "Obeisance to the one whose path in the sky is invisible; obeisance, obeisance to Vāyu here," and having chosen two priests—one for the *Ṛgveda* and one for the *Atharvaveda*—and having offered the *bali* with the mantra: "Oṃ, to the one armed with a goad, whose vehicle is a deer, O Vaiśampāyana among sages, to the Wind-god (Pavana), svāhā," he should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). Then, having established a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the north, [he should face] the direction of the universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*).
Having worshipped him and chosen two officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who were knowers of the *Atharvaveda*, [the Lord] said:
"O Śaṃpāyana, best of sages, may you become my priest in this sacrifice. Having been chosen and worshipped with the mantra beginning with "śaṃ naḥ divīḥ," and having meditated upon Soma, he [said]:
"Come, O Lord of Sacrifice, intending to perform the protection of the sacrifice, together with the hosts of stars, all medicinal herbs, and the ancestors, as well as the planets..."

Having performed the oblation and worship with *hārṇa* [mantras], and having invoked [the deity] with "O Blessed One, salutations to you" (*bhagavan namaste*), one should raise a green banner (*haritāpatākā*) while reciting "Come here" (*āyāsya*). Having worshipped it thoroughly, and having offered obeisance with "Salutations to Soma, the King who is established in the midst of all the constellations (*nakṣatra*)—to that Soma, the Lord of the Constellations" (*tasmai somāya nakṣatrapataye namaḥ*) nine times, one should sprinkle the northern door with water from the *arghya* vessels. Above that, on the lintel, one should worship with "Oṃ, salutations to Vaṭuka" (*oṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ*) and "Oṃ, to the Goddess of the Door" (*oṃ dvāraśriyai*).

*Oṃ namaḥ* to the right and left branches: *Oṃ saṃ śaṃ* to the Śaṅkhanidhi and Vasudhārā goddesses; *Oṃ paṃ* to the Padmanidhi and Sumatī goddesses. Above those two: *Oṃ gaṃ* to Gaṇeśa; *Oṃ kṣaṃ* to Kṣetrapāla. Then above those two: *Oṃ gaṃ* to Gaṇadevī; *Oṃ yaṃ* to Yamunā. Above those two: *Oṃ dhātre*, *Oṃ vidhātre*. Below, at the threshold (*dehalī*): *Oṃ aṃ* to Aṅka.
Having offered the bali-oblation to Kubera, who holds a mace as his weapon and a man as his vehicle, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana). Thus concludes the worship at the northern gate.
Then, having placed a water-pot (kalaśa) in the northeast and worshipped Supratīka and Maṅgala, and having meditated upon Īśāna in the northeast, [one recites]: "O Rāhu, come!
O Viśveśvara, together with the one who holds a trident and a khaṭvāṅga in hand, O Grahas, for the sake of the success of the sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice!"

Having performed the worship with "O Blessed One, salutations to you," and having raised a white banner and a flag with the mantra "Ā vaha deva savitaḥ," and having worshipped them, [he should say]: "I invoke [the deity] mounted upon the shoulders of a bull, trident in hand, three-eyed; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice. O Sovereign of all, Great Goddess, Śāna, Śukliśvara, Trident-bearer, Virūpākṣi!"

Having thus bowed and worshipped him with the words "Salutations, salutations eternally to Him," and having sprinkled [the area] with nectar-like waters, one should offer the *bali* oblation with the mantra "Oṃ hrāḥ, O you who ride upon the bull and wield the trident as a weapon! and then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, having meditated upon Ananta between the northeast and the east, [one should recite]:

"Come, come! You who bring about the welfare of the worlds of the gods, the lords of the serpents, the Yakṣas, and the Kinnaras, whose praises are sung by the women of the serpent-kings and the lords of the Maruts, and who support the earth and the underworld."

Having invoked [the deity] with the mantra "naṃtarakṣādhvaramasyadīyam," and having raised the white banner and the flag, one should worship with "āyagaurī. Then, bowing with the words, "Obeisance, obeisance to Him who, in the form of the *nyagrodha* tree, holds the universe of moving and unmoving beings like a flower upon His head (mūrdhni)," one should thereafter sprinkle [the vessel] with nectar (*amṛta*) and offer the *bali* with the mantra "oṃ hrīṃ cakrāyudhakurmavāhanānatāyi. Then, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*). Thereafter, pa...

Having meditated upon Brahmā in the center of the western *ṛtvij*, one should invoke him with the mantra: "Come, come, O Lord of All, Indra of the gods, together with the world and the ancestral deities; you are the sustainer of all, possessed of immeasurable power; for our sake, protect this sacrifice night and day for our welfare.

Then, having worshipped the red banner and the raised flag with the mantra "Brahma-jñānam" and "Oṃ," one should recite: "The Grandfather (Pitāmaha), the source of the six paths, possessing four forms, is indeed the protector of the sacrifice."

"Salutations again and again to that four-faced Lord, the Overseer. Having thus bowed, he should sprinkle [the area] with the nectar of the *arghya* water. Then, having offered an oblation (*bali*) to Brahmā with the mantra "Oṃ Āṃ, to Brahmā, whose weapon is the lotus and whose vehicle is the swan," he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, in the center of the pavilion, having hoisted the great banner of Indra with the mantra "Indrasya vṛṣṭā," and having worshipped Brahmā with the mantra "Brahma yajñānam," he should offer an oblation right there with the words "Salutation to Antarikṣa."

Then, between the northeast and the east, one offers the oblation (*bali*) with "Oṃ bhūmyai namaḥ" (Salutation to the Earth). Then, on the pillars of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), [one offers to] all the gods;
in the rafters, to the *kinnaras*; on the roof, to the *pannagas*. Then, in the northeast of the pavilion, to all the spirits (*bhūtas*);
in the southeast, to all the *varṇa-yoginīs*; in the southwest, to Kurukullā; in the northwest, to Vārāhī. Then, in the west...

Oṃ roṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Great Goddess; O dispeller of the minds of all bound souls (paśus), grant [this]! Svāhā! Having offered a separate sacrificial cake (bali) to each of the following—Tiraskāriṇī, Agni in the southeast, Rudra in the east, Īśāna in the northeast, Brahmā in the west, and Gaṇeśa in the center—and having worshipped Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī, then outside that pavilion in the east... what?

May all beings, both stationary and moving, that exist within the three worlds—having been anointed upon the ground of consciousness (cid-bhūmi)—along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, grant me protection.

May the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pannagas, sages, ascetics, cows, and the divine mothers, all filled with joy, provide protection for my sacrifice. May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, together with the hosts of Kṣetrapālas, likewise protect me.

May all protect the pavilion; may they destroy the *rakṣas* on every side from the beings moving and stationary in the three worlds, and from the beings moving in the three worlds. To Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; again at the southern door, to the right and left: *Oṃ svāhā* to the Goddess Śubhaṅkarī; above that, to Gau and Gaurī; *Oṃ* to the divine ones; above that, *Oṃ* to the perfected (*siddha*) ones; *Oṃ* to the celestial beings (*bhauvana*), to the gods, to the *gandharvas*, and to the *yakṣas*.
Oṃ, having worshipped and offered the *bali* oblation to the *bhūtas*, *rākṣasas*, *pannagas*, *ṛṣis*, *manuṣyas*, *gods*, and *mātṛs*, one should rinse the mouth (*ācamana*).

Then, having circumambulated the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), at the eastern door, on the right and left [sides], [one worships]: Oṃ, obeisance to Bhā-bhadrakālī; Oṃ, obeisance to Svā-sarasvatī. Above that, Oṃ, obeisance to Gau-gaurī. Above that, Oṃ, obeisance to the divine hosts (*divyaudhas*); above that, Oṃ, obeisance to the perfected hosts (*siddhaudhas*); Oṃ, obeisance to the human hosts (*mānavaudhas*). Then again, on the south...

At the right and left of the door: *Oṃ svāhā* to the Goddess; *Oṃ saṃ* to Śubhaṃkarī; above those, *Oṃ gauḥ* to Gaurī; *Oṃ divyaiḥ* to the divine hosts; *Oṃ siddhaiḥ* to the Siddha hosts; *Oṃ mānavaughebhyaḥ* to the human hosts. Then, having gone to the western door as before, at the right and left: *Oṃ saṃ* to Sarasvatī; *Oṃ maṃ* to Mahālakṣmī; *Oṃ gauḥ* to Gaurī; *Oṃ divyaughebhyo siddhaughebhyo mānavaughebhyaḥ* [to the divine hosts, the Siddha hosts, and the human hosts]. Then, as before, at the north, at the right and left.

Oṃ to Māyādevī; Oṃ to Durgā; Oṃ to Gaurī, to the divine ones, to the Siddhas. Then again, having approached the western door with the right side forward, one enters the great temple of Bhavānī at the western door, which is protected on the outside by Indra and the other gods and adorned with supreme sovereignty.

Having meditated thus, one should worship the pavilion with the mantra: *oṃ paścimadvārāyaratnamaṇḍapāya imaṃ maṇḍapaṃ saṃpūjya*. Then, preceded by three *tāla* gestures, one should gaze at the door and say: "May the bhūtas, piśācas, pretas, and guhyakas depart; and those deities who reside here upon the earth, depart! May those bhūtas residing here depart, and may those bhūtas who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva! *oṃ sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*."

Having entered the pavilion of the earth (*bhū-maṇḍapa*), one should drive away the obstructors dwelling on the ground with three blows of the left heel; those moving through the intermediate space (*antarikṣaga*) with both hands joined in the *tāla* gesture; and the divine obstructors (*divya-vighna*) by gazing with divine vision (*divya-dṛṣṭi*). [One should recite: "May the aerial elephants (*bhāṇḍakariṇaḥ*) who have descended to the earth and those situated in the celestial realm perish by the command of Śiva! Whatever natural impurity (*prakṛta-pāpa*) has overcome me in the sky, may you expel that from my consciousness. [Then,] having purified the site, one should proceed.

*Mepāpaṃ phaṭ phaṭ, obeisance to him! Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, the great elements, and the Earth—be witnesses here to this rite for the sake of [determining] the auspicious and inauspicious of the night.* Thus is the worship of the door. Here, when the first lunar day (*pratipad*) coincides with a Tuesday, one should stand at the western door of the sacrificial ground, fashion the four doors, and perform the worship. Alternatively, some say that one should worship only the western door.

If one is unable to perform the worship due to incompleteness, one should consecrate water placed in a vessel of copper or similar metal with the *praṇava* and the root mantra, transform it into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of a mudrā, and sprinkle [the area] with that water. Herein, the sequential meditation on the deities of the door is not written out for fear of excessive length. Then, having entered within the pavilion, having rung the Kāśyapa bell, and having covered the door with a cloth, [one should perform the rite] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the *arghya*.

One should sprinkle [water] toward the south within the interior of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). Then, in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), having worshipped Dīpanātha with: *oṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ* and *oṃ raktadvādaśāktiyutaśrīpadena yanāthāya namaḥ*, one should pray: "In this lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), for the sake of the unimpeded accomplishment of the worship of Śrī Caṇḍī, you ought to grant permission. Thereafter, one should worship the eight Śaktis in pairs in the directions starting from the east.

Then, having worshipped at the western gate with: *Oṃ purandaryai vādiṅmātre*, *Oṃ vaśinyai diṅmātre*, *Oṃ dūtaryai vādiṅmātre*, *Oṃ sumukhyai vādiṅmātre*, *Oṃ virūpāyai vādiṅmātre*, *Oṃ vimalāyai vādiṅmātre*, *Oṃ puṣpamardinyai vādiṅmātre*, and *Oṃ vadyai vādi*—one should worship Sundarī as the ninth in the center. Then [worship] Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra Mahākāya...

"O you who are like the fire at the end of an aeon, salutations to you, O Bhairava; you should grant me permission. Having thus received the command of Bhairava, [the practitioner] goes with the sound "Ā-phaṭ," purifies the site, and having gazed upon the ground there, sprinkles it with water from the *argha* vessel while reciting "Astrāya phaṭ.

Then, having struck it with that same weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and protected it with "Eka-cāpa-haṃ," these are the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the ground. Thus [ends the section on] the Ācārya.

Having performed the ritual worship of the nine planets, beginning with their installation on the *navagraha-vedi* (the altar for the nine planets) such as the *Sarvatobhadra*, and ending at the conclusion of the worship, one should sit upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*) of the altar in the western portion.

Here, the sequence of the *brāhmaṇa-muhūrta* and other procedures is as before; having performed the rites up to the *saṃdhyā*, one recites the *gāyatrī*: "cāmuṇḍāyai vidmahe varadāyai dhīmahi tanno lakṣmīḥ pracodayāt. All else, up to the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), is as previously described.

Oṃ, having driven away the elemental spirits (bhūtas) with the mantra "Oṃ kramaḥ apasarpatu," and having established the seat with the mantra "Pṛthivī," one should sit down in the sequence beginning with the lotus posture (padmāsana). Then, having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra (mūlamantra), and having offered the disciple's joined palms (añjali) while reciting "I bow to the mind" (namo manasi) for each in the lineage succession starting from Brahmā down to one’s own guru’s sandals, [the teacher] should place the sandals of the Guru on his left shoulder, Gaṇapati on his right shoulder, and Sarasvatī at his navel.

Having remembered Kāla in the heart, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the sake of pleasing Śrī Mahālakṣmī, in this rite of Caṇḍī and others, I shall perform the worship, the recitation (*japa*), the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa-sthāpana*), and so forth. Then, first making the resolve, "For the sake of establishing my authority, I shall perform the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*) and so forth," one should perform the *bhūta-śuddhi*.
Having placed the two hands in the *svastika* posture, one should meditate upon the Śrī-kuṇḍalinī at the *mūlādhāra*, who is serpent-like in form, endowed with three and a half coils,
as slender as a grain of *nīvāra* rice, the embodiment of all deities, possessing the brilliance of a flash of lightning, and coiled around the *svayambhū-liṅga*. Then, by the method of *kuñcana*,
contracting the anus while reciting the *haṃsa-mantra* and performing *praṇāma*, one should draw up that serpent-like power from the *mūlādhāra*.

Having meditated upon the void (*śūnya*), which consists of Brahman situated within the central triad known as Suṣumnā and Vajra— the oneness of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the supreme soul (*paramātman*)— one should contemplate that water, which is the portion of Brahman corresponding to the letter *Oṃ*, dissolving into the water of universal form (*viśvarūpa*) corresponding to the letter *U* (the portion of the *praṇava* belonging to the Svādhiṣṭhāna), which is four-cornered, composed of the letters from *Va* to *Sa*, and associated with the earth element; and that water, along with the letters from *Va* to *La*, dissolves into the Maṇipūra.

Having dissolved that wind— which is of the nature of deep sleep, accompanied by the *praṇava* portion of the *rasya*, and in the form of the Lord who is the half-moon— into the space (ākāśa) consisting of Sadāśiva, which is the seat of the pure *praṇava* portion and is associated with the six-cornered [figure] along with the flame of a lamp, together with the individual soul (*jīva*) and the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*; then that space, together with the sixteen-petaled lotus, the vowels, the circle, and the previously mentioned *ājñā* [cakra], dissolves into that *praṇava*.

One should contemplate the dissolution of the mind into the Bindu, which consists of Śiva and Śakti in the form of a bamboo-bundle; then that Ignorance (avidyā), together with the Bindu and the mind, dissolves into the syllable *Oṃ*; that living self (*jīvātman*), accompanied by the *haṃ* sound, dissolves into the Great One who is all-pervading and possesses great power; that Great One dissolves into the Supreme Nature (*prakṛti*) through the highest activity. One should contemplate that [Nature] as being of the nature of light, eternal, the very essence of the knowledge of Brahman, solitary, and pure.

Having contemplated that "the Valāśāntas, Nirguṇa, and Paramātman" as previously described dissolve into the Supreme Śiva in the form of the supreme *bindu* within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus— that which is called the supreme state, free from disease— one should then contemplate the wind-seed syllable *yaṃ*, smoke-colored, at the heart. By reciting it sixteen times, one should fill the lungs with air, and by holding the breath (kumbhaka) sixty-four times, one should [retain] the left [side].

One should meditate upon that sinner, who has the sin of killing a Brahmin as his drawn-out head situated in the belly, the two arms for stealing gold, the heart for drinking liquor, and the two hips for violating the Guru’s bed;
likewise, one should remember him with all his major and minor limbs as the various sins, his body-hairs as the secondary sins (upapātaka), and his fangs as terrifying;

holding a sword and a shield, and filled with rage, one should contemplate him in the left side of the belly, visualizing that sinner dried up along with his body, and then recite the mantra thirty-two times.

One should exhale the breath through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] while reciting "im," visualizing the fire-seed (*vahni-bīja*) as red-colored at the navel; by reciting it sixteen times, one fills the breath through the *piṅgalā*; having retained the breath by reciting it sixty-four times, one should contemplate the body along with its sins as being incinerated; then, one should exhale by reciting it thirty-two times. One should visualize the moon-seed (*candra-bīja*) as "vam" as white-colored within the lunar orb at the head; [one should recite it] sixteen times.

Having filled [the body] with air by reciting the mantra sixty-four times, one should contemplate one's own body as being saturated with the nectar produced therefrom; then, having visualized the seed-syllable *vaṃ*—white in color—at the head, one should exhale the air by reciting it thirty-two times. Then, having filled the air with the *piṅgalā* [channel] by reciting the syllable sixteen times, one should subsequently bathe the divine body with the nectar produced therefrom by reciting it sixty times.

Having visualized the letter *va* (the seed-syllable of wind), one should exhale the breath while reciting it thirty-two times. Then, having contemplated the letter *la* (the earth-seed syllable) at the *mūlādhāra*, which is of yellow color, one should fill [the body] with air by reciting it sixteen times, and hold the breath (*kumbhaka*) by reciting it sixty-four times. Having firmly fortified the body with the earthly elements produced thereby, one should exhale the breath through the *piṅgalā* channel by reciting the syllable thirty-two times. *Haṃ* is the white-colored seed-syllable of space (*ākāśa*).

Having recited the *Kaṇḍe-vicintya* mantra sixteen times while filling the breath with *piṅgalā*, one should perform *kumbhaka* (retention) by reciting it sixty-four times. Then, having meditated on the gross body being consumed by those elements, one should exhale the breath through *iḍā* by reciting the mantra thirty-two times. Thereafter, one should bring the *jīva* (individual soul) into the heart with the mantra "Sāham" (I am That). One should then bring the *kuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra* up to its own place through the *tattvas* in the direct order (*anuloma*). This is the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Without ritual action—such as recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and worship—the *niṣkala* [form] becomes accomplished in every way; thus concludes the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Now, for the mantra of the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*): Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers (*ṛṣis*); the *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman* are the meters (*chandās*); the deity is the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*) whose form is consciousness (*cidrūpinī*); *āḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *kroṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*); having established that the application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation of the vital breath, one should perform the *añjali* [gesture] and recite the [seers] over the head: "O Brahman, O Seer..."

With "Oṃ, salutation to the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas; salutation to the one whose form is consciousness (cidrūpin) in the heart; salutation to the deity Prāṇa-Śakti in the secret place; salutation to the seed-syllable 'Āṃ' in the feet; salutation to the Śakti 'Hrīṃ' in the feet; salutation to the Kīlaka 'Krīṃ' in all limbs"—thus is the Nyāsa of the Seer and others. Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ Aṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ, salutation to the thumbs (Aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ Namaḥ) for the self consisting of Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether. Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ Iṃ Caṃ Chaṃ... [and so forth].

*Jāṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ śabda-śarīra-rūpa-rasa-gandhātmane itarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ.* *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ śrotra-tvak-cakṣu-jihvā-ghrāṇātmane oṃ madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ.* *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ e taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ na vāk-pāṇi-pāda-pāyu-upasthātmane rau anāmikābhyāṃ huṃ.* *Oṃ āṃ oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ ma nāda-ādāna-gamana-visarga-ānandātmane au kaniṣṭhābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ.*

*Kābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ; Oṃ Āṃ Aṃ Ya-manobuddhyahaṃkāra-cittajñānātmane akara-tala-kara-pṛṣṭhābhyāṃ phaṭ*—thus is the *karanyāsa*. Likewise for the heart and other limbs. Now, the *kṣaranyāsa*: *Oṃ Āṃ Namaḥ* from the feet to the knees; *Oṃ Hrīṃ* from the heart to the navel; *Oṃ Krāṃ* from the head down to the heart. *Ayaṃ tvagātmane*; *Oṃ Raṃ* to the blood (*asṛgātmane*); *Oṃ Laṃ* to the flesh (*māṃsātmane*); *Oṃ Vaṃ* to the fat (*medātmane*).

Oṃ neoṃ kṣaṃ to the self of the soul; oṃ ṣaṃ to the self of Pūṣan; oṃ saṃ to the self of Maja; oṃ haṃ to the self of the power of space (Ākāśa-śakti); oṃ laṃ kṣaṃ to the self of the individual soul (Jīva). Thus one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart. The visualization (*dhyāna*): Seated upon a red lotus arising from the middle of a sea of blood, she rests upon a crimson lotus. With her lotus-like hands, she holds a noose, a bow made of sugarcane, a goad consisting of a string of jewels, and a five-feathered arrow; she bears a blood-stained sword and possesses three eyes.

One should meditate on the Goddess, who is white-complexioned, adorned with breasts and hips, possessing the luster of the rising sun, the bestower of happiness, the supreme life-force (*prāṇa-śakti*), and the very self. Having thus meditated, one should visualize the weapons: the first pair above the left [hand], the second pair below it, the third pair above the right [hand], and the fourth pair below it. Then, having placed the *hṛdaya* (heart) and *liṅga* mudrās, one should recite: *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ mama prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ*.

"Oṃ āṃ maṃ, may my life-breath (jīva) abide here"—thus one should place [the mantra] on the head. "Oṃ haṃ maṃ, may all my sense organs (sarvendriyāṇi)"—thus on the two eyes. "Oṃ haṃ maṃ, may my speech, mind, sight, hearing, tongue, nose, and vital breaths (vāk-manas-kṣu-śrotra-jihvā-ghrāṇa-prāṇāḥ), having come here, remain happily for a long time, svāhā"—with this, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) over all the limbs. Having performed this placement three times, then, placing the hand upon the heart and performing fifteen repetitions of the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should contemplate in sequence: "My purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been accomplished."

Then, having performed the *itiprāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the ritual installation of the vital breaths) and the offering of the *ajapā*, one should perform the *mātṛkānyāsa*. Having filled [the body] with air through the *iḍā* [left nostril] by means of the vowels, one should retain it (*kuṃbhaka*) and exhale through the *piṅgalā* [right nostril] by means of the consonants. Thus, having performed the three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, for this *mātṛkānyāsa-mantra*:
Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*, Gāyatrī is the *chandas*, Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity, the consonants are the seeds (*bījas*), the vowels are the powers (*śaktis*), and the *kīla* is [the syllable] *Haṃ*.

Having performed the ritual service (*upāsana*) of the Caṇḍī-mantra, this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the Nyāsa of the Mātṛkās as its limbs. With palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should then perform the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣis and so forth: One should place [the syllables] with the fingers excluding the thumbs: *brahma* on the head, *gāya* on the face, *tri* on the eyes, *nama* on the heart, *adhi* on the private parts, *mātṛkā* on the feet, and *namaḥ* on the anus. *Haṃ* is for the seed-syllable (*bīja*) on the private parts; *namaḥ* is for the vowels on the feet; *ka* through *kṣaṃ* is for *namaḥ* on the navel. "May there be my application" (*mamaviniyogaḥ*) is said while forming a hollowed cup with the hands (*karasaṃpuṭa*). *Oṃ aṃ na*. *(Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a liturgical manual detailing the ritual placement of phonemes. The sequence of mantras and their locations follows the standard pattern of Mātṛkā-nyāsa.)*

The *nyāsa* is as follows: *oṃ āṃ* on the palm of the right hand; *oṃ īṃ* on the palm of the left hand; *oṃ uṃ* on the back of the left hand; *oṃ eṃ* on the back of the right hand; *oṃ aiṃ* on the palm of the left hand; *oṃ auṃ* on the palm of the right hand; *oṃ aṃ* on the back of the left hand; and *oṃ aḥ* on the back of the right hand. Then, one should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* by placing the ten vowels—*ṛṃ, ṝṃ, oṃ, ḷṃ, aiṃ, aiṃ, auṃ, aṃ, aḥ*—preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, individually from the right thumb to the left thumb, in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Now, the *sthitinyāsa*: namely, *oṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ namaḥ* on the two thumbs; *oṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ namaḥ* on the two index fingers; *oṃ*... [and so on].

*Sthitinyāsa*: *Aiṃ* on the two middle fingers; *Oṃ Auṃ Auṃ* on the two ring fingers; *Oṃ Aṃ Aḥ* on the two little fingers. *Saṃhāranyāsa*: Beginning from the base of the right index finger and ending at the tip of the left little finger, one should place the letters from *Ka* to *Kṣa*, preceded by *Oṃ* and followed by *Namaḥ*, upon each joint of every finger. *Akṣasūkṣmakaranyāsa*: *Oṃ Aṃ* (16) on the thumb; *Ka* (12) on the index finger; *Ṅa* (10) on the middle finger; *Va* (6) on the ring finger; *Ba* (4) on the little finger.

"Ni-haṃ-kṣaṃ-ka-ra-taḥ"—this is the subtle finger-placement (*sūkṣma-kara-nyāsa*). Having performed the placement on the heart and other limbs in this very manner, one should perform the gross finger-placement (*sthūla-kara-nyāsa*):

Oṃ aṃ kaṃ (5) to the thumbs; Oṃ iṃ caṃ to the index fingers; Oṃ ṭaṃ (5) to the middle fingers; Oṃ paṃ taṃ (5) to the ring fingers; Oṃ aiṃ auṃ (5) to the little fingers; Oṃ aṃ aṃ paṃ (9) aḥ to the palms—this is the finger-placement (*kara-nyāsa*). Oṃ a kaṃ (5) ā haḥ (0)—this [is performed] at the heart with the fingers excluding the thumb.

*Oṃ draṃ caṃ* (590) *śī* (0) *tābhir ekha-śiras-oṃ-oṃ ṭaṃ* (5) *oṃ ūṃ śikhā* (0)—thus, with the fist and the downward-pointing thumb at the place of the crest (*śikhā*); *oṃ eṃ taṃ ro ka ca*—thus, with the fingers of both hands from the throat down to the navel at the place of armor (*kavaca*); *oṃ oṃ paṃ* (5)—thus, with the index, middle, and ring fingers for the three eyes; *oṃ aṃ paṃ* (9) *aḥ astrā* (0)—thus, with the sound of the thumbs and index fingers of both hands in the cardinal directions. This is the Mātṛkā [mantra].

Having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and having bound the flower-offering with the two *taraṃ* mantras, one should perform subtle meditation (*sūkṣmadhyāna*). [One should meditate upon] Mṛtyuñjaya, who stands on the tip of a sword, destroying poison and disease; he resides in the city of the earth (*akṣoṇīpura*), which has the syllable *vaṇā* as its stalk, is surrounded by the directions, possesses a golden stem, and is adorned with the letters of the five groups (*pañcavarga*) moving within its petals, its filaments flashing with pairs of *ṛc*s, and its pericarp marked by the sequence of the three *gaṃ*s. Then, in the mass of nectar...

Having meditated upon the *Kārttikāya* mantra— which is like fresh butter, which has emerged from the heart of Śiva, whose seed-syllable (*bīja*) is situated in the pericarp, whose filaments consist of the eight groups of consonants,
which is surrounded by a square with its seed-syllables and the syllable *bhūti* and adorned with thunderbolts (*vajra*), and which consists of the essence of nectar— upon one's head;
and having raised the *Kuṇḍalinī* from the *Mūlādhāra* by hearing the sound on the path of the *Mūlādhāra*, the *Kuṇḍalinī* power, awakened and resembling a blazing fire, [becomes] subtle...

The wise one should meditate on the form of the Goddess, whose nature is brilliance (*tejas*), shining from the *mūlādhāra* up to the lotus of the head. Through her, the letters of the *mātṛkā*—which have emerged from the head-lotus in the form of a flood of nectar and have entered the *suṣumnā*—should be visualized as having pervaded all things in the form of that very flood. Having thus meditated upon them in their subtle form, one should remain and meditate upon them in their gross form, and then install all those letters of the fifty-fold *mātṛkā*. Thus, having meditated on the subtle form, one should meditate on the gross form of the fifty letters.

I bow my head to her who is depicted in the *Mātṛkā* lotus of the mind—she whose face, arms, feet, belly, and chest are marked by the divisions [of the letters], whose radiant matted hair dishevels the crescent moon, whose jar-like breasts are as white as the moon, jasmine, or a conch, whose excellent hands are drawn in the gesture of granting boons, whose eyes are those of a woman, who sits upon a lotus, who is of pure complexion, and whose heavy hips do not breathe [with exhaustion]. Having thus meditated upon her and worshipped her with the syllables of the alphabet beginning with *Ha Sauṃ* and ending with *Ha Sauṃ*, he [performs the rite]. *Akā...* [The text continues with the sequence of vowels.]

Having performed the three-fold pervasive nyāsa (*trivyāpakanyāsa*) with the letters of the Mātṛkā from *ra* to *kṣa*, and having visualized one's own body as being of that very nature, one should perform the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa followed by the external Mātṛkā-nyāsa. Therein, for the internal Mātṛkā, having visualized a triangle of Śiva at the Brahma-randhra in the head, one should place the sixteen vowels—beginning with *ya*, *ī*, and *u*—on the eastern line starting from the northeast corner (*īśakoṇa*), ending with *ṣoḍaśasvara*. On the southern line starting from the southeast corner (*agnikoṇa*), [one places the consonants], and on the western line in the west (*vāruṇyāṃ*), [the remaining two sets].

In the middle of the triangle at its extremity, one should place *haṃ* at the junctions of the northeast, west, and south. Having meditated upon the sixteen-petaled lotus called Viśuddhi in the throat, one should place [the syllables] *aṃ namaḥ* and so forth on its petals, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise. Then, having meditated upon the twelve-petaled lotus in the heart called Anāhata, which has the letters *ka* through *ṭa* as its doors, one should place *kaṃ namaḥ*, *so'haṃ*, and likewise *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *ṅaṃ*, *caṃ*, *chaṃ*, *jaṃ*, *jhaṃ*, *ñaṃ*.

One should place the twelve syllables beginning with *ṭaṃ* and *ṭhaṃ*. Then, having meditated upon the ten-petalled lotus of the *maṇipūra* as being one's own name, one should place the ten syllables beginning with *ḍaṃ namaḥ so 'haṃ*, followed by *ṭaṃ* (four times), *ṇaṃ* (four times), *taṃ* (four times), *thaṃ* (four times), *daṃ* (four times), *dhaṃ* (four times), *paṃ* (four times), and *phaṃ* (four times). In the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, having meditated upon the six-petalled red lotus, one should place the syllables *baṃ*, *bhaṃ*, *maṃ*, *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, and *laṃ*—conjoined with the central principle (*tatva*)—along with the mantra *namaḥ so 'haṃ*. In the *mūlādhāra*, having meditated upon the four-petalled lotus known as the *ādhāra* as being yellow in color, [one should place the syllables].

*Oṃ syadaleṣu īśādivaṃśaṃ saṃ namaḥ so'ham*—ending thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *tattvas*. Having meditated upon the pure, eight-petaled *ājñācakra* between the eyebrows with a concentrated mind, this is the internal *mātṛkā-nyāsa*. From the *maṇipūra*, one should place [the letters] from *ṭa* to *ṭha*, ending with *nyāhataparyaṃta*; this is the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of internal abiding. From the *ājñācakra*: *tayoda-chavāme haṃ namaḥ so'haṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ so...*

Thus, having meditated upon the syllable *Haṃ* as the space (*ākāśa*) conjoined with the purpose of the *ājñācakra*, and having contemplated the form of the phonemes (*varṇa*) residing there—pervading the entire body—through the contemplation of the unity of Brahman and the Self, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters from *Kṣa* down to *A* in reverse order across the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*). Beginning with *Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ* and ending with *Ityaṃtaḥ saṃhṛtiḥ*, this is the placement within the heart. Furthermore, according to the *Jñānārṇava*, the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (creation placement) and *sthiti-nyāsa* (maintenance placement) should be performed by one established in the state of a householder; however, in the *Vaikhānasa* tradition, they are to be performed by the husband.

"By the placement of the Kuleśvarīs during withdrawal, ending with maintenance (sthiti), it is described as being from creation (sṛṣṭi). Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇuyāmala: 'Withdrawal is for the destruction of enemies; creation is for auspicious creation; and the placement of peace (śānti) is for maintenance. Therefore, the wise should perform this threefold [rite].
Regarding the five-fold Mātṛkā: on the ring finger at the head, 'Oṃ Aṃ Namaḥ'; likewise, on the middle finger at the face, proceeding clockwise..."

With the index, middle, ring, and little fingers [one touches] the two eyes; with the thumb [the two] ears; with the upward-pointing little finger and thumb [the two] nostrils; with the index, middle, and ring fingers [the two] cheeks; with the middle finger [the two] lips; with the ring finger [the two rows of] teeth; with the middle finger [the top of] the head; with the ring and middle fingers [the] face;
and with the little, ring, and middle fingers [the rest of the body].

One should not touch [the letters] with the hands or feet; [place] *sa* and *ṇa* on the two sides of the fire (navel), *ṭa*-group on the back, and *ta*-group on the right hand. Place *pa*-group on the left hand, *ta*-group on the two sides, *pha* and *ba* on the back, and *ma* with the little finger (*kanīṣṭhā*), middle finger (*madhyamā*), and ring finger (*anāmā*) on the navel. With all fingers, place *ya* on the belly; with the palms, place *ra* on the heart.

With all fingers, place *la* on the skin-element (*tvag-dhātu*) at the right shoulder; place *va* on the blood-element (*asṛg-dhātu*) at the back of the neck; and *ma* on the flesh-element (*māṃsa-dhātu*) at the left shoulder. [Place] *ba* on the fat-element (*medas-ātman*).

To the bone-element (asthi-dhātu), preceded by the heart [syllable], on the right hand; to the marrow-element (majjā-dhātu), preceded by the heart, on the left hand; to the semen-element (śukra-dhātu), preceded by the heart, on the right foot; to the life-force-self (prāṇātman), preceded by the heart, on the left foot; to the living-soul-self (jīvātman), preceded by the heart, at the navel; to the supreme-self (paramātman), preceded by the heart, at the mouth. One should perform the pervasion (*vyāpaka*) three times with the Mātṛkā as before. This is the external Mātṛkā-nyāsa. When this nyāsa has been performed, all sins are [removed] from the mantra...

One shall be liberated from sins in three moments; by performing the twilight rituals (*sandhyā*) thrice, one attains the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). If one is capable here, one should perform the tenfold *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of creation and so forth as previously described. If one is incapable, one should perform the two-fold *kalā-nyāsa*.
If even that is impossible, one should first perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) *mātṛkā-nyāsa* for all [mantras], and afterwards perform those [nyāsas] prescribed in the Tantras. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that after the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should perform the *nyāsa*s mentioned in the *Svatantra-tantra*. Now, for the *mūla-mantra-nyāsa*: Then the practitioner, having restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*) upon the root [mantra], [should know] that for this nine-syllabled mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers (*ṛṣi*); Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Anuṣṭubh are the meters (*chandas*); Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī are the deities (*devatā*); Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmari are the seed-syllables (*bīja*); Nandinī, Jālandharī, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā are the powers (*śakti*).

The *ṛṣis* are Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya; the *tattvas* are the divisions [of the mantra]. For the sake of attaining desired success, this is the *viniyoga* for recitation (*japa*). Now, for the *ṛṣyādi* (assignment of seers and so forth):

with the fingers excluding the thumbs, one says "Obeisance to the seers Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra" at the head; "Obeisance to the meters Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Anuṣṭubh" at the mouth; "Obeisance to the deity Mahākālī" at the heart; and "Obeisance to the seed-syllables Raktadaṃtikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmari" at the private parts. The feet [are assigned to the weapon-syllable].

One should perform the three-fold pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) for the two days [of the fortnight] using the mantras of Nandajā, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā from the *Śaktis*, and for the *Sarvāṅga* [placement], one should use Agni and Sūrya from the *Tattvas*.

One should perform the eleven placements (*nyāsa*) starting with: *Oṃ hrīṃ aṃ namaḥ* on the head, and so on, ending with *kṣaṃ* in the state of the deceased (*mṛtakāvasthā*). By performing this sixfold placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), a person attains the form of the Deity. This is the first placement. *Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ* on the little finger... [and so forth].

To the two little fingers (4), to the two ring fingers (4), to the two middle fingers (4), to the two index fingers (4), to the two thumbs (4), to the palms and backs of the hands (4), to the two wrists (4), to the two elbows (4)—*namaḥ* to the heart (4), *svāhā* to the head (4), *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (4), *huṃ* to the armor (4), *oṃ vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes (4), *phaṭ* to the weapon. When this Sārasvata nyāsa has been performed, all obstacles perish. Thus ends the Sārasvata nyāsa.
With a companion: *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutations to Brāhmī—may she protect [me] in the east; salutations to Māheśvarī—may she protect [me] in the southeast;

salutations to Kaumārī—may she protect [me] in the south; salutations to Vaiṣṇavī—may she protect [me] in the southwest; salutations to Vārāhī—may she protect [me] in the west; salutations to Indrāṇī—may she protect [me] in the northwest;

salutations to Cāmuṇḍā—may she protect [me] in the north; salutations to Mahālakṣmī—may she protect [me] in the northeast; salutations to Vyomeśvarī—may she protect [me] in the zenith; salutations to Saptadvīpeśvarī—may she protect [me] in the nadir.
*Oṃ*, salutations to Pātukāmā; salutations to Īśvarī, may she protect me on the ground. In this third *nyāsa* performed, one shall become victorious in the three worlds.

Thus ends the third group of Mothers. *Oṃ*, may Anandajā, holding a lotus and a goad, protect my front limb. *Oṃ*, may Raktadaṃtikā, with a sword in her hand, protect my right side. *Oṃ*, may Kṣākaṃbharī, adorned with flowers and sprouts, protect my west. *Oṃ*, may Durgā, with four arrows in her hands, protect my north.

May she who is terrifying with her head, bowl, and hands protect [me] from the top of the head down to the feet; may Bhrāmarī, bearing variegated luster, protect from the feet up to the crown of the head. The man who performs this *yaṃ-nyāsa* is liberated from old age and death. Thus ends the fourth, the Ṣaḍdevī-nyāsa. May Brahmā protect from the feet up to the navel; from the navel... [the rest of the text is missing].

May Janārdana protect the head up to the neck; may Hari, who consists of all bliss, protect the two parts of the body beyond that. In this fifth Nyāsa dedicated to Brahmā and the others, may one obtain all auspiciousness. Thus ends the fifth Nyāsa of Brahmā and the rest. May Mahālakṣmī with eighteen arms protect the middle;
