may Mahāsarasvatī with eight arms protect the upper part; may Mahākālī with ten arms protect the lower part; may Siṃha protect the two hands; and may Paramahaṃsa protect the eyes.

May Maheśa, joined with Caṇḍikā, protect both feet as he rides upon his divine buffalo; may he protect every limb. By performing this Nyāsa on the sixth day, a person shall attain the state of Sadāśiva. Thus ends the Lakṣmyādi-nyāsa. Oṃ Aiṃ Namaḥ to the Brahma-randhra (the aperture at the crown of the head).
Oṃ Hrīṃ Namaḥ to the right eye. Oṃ Klīṃ Namaḥ to the left eye. Oṃ Cāṃ Namaḥ to the right ear. Oṃ Muṃ Namaḥ to the left ear. Oṃ Ḍāṃ Namaḥ to the right nostril.

*Oṃ ya~ namaḥ* on the left nostril; *oṃ viṃ namaḥ* on the mouth; *oṃ cc~ namaḥ* on the anus—one should perform the seventh placement (*nyāsa*) thus. When this seventh placement is performed in direct order (*anuloma*), there shall be imperishability. This is the seventh placement in direct order. *Oṃ cc~ namaḥ* on the anus; *oṃ viṃ namaḥ* on the mouth; *oṃ ya~ namaḥ* on the left nostril; *oṃ ḍāṃ namaḥ* on the right nostril; *oṃ muṃ namaḥ* on the left ear; *oṃ cā~ namaḥ* on the right ear; *oṃ klīṃ namaḥ* on the left [ear].

"Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ to the eyes; namaḥ to the right [eye]; when this eighth nyāsa is performed in the *brahmarandhra*, all suffering is destroyed. Thus ends the eighth practice in reverse order. "Aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutations to Cāmuṇḍā, the All-pervading One (*vicce*). One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) from the head to the feet and from the feet to the head, thinking: "May the eastern limb be protected. Likewise, from the head to the feet and from the feet to the head, one should perform the pervasive placement for the southern limb, thinking: "May [the southern limb] be protected. (9) Head... (0) ...feet.
May the pervasive [deity] protect the left limb; may the pervasive [deity] protect the right limb. "The other [mantra] is made by the root-mantra; salutation is made to the attainment of the deity.

Thus is the *nyāsa* of the nine corners (*koṇava*) consisting of the nature of mantra-pervasion. Heart (9), Head (9), Crest (9), Armor (9), Eyes (9), Weapon (0). When this tenth *nyāsa* has been performed, the three worlds shall come under one's control. Thus is the tenth *nyāsa* with the root-mantra. [Kṣetrapālas: Khaḍginī, Śūlinī, Ghorā, Gadinī, Cakrinī...

O Goddess who holds the conch, the bow, the arrow, and the *bhuśuṇḍī* and *parigha* weapons; O most gentle one among all gentle beings, you are exceedingly beautiful. You alone are the Supreme Sovereign (*Parameśvarī*), the highest among the high and the low. Whatever object exists anywhere—whether real or unreal, O Soul of All—you are that power (*śakti*) of it all; so why do you praise me? By you the world was created, by you the world is protected, and even he who governs the world is under the sway of your sleep (*nidrā*).

Who indeed would be capable of praising you? Maheśvara, Viṣṇu, and I myself have been made to assume bodies by you; therefore, who could possibly have the power to praise you? Having meditated upon this five-fold *ślīpa* (the syllable *Hrīm*), which is drawn from the letters and is the very form of Mahākālī, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) so as to pervade all limbs, protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambikā; protect us with the sound of your bell, and with the bowstring.
By your roar, protect us in the east; O Caṇḍikā, protect us in the west; by the whirling of your trident, protect us in the south;
and likewise, O Sovereign Lady, with those gentle forms and those terrible forms fashioned throughout the three worlds, protect us from all sides.
O Vike, with the sword, the trident, the mace, and other weapons held in your lotus-like hands, protect us in this world. (Thus ends the four verses.)

Having meditated upon that which resembles the rising sun, the very form of Mahālakṣmī, one should place it pervading all limbs: "O Goddess who possesses all forms, who is the sovereign of all, and who is endowed with all powers; O Durge, protect us from fear! O Goddess, salutations to you! This gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes—O Kātyāyanī, may it protect us from all terrors! Salutations to you! [This] trident, extremely fierce and formidable with its flames, [is held by] the destroyer of all the beautiful asuras."

Salutations to you, O Bhadrakālī, who are terrifying to those who fall [into sin]; salutations to you who destroy the splendor of the Daityas by filling the world with your roar. O Goddess, may your bell protect us from evils; salutations to you who are like a mother to her sons. May your radiant hand, smeared with blood and mud, be for our welfare—O Caṇḍikā, we bow to you. Having meditated upon the entire form of the Great Asura-slayer, which resembles pure crystal, one should recite these five verses.

One should place the pervasive [mantra]: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Taḥ Hrīṃ* for the head (*śiras*), *Klīṃ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *Cāmuṇḍāyai* for the armor (*kavaca*), and *Vicce* for the eye (*netra*). With the root-mantra, one places the weapon (*astra*).

*Oṃ Aiṃ Namaḥ* on the crest-lock; *Oṃ Hrīṃ Namaḥ* on the right eye; *Oṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Namaḥ* on the left eye; *Oṃ Cāṃ Namaḥ* on the right ear; *Oṃ Suṃ Namaḥ* on the left ear; *Oṃ Ḍāṃ Namaḥ* on the right nostril; *Oṃ Yai Namaḥ* on the left nostril; *Oṃ Viṃ Namaḥ* on the right cheek; *Oṃ Maṃ Namaḥ* [on the left cheek].

*Oṃ ḍāṃ namaḥ* on the left ear; *oṃ yai namaḥ* on the right nostril; *viṃ namaḥ* on the left nostril; *ce namaḥ* on the mouth; [and] *naḥ* on the anus. Then, having meditated upon the form from the head to the feet and from the feet to the head as pervading the root-mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) over all limbs: *Aiṃ* at the heart, *Hrīṃ* at the head, *Klīṃ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Having performed this once, and having performed the eleven-fold placement (*ekādaśa-nyāsa*), the three worlds shall become subject to one's power. Thus ends the eleven-fold [placement].

Now, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Yoga-pīṭha: Having meditated upon one’s own body as the Yoga-pīṭha—conceived here as having four legs at the two sides of the face and a body conceived in the middle—one should perform the placement. At the *ādhāra*: "Oṃ Maṃ, svāhā to Maṇḍūkāya. At the navel: "To Kālāgnirudra, who is the primordial source (*mūlaprakṛti*). At the heart: "To Ādhāraśakti; there itself, to Prakṛti, to Kūrma, to Ananta, to Varāha, and to Pṛthivī."

Oṃ! To the great sacrificial hearth (mekha) of the salt ocean; to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) consisting of a jewel-maṇḍala; to the jewel-altar (vedikā); to the jewel-lion throne (siṃhāsana). One should place [the following] upon the heart: to Dharma, red in color, in the form of a bull, on the right thigh; to Adharma, dark green in color, in the form of a lion-throne, on the left thigh; to Jñāna, yellow in color, the source of all beings, on the left knee; to Vairāgya, like sapphire (indranīla), at the navel; and to Avairāgya, on the right knee.

"For sovereignty"—thus [are the mantras for] the deities residing on the seats (pīṭhas), beginning with Agni and the others, who are to be meditated upon with their previously mentioned forms and colors: for unrighteousness (adharma) on the left side of the face; for ignorance (ajñāna) at the navel; for lack of dispassion (avairāgya) on the right side; and for lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya). These are the Gāyatrīs of the seats. [Then the mantras for] the central [deities]: for Māyā; for the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti); for Ananta, who is endowed with seven coils and possesses a thousand hoods; and in the center of that, above the hood, for the bulb of bliss (ānanda-kanda), for consciousness (saṃvit)...

Salutation to the stalk consisting of all principles (*sarvatattva*), to the petals which are the nature of the [eight] lower realms (*apāya-prakṛti*), and to the filaments consisting of transformations (*vikāra*). Salutation to the pericarp enriched with the fifty seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the center of the lotus. Within that lotus-center, salutation to the solar disc (*arka-maṇḍala*) consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*); *Oṃ*, to the lunar disc (*soma-maṇḍala*) consisting of sixteen digits; *Oṃ*, to the fiery disc (*vahni-maṇḍala*) consisting of ten digits; *Saṃ*, to the quality of purity (*sattva*) whose nature is awakening; *Raṃ*, to the quality of passion (*rajas*) whose nature is intense activity; *Taṃ*, to the quality of darkness (*tamas*)... [the text ends].

One should place [the mantras] upon each [of the petals] everywhere as follows: *Hrīṃ* to the Self (Ātman) on the right; *Aṃ* to the Inner Self (Antarātman) in the west; *Puṃ* to the Supreme Self (Parātman) in the north; *Hrīṃ* to the Individual Self (Nātman) in the east; and *Kaṃ* to the principle of Kalā, *Viṃ* to the principle of Vidyā, *Paṃ* to the principle of Para, and *Maḥ* to the principle of Pradhāna in the center. Then, one should contemplate the nine Śaktis in the eight petals and the pericarp, starting from the east.

With dexterity, [one should worship] Oṃjayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Mityavilāsinī, Aghorā, Maṅgalā, and in the center, likewise, Śrī Mahākālī. These eight Śaktis—granting boons and fearlessness, holding lotuses, and red in color—are to be meditated upon. Then, having performed the eight-fold pervasive sprinkling (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, and having bound the "tortoise-like" hands together with flowers, one should meditate on the six [limbs].

Wielding in her hands a sword, arrows, a bow, a mace, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī*, a skull-topped weapon, and a conch; three-eyed and adorned with ornaments on all her limbs, the lotus-born Brahmā praised Mahākālī—who had ten feet and faces as dark as a sapphire—as she was about to slay the sleeping Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

Having thus meditated upon Mahākālī, [one should visualize her] holding a sword, a discus, an arrow, a skull, and a conch in the right hands in sequence, and a mace, a club, a bow, and a trident in the left.

Having displayed those mudrās, beginning with the *bhuśuṇḍī*, one should then meditate upon Mahālakṣmī: "One should worship her who possesses the radiance of coral, who stands upon a lotus, who tramples an elephant, and who holds in her hands a garland, an axe, a goad, arrows, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a *dhenu* (cow), a staff, a spear, a sword, a shield, a conch, a bell, a wine-vessel, a trident, a noose, and the *sudarśana* discus—this is Mahālakṣmī. Having thus meditated upon Mahālakṣmī, [one should perform] the *akṣamālā*...

One should display these mudrās in the right hands: a lotus, arrow, sword, vajra, mace, discus, and water-pot; and in the left hands: a bell, axe, thunderbolt, staff, shield, trident, bow, noose, and vessel. Then, one should meditate upon Mahāsarasvatī, who holds a bell, trident, plough, conch, mallet, discus, bow, and arrows in her lotus-hands; whose radiance is like the cool-rayed moon shining at the end of the clouds; and who emerged from the body of Gaurī to protect the three worlds.

"I worship that Sarasvatī, the primordial great source, the support of all, who destroys the hosts of demons such as Śumbha. Having thus meditated upon Mahāsarasvatī, one should display the hand-gestures (*mudrās*) corresponding to her weapons: a conch, mace, discus, and arrow in the right hands, and a bell, trident, plow, and bow in the left.

Here, the sequence of weapons differs according to the specific *tantra*, as the secret tradition prescribes a sequence starting from the right. Now, one should worship with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*). As long as...
"I am indeed that very Jīva-Brahman, offering the 'I'-consciousness"—the knowers of Yoga know this alone to be the meditation on the Nirguṇa.

Thus, O Goddess, having meditated upon the Heart, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the feet of the Goddess, who resides right there within the vessel of Kuṇḍalinī. Having worshipped the mind with thousands of delightful ornaments, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) into the mouth; and from the secret support (*guhādhāra*), one should unite Kuṇḍalinī with the face of Sadāśiva.

Having contemplated the state of *sāmarasya* (unified equilibrium) which has been made to flow forth by the nectar from the multitude of lotus-feet [of the Guru], and having bathed oneself by sprinkling that nectar upon one's own body, one should meditate thus. At this time, the union of Śiva and Śakti arises from the *mūlādhāra*; dissolving for a short while into *samādhi*, one performs the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) with "Oṃ. One should then satisfy [the deities] with that nectar produced from the digits (*kalā*) of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, which have flowed down intensely during the union of Śiva and Śakti.

The offering of water for the feet consists of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). The wise know the ten flowers to be: freedom from illusion (*amāyā*), absence of ego (*anahaṅkāra*), absence of death (*amaraṇa*), absence of delusion (*amoha*), absence of pride (*amada*), absence of hypocrisy (*adambha*), absence of fear (*abhaya*), absence of hatred (*adveṣa*), absence of envy (*akṣābhaka*), and absence of greed (*alobha*). Furthermore, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the supreme flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower;

compassion (*dayā*) is a flower; forgiveness (*kṣamā*) is a flower; and knowledge (*jñāna*) is the fifth flower. Having worshipped with these fifteen flowers, [one should offer] the sound of the unstruck resonance (*anāhata-dhvani*).

Sounding the *yīṃ* bell, he visualizes incense in the form of wind, a lamp in the form of fire, and then, for the purpose of the food offering (*naivedya*), he visualizes nectar, intellect, mountains of various side-dishes (*vyañjana*) along with foods to be chewed,

eaten, sucked, and licked, mountains of various cakes (*pūpa*) and the like, and mountains of heaps of sugar; as well as the crescent moon, its root, the sky, the fly-whisk (*cāmara*), the moon-umbrella, the sun, a mirror, a lotus, a girdle, and a radiant necklace of bliss.

Having fashioned [the image] in one's mind, one should please the Supreme Goddess with dances, songs, and food offerings arising from the sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which are like a stage for the dance of the mind. One should perform the offering of worship, the presentation of food, and the recitation (*japa*), saying: "Welcome, O God of gods! O Goddess, remain firm! O Caṇḍikā, accept this mental worship; it is offered according to what is fitting. Then, having performed the recitation one hundred and eight times with the rosary, one should offer the recitation with the mantra beginning with "O Guhya... while remaining mentally focused.

One should perform the *homa* in the triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) at the *mūlādhāra*. Having kindled the fire, which is the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and consists of both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), one should offer oblations there into that fire with a ladle (*sruva*) from which the clarified butter (*ājya*) flows well. Therein, having reflected deeply, one should offer the oblation of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, saying: "I offer this oblation of ignorance; *svāhā*! In this manner, having offered nine oblations for falsehood, backbiting, lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, one should then proceed with the worship and other rites.

O Mother of the Universe, that which was created by the gods became drinkable through your grace; you are the refuge. Having been told, "Offer the splendor that has entered the path of the breath," he remained at that very moment, becoming one with That, consisting of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. Having thus performed the propitiation, one becomes directly identical with Brahman;

for such a person, there are no flowers or sins, and they certainly become liberated while living. This is the yoga; thereafter, having prepared the *Sarvatobhadra* diagram upon the altar, [one should proceed].
Oṃ. Having established [the vessel] according to the ritual for the deities and having worshipped it, one should touch the ground in the middle above that with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ";
then, having placed the seven grains with the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ sīmataḥ," one should place a water-pot (kalaśa)—either made of gold, silver, copper, or clay—into the pot.

As for the characteristics of the pot, the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states: "Those made of gold, silver, copper, or clay should possess the required characteristics. [This concludes] the mantra for the installation of the marriage ceremony.

For the consecration (abhiṣecana), one should obtain a water-pot (kalaśa) with a spout of ten finger-breadths; for nourishment (puṣṭi), it should be ten finger-breadths [in height]; for elevation (utsedha), sixteen finger-breadths; twelve finger-breadths thick at the base; eight finger-breadths at the mouth-opening; and fifteen finger-breadths wide at the middle. According to the *Padārthādarśa*, however: "Because this was fashioned by Viśvakarman for the gods, and since it is a vessel (kalaśa) for the deities, it is called a *kalaśa*. Thus says Padmapādācārya.

Having filled the *kalaśa* (water-pot) with water using the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," having added fragrance with "gaṃdhadvārām," all medicinal herbs with "oṣadhīḥ," *dūrvā* grass from every joint with "kāṇḍātkāṇḍāt," five sprouts with "aśvatthe vo niṣadanam," seven types of grain with "syonā pṛthivi," fruit with "tyāḥ phalinīḥ," gems with "sa hi ratnāni," and gold with "hiraṇyarūpaḥ," and having cast [these] into it... [he should recite] "cakṣuḥ."

Having wrapped it with a cloth dyed with *vāsā* and *āsava*, and having placed a thick vessel full of grain upon it, one should draw a diagram there—either on a copper plate or a stone—with a stylus (*śalākā*). As follows:

a dot, a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a circle, and a twenty-four-spoked wheel, along with the earth-diagram (*bhūgraha*). Within that earth-diagram, in the outer ring, starting from the northeast and proceeding to the east, and then in the intermediate directions and so forth, one should draw three sets of eight triangles in the eight intermediate directions.

Having fashioned sixty-three triangular [sections] for the *vaṃcata* [diagram], and having thus drawn the *yantra*, one should place it in a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*). Then, having performed the invocation of fire (*agnyutthāpana*) over the previously mentioned image, one should establish it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and set it down below. Thereafter, one should perform the external worship: having placed a water-pitcher (*kalaśa*) to one's left and having fashioned a triangle within a square, one should worship [the base] with "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti" and then place the *arghya* vessel upon that, together with its stand (*sādhāra*).

Having filled [the vessel] with water and offered fragrance and other items, one should invoke the *tīrtha* from the solar orb using the *Gaṅge ca* mantra and the *kuśa-mudrā*. Then, having consecrated it eight times with the *praṇava*, one should transform it into nectar using the *dhenu-mudrā*. This is the installation of the conch (*śaṅkha-pratiṣṭhā*). Next, sprinkling the materials for worship and oneself with that water, one should place the vessels for the *pādya*, *arghya*, *ācamana*, *madhuparka*, and the bath (*snāna*) to the north of that, like the conch. Now...

One should establish one of the five [vessels] beginning with *vāpa*. To its north, having fashioned a square, a circle, a six-cornered figure (*ṣaṭkoṇa*), a triangle in its center, and a dot (*bindu*), and having inscribed these with conch-water, one should worship them with "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti and the others. Then, in the square, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, [one should worship]: *Oṃ* to Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha, Uḍḍiyāna-pīṭha, Kāmarūpa-pīṭha, and Ṣa...

Having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the [six] corners, the root mantra in the central triangle, and the primary triangle with the root mantra, one should say, "I establish the special *arghya* vessel for Śrī Mahākālī," and with *phaṭ*, having placed the tripod (*tripādikā*) which has been washed, one should worship the ten fire-calorific powers (*vahni-daśakalā*) there in a counter-clockwise direction: *yaṃ* to Dhūmrārcis, *rūṣmā* to Ūṣmā, *laṃ* to Jvālinī, *śāṃ* to Visphuliṅginī, *ṣaṃ* to Śuci, *saṃ* to Surūpā, *haṃ*...

Having worshipped [the goddesses] with "Oṃ Kapilāyai," "Oṃ Laṃ Havyavāhāyai," and "Oṃ Kṣaṃ Kavyavāhāyai," and having worshipped the center of the fire-mandala with "Oṃ Maṃ Vaṃ Vahnimaṇḍalāya Daśakalātmane," one should place the arghya vessel—
which has been washed with "Tadūpa Riphaṭ"— therein, and worship the twelve kalās of the Sun there in counter-clockwise order (vāmāvarta):
Kaṃ Bhaṃ Tāpinyai, Khaṃ Baṃ Tāpinyai, Gaṃ Phaṃ Dhūmrāyai, Ghaṃ Paṃ Marīcyai, Ṅaṃ Naṃ Jvālinyai, Caṃ Dhaṃ Rucyai, Chaṃ Daṃ Suṣumṇāyai, Jaṃ...

Having worshipped Thaṃ to Thaṃbhogadāyai, Jñaṃ to Jñaṃtaviṇvāyai, Śaṃ to Śaṃṇaṃbodhinyai, Ṭaṃ to Ṭaṃḍhaṃdhāriṇyai, Ṭhaṃ to Ṭhaṃḍaṃkṣamāyai, and in the center Jaṃ with "Jaṃ Arkamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane," one should then fill the special *arghya* vessel for Śrī Caṇḍikā with water from the pitcher using the root mantra and the reverse-order Mātṛkā beginning with 'A' and ending with 'Ha', saying: "I fill the special *arghya* vessel for Śrī Caṇḍikā. Then, one should worship the sixteen digits (*kalās*) of the Moon, starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise, beginning with: "Aṃ Amṛtā... [and so on].

*Tāṃ* (to her), *namaḥ* (salutation); to *Ānandā*, *Iṃ* (to *Pūṣā*), *Ī* (to *Tuṣṭi*), *I* (to *Ṛti*), *Ṛ* (to *Ūdhi*), *Ṝ* (to *Śaśinī*), *Ḷ* (to *Caṇḍikā*), *Ḹ* (to *Kālī*), *Aiṃ* (to *Jyotsnā*), *Aiṃ* (to *Śrī*), *Oṃ* (to *Prīti*), *Auṃ* (to *Aṅgadā*), *Aṃ* (to *Pūrṇā*), *Aḥ* (to *Pūrṇāmṛtā*), *Oṃ* (to *Yamā*), *Oṃ* (to *Madhyā*), *Oṃ* (to the *Soma-maṇḍala*, the essence of the sixteen *kalās*). Having thus worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, and having prepared the *arghya* offering with the mantra beginning "O Gaṅgā... and so forth, [one should perform the *kuśa* rite].

Having invoked the holy water (*tīrtha*) from the solar maṇḍala with the *mudrā*, one should envelop it with the syllable *huṃ*. Protecting it with the *astra-mantra* by means of finger-snaps (*choṭikā*), one should perform the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the six-limbed mantra and transform it into nectar with the *vam* syllable. Having shown the *dhenu-mudrā*, the *amṛta-mudrā*, and the *śaṅkha-cakra-mudrā*, one should place the five offering vessels for the *laṭaka-yoginīs* and all spirits in sequence like a conch shell, using the *accha-mudrā*. If one is unable [to do this], [the following applies].

Or else, one should arrange twelve vessels in this manner; if unable to do so, five [should be used]: the conch, the *pādya*, the special *arghya*, the *bali*, and the *sāmānyārghya*. If unable to do even that, three [should be used]: the conch, the special *arghya*, and the *bali* vessel. Among these, for the *pādya* there should be *dūrvā* grass, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and leaves of *śyāmāka*;
for the *arghya*, fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, tips of *kuśa* grass, mustard seeds, barley, and *dūrvā*; and for the *ācamanīya*, nutmeg and camphor.

Lavaṅga (cloves), madhuparka, curd, and honey—these are placed in water. Having poured a little *arghya* water into them, one should consecrate them with the root mantra while visualizing a pure seal (*mudrā*). Next is the placement of the second vessel. Then, upon the previously drawn *yantra* in the *kīrṇakā* [area], one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) in the full vessel.
Therein, to the right of the Goddess, one worships: *yaṃ* to the Gurus, *yaṃ* to the Paramagurus, *yaṃ* to the Parātparagurus, and *yaṃ* to the Parameṣṭhis.

To the Gurus established from beginningless time (Oṃ); to the Gurus who are the former teachers (Oṃ); to the Goddess on the left (Oṃ); to Gaṇapati on the right (Oṃ); to Sarasvatī, the consort of Brahmā, on the right (Oṃ); to Durgā, the Goddess of the navel, on the left (Oṃ); to Kṣetrapāla on the left side (Oṃ); to Vāstupuruṣa on the right side (Oṃ); to Caṇḍī in her own form in front (Oṃ); at the base: Oṃ Maṃ, salutation to Maṇḍūka; Oṃ Kaṃ, salutation to Kalāgnirudra; to Mūlaprakṛti; to Ādhāraśakti; to Prakṛti...

Having thus worshipped those [deities]: to Kūrma, Ananta, Varāha, Pṛthivī, the Ocean of Milk, Śvetadvīpa, Mahāmeru, the Jewel Pavilion, the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, the Jewel Altar, and the Jewel Lion-throne; then, in that [mandala], from the southeast to the northeast, one should worship in the intermediate directions:
Dharma, who is red-colored and has the form of a bull; Jñāna, who is dark-colored and has the form of a lion-throne; and Bhūta, who is yellow-colored.

Oṃ! To Kāra; to Vairāgya; to him who has the luster of sapphire; to the one in the form of an elephant; to the Lord endowed with the seven coils of the serpent; to Ananta, who possesses a thousand hoods—thus, in the center of the *pīṭha-gāyatrī*, one should arrange a binding silken thread. Upon the central hood, [one worships] Ānandaka, the giver of bliss; to the stalk of consciousness; to the lotus-throne of all; to the petals of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); to the filaments beginning with the syllable *ki*; to the five... [etc.]
To the pericarp enriched with the six seed-syllables; (0) Oṃ, to the solar orb consisting of twelve kalās; (0) Oṃ, to the lunar orb consisting of sixteen kalās;

maṃ, to the fire orb consisting of ten kalās; (0) saṃ, to Sattva, whose nature is awakening; (0) raṃ, to Rajas, whose nature is primordial matter (prakṛti); (0) taṃ, to Tejas, whose nature is the Moon; thus having worshipped in the center of the seat, [one worships] on the seat in the directions starting from the east: Ātman, Antarātman, Parā...

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with "namas" for the Self (*ātman*), the Principle of Illusion (*māyā-tattva*), and likewise again for the Principle of the Self (*ātma-tattva*), the Principle of Limited Agency (*kalā-tattva*), and the Supreme Principle (*para-tattva*). Then, on the eight petals, proceeding clockwise starting from the east: Oṃ to Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityāvilāsinī, Dogdhī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā; and in the center, to Ṛddhi. Therein, [is] Śrī.

To the Goddess Mahākālī, whose nature is the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), these eight powers (śaktis) are offered as her throne. They are red in color, bestowing boons, and holding lotuses; they should be meditated upon. Having tied the eight-fold root-thread (mūla-sūtra) as before, and having meditated on the collection of flowers in the water-vessel, one should visualize [the deity] in the form of light (tejas) entering through the path of the breath. Then, taking those flowers in the water-vessel, one should invoke her into the presence.

"O Mother, whose form is the bliss of the internal cause beyond all worlds; O Supreme Goddess, who acts for the welfare of all beings; O Queen of Gods, easily attained through devotion, accompanied by Your retinue—remain steadfast as long as I worship You.
Having thus visualized the Goddess in the form of light, one should display the *āvāhana* (invocation) and other mudrās to Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī.

"Come here! Stay here! Be present! Be near! Face me!"—having performed these five [steps] beginning with the invocation, and having displayed the *mudrās*, and having performed the rites of *sakalīkaraṇa*, *paramīkaraṇa*, and *amṛtīkaraṇa* while displaying the *yoni-mudrā*, [one recites]: *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kro yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ mahākālabhyaḥ praṇā iha prāṇāḥ | Oṃ haṃ mahākālabhyaḥ jīva iha sthitaḥ | Oṃ haṃ mahākālabhyaḥ sarvendriyāṇi | Oṃ haṃ...*

"O great [deities] of speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and breath, come here and remain for a long time in happiness; Svāhā! Having thus performed the ritual installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), he held a sword, arrow, mace, trident, conch, discus, *ṛṣuṇḍi*, iron club, bow, and heads dripping with blood. In this manner, according to the sequence taught in the secret [tantras], he displayed the mudrās, as well as a rosary, a lotus, an arrow, a thunderbolt, and a mace.

One should display these mudrās in sequence: the discus, trident, axe, conch, bell, noose, spear, staff, shield, bow, drinking vessel, and water-pot. Likewise, one should display the mudrās of the arrow, mace, sword, discus, shield, conch, bell, plough, and bow according to the secret order mentioned, starting from the lower right hand. Then, [one should meditate on the Goddess] who has four arms, three eyes, and bestows boons and fearlessness.

[One should meditate on] the Goddess who wears red garments, the Great Goddess who bestows boons; [reciting] "Hiraṇyavarṇā," at the end of the root mantra, [one says] "Salutation to Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī. One should announce the invocation with "Salutation, I offer [this]," and present flowers and other offerings. One should pour out the water from the conch. In this same manner everywhere [one should worship her] who resembles molten gold, the lotus-eyed one, the bestower of boons, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, the Great Sovereign Caṇḍikā.

O Āmā Mahākālī, I prepare this seat for you; may the Blessed One be seated here. Having placed the flower-seat on the left side and displayed the *āsana-mudrā*, one should prostrate. Having greeted her with "Welcome! and inquired after her well-being with "Are you well?", [one should worship] the auspicious Great Goddess, who holds a sword, a trident, and a mace in her hands, bestows fearlessness, is mounted upon an elephant, and grants all sovereignty—[this is] for Aśvapūjāmatī... this white [garment]... Anā...

Having placed the two feet with the *māṅguṣṭha* (thumb-toe) yoga and displayed the *pādya* mudrā, one should worship the Great Goddess Vidhādharā, Yamā, Kṣī, Lokanāyakī, and the Great Goddess endowed with all sovereignty (*sarvaiśvarya*). Having offered the *arghya* with the mantra "Kāṃso'smi śū... tyai eṣo'rghyaḥ svāhā," and having offered the *arghya* with the *mudrā*, [one worships] the Goddess who grants various boons, the delightful Nārāyaṇī, Mahālakṣmī, the Infinite One (*Nantā*), the beloved of Viṣṇu, and Candā.

Having offered water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) into the mouth with the mantra *mūla-mantra* and *idam ācamanīyaṃ namaḥ svadhā*, he should present the gesture of sipping (*ācamana-mudrā*). Then, having offered the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) combined with curd, honey, and clarified butter, mixed with sugar and jaggery, he says: "O Supreme Goddess, accept this *madhuparka*; be gracious. Having offered the *madhuparka* to the consort of the *mūla-mantra* with the *madhuparka-mudrā*, he should again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Then, having performed the cleansing bath (*malasnāna*), he should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) using Vedic mantras, and then perform a bath with pure water in another vessel.

One should perform the *Vājapeya* [recitation] one thousand, one hundred, or twenty-eight times of the eight-verse hymn beginning with "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe," the fifteen verses beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇām," the fourteen-verse hymn beginning with "Iyam adāt," the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Suvarṇadharma-anuvāka*, and the *Mahāyusvidyā* along with its root mantra.
Then, [one should meditate on] the Great Goddess, who is radiant, subtle in form, three-eyed, mounted upon a lion, and who has bathed; [offering] this [oblation] to Mūmā.

I offer a bath; again, I offer water for sipping (ācamana). To the goddesses who bestow various supernatural powers, who are enchanting with manifold virtues, and who grant various merits—O Goddess, I offer two garments. [To the goddess] whose color is like the sun, who is the mother of the world, this garment... [to her] who resembles molten gold, who holds a lotus, and who grants boons—I have offered this sacred thread (upavīta);
accept it, O Supreme Sovereign. Come to me, O Mother; [this is] the sacred thread; the sacred thread, the giver of joy; [to] the Mother.

Having adorned [the deity] with ornaments such as a single-kaṇṭha necklace and a crown, and having offered the mudrā; and having offered fragrance consisting of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and yellow pigment (rocanā), along with perfumes such as musk; and having offered the mudrā for the removal of hunger, thirst, and fatigue; then, having offered five handfuls of flowers with the root mantra upon the head, heart, secret place, feet, and all limbs, one should perform the worship of the enclosures (*varaṇapūjā*). O Goddess, this is the supreme nectar within the three-fold contemplation.
"O beloved of Taruci, this is for the worship of the retinue of the Great Caṇḍī by command. Having received this command, one should worship with flowers or unbroken grains (akṣata).

One should contemplate that in the six corners—in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Indra, Vāyu, the center, and the [western] direction—the presiding deities have emerged from the body of the Goddess as the attendant deities (varaṇadevatā).
These principal female deities possess the luster of frost, crystal, dark blue, black, and reddish-brown, and they hold the gestures of granting boons (varada) and fearlessness (abhaya).

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ naṃdajāyai hṛdayāya namaḥ; I worship the heart-śakti śrīpādukā, namaḥ*. In this same manner for all [limbs]: *Oṃ raktadaṃtikāyai śirase svāhā* (Heart: Śiras-śakti); *Oṃ śākaṃbharyai śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (Heart: Śikhā-śakti); *Oṃ durgāyai kavacāya huṃ* (Heart: Kavaca-śakti); *Oṃ bhīmāyai netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (Heart: Netra-śakti); *Oṃ bhrāmaryai astrāya phaṭ* (Heart: Astra-śakti). *A*.

One should perform the libation with the special *arghya* water, saying: "I satisfy the Weapon [deity], the Heart Goddess. In this same manner for all [the other limbs]: from the Head Goddess, the Tuft Goddess, the Armor Goddess, the Eye Goddess, and the Weapon Goddess. Then, taking flowers and the special *arghya* water in the palm of the right hand with the *tāna-mudrā*, one should offer them with devotion, saying: "O You who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the attainment of my desired goal; I offer this to You as the first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*)."

"Obeisance to [Name] together with the six-limbed enclosure"—having thus offered a flower at the feet in the southeast, there is an *ūha* (modification) at the beginning of the worship of the first enclosure.
This concludes the first enclosure. Then, in the drop (*bindu*) in the center of the triangle, worshipping the *śrīpādukā* at the end of the root mantra:
"Obeisance to Vidhātṛ in the eastern corner of the triangle; to Dhātrī-Śrī in the southwest; to Viṣṇu together with Śrī in the northwest; and to [the deity] accompanied by Umā in the north."

To Śiva, to the lion of the illustrious learned Śiva-Śrī, and to the buffalo of the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti—to the buffalo, the fulfillment of all desires—having thus offered [the worship], this is the second enclosure (dvitīyāvaraṇa). Now, in the center of the triangle, from the northwest (vāyavya) to the northeast (īśa), one should worship the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti). One should meditate upon them as being adorned with beautiful red garlands and excellent ornaments, well-adorned, seated upon lotus-thrones, all established in the yoga of support (ālambana-yoga), and possessing complete sovereignty.
Having meditated thus upon the two who possess the eight qualities: *Oṃ gurubhyaḥ guru-śrīḥ; Oṃ paramagurubhyaḥ paramaguru-śrīḥ; Oṃ parātparagurubhyaḥ parātparaguru-śrīḥ;

Oṃ parameṣṭhigurubhyaḥ parameṣṭhiguru-śrīḥ*, one should offer [these] as before to the desired [deities]. This is the third enclosure (*āvaraṇa*). Now, in the middle of the eight petals, one should worship the Mothers beginning with Brahmāṇī, starting from the east and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction (*vāmāvarta*). As for their meditation (*dhyāna*): whatever form a deity has, and whatever their ornaments and vehicle may be...

Having meditated thus: "She who has stationed her power at the gate has come forth to fight the Asuras," one should offer oblations as before with the mantra: *Oṃ Brahmāṇyai Śrī Oṃ Māheśvaryai (0) Māheśvaryai Śrī Oṃ Kau Oṃ Māryai Śrī Oṃ Vaiṣṇavyai Vaiṣṇavī Śrī Śrī Oṃ Vārādyai Vārāhī Śrī Oṃ Nārasiṃhyai (0) Nārasiṃhyai Hrī Śrī Oṃ Aiṃ Glai Aiṃdryai Śrī (0) Oṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Cāmuṇḍā Śrī Abhī*. This concludes the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇam*). Then, on the twenty-four petals, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise—
With the [respective] syllables: *Oṃ* to Viṣṇumāyā, *Viṣṇumāyā-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Cetanā, *Cetanā-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Buddhi, *Buddhi-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Nidrā, *Nidrā-Śrī*;

*Oṃ* to Kṣudhā, *Kṣudhā-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Chāyā-Śakti, *Chāyā-Śakti-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Tṛṣṇā, *Tṛṣṇā-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Kṣānti, *Kṣānti-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Jāti, *Jāti-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Lajjā, *Lajjā-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Śānti, *Śānti-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Śraddhā, *Śraddhā-Śrī*; *Oṃ* to Kīrti, *Kīrti-Śrī*.
Śrī(0) Oṃ Lakṣmyai(0) Lakṣmī-Śrī; Oṃ Dhṛtyai(0) Dhṛti-Śrī; Oṃ Vṛttyai(0) Vṛti-Śrī; Oṃ Śrutyai Śruti-Śrī; Oṃ Smṛtyai Smṛti-Śrī;
Oṃ Tuṣṭyai(0) Tuṣṭi-Śrī; Oṃ Puṣṭyai Puṣṭi-Śrī; Oṃ Dayāyai Dayā-Śrī; Oṃ Mātre(0) Mātā-Śrī; Oṃ Lajjāyai Lajjā-Śrī; Oṃ Bhrāntyai Bhrānti-Śrī.
(24) Having offered [these] as before, this is the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*). Then, outside [that], in the directions of Earth, Lord of the House, Fire, Nirṛti, Wind, and Water...

In those [vessels], one should offer as before: Oṃ to Gaṇeśa, Gaṇeśa-Śrī; Oṃ to Kṣetrapāla, Kṣetrapāla-Śrī; Oṃ to Vaṭuka, Vaṭuka-Śrī; Oṃ to the Yoginīs, Yoginī-Śrī. Thus ends the sixth enclosure. Then, from the east to the northeast, there are eight triangular [vessels]; in each corner there is one vessel. Starting from the northeast and ending at the southeast, starting from the north and ending at the northwest, starting from the northwest and ending at the west, and starting from the west and ending at the southwest—[these are the locations].

Having drawn sixty-four triangles with a *bindu* in the four corners—starting from the southwest (Nairṛti) to the south, from the south to the southeast (Āgneya), and from the southeast to the east—on the third line of the earth-pavilion (*bhūgṛha*), one should worship the sixty-four Yoginīs there in order, starting from the east and ending with Īśāna, either clockwise or counter-clockwise. Now follows the visualization (*dhyāna*) of the first group of eight Yoginīs: they are white in color, [holding] a trident and a *ḍamaru*...
To be meditated upon as holding a rosary, a water-pot, a book, and a lute: Oṃ Jayāyai Jayaśrī; Oṃ Vijayāyai Vijayaśrī; Oṃ Jayantyai Jayantīśrī; Oṃ Aparājitāyai Aparājitāśrī;

Oṃ Divyayoginyai Divyayoginīśrī; Oṃ Mahāyoginyai Mahāyoginīśrī; Oṃ Siddhayoginyai Siddhayoginīśrī; Oṃ Gaṇeśaśvaryai Gaṇeśaśrī. Then follows the second group of eight: she is to be meditated upon as holding a rosary, a water-pot, a book, and a lute; Oṃ Pretā.

To Śinī: Oṃ! To Ḍākinī: Oṃ Ḍākinī! To Kālarātri: Oṃ! To Niśācarī: Ni! To Ṭaṅkāriṇī: Ṭaṃ! To Rudravetālī: Ru! To Huṃkāriṇī: Huṃ! Then, on the third [level], those of red color, holding a flaming spear and granting protection, are to be meditated upon: To Ūrdhvakeśinī: Ū! To Virūpākṣī: Vi! To Śuṣkā: Śu! To Taramojinī: Na! To Phaṭkāriṇī: Phaṭ! To Vīra...

To Bhadrā, Vī; to Dhūmrā, Dhū; to Kalahapriyā, Ke. Then, the fourth [is] like lightning, endowed with a banner, arrow, bow, and noose: to Rākṣasī, Rā; to Raktākṣī, Rā; to Viśvarūpā, Vi; to Bhayaṅkarī, Bha; to Vārakāmārī, Vīra; to Caṇḍikā, Caṃ; to Vārāhī, Vārā; to Muṇḍadhāriṇī, Muṃ. Then, the fifth is the color of the sun.

Those to be meditated upon as holding a lotus, a rosary, the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of bestowing boons (*varada*): *Oṃ bhairavyai*, *Oṃ dhvāṅkṣiṇyai*, *Oṃ dhūmrāyai*, *Oṃ pretavāhinyai*, *Oṃ khaḍginyai*, *Oṃ dīrghalaṃvoṣṭyai*, *Oṃ mālinyai*, *Oṃ mantrayoginyai*. [Then] those to be meditated upon as holding a beautiful blue lotus, a conch, a discus, and a mace, while displaying the gesture of granting fearlessness: *Oṃ kaulinyai*, *Oṃ cakriṇyai*, *Oṃ kaṅkālyai*, *Oṃ bhūva*.

Not with non-sovereigns: Bhū (0), Oṃ Troteṭakye (0) Tro (0), Oṃ Mahāmāye (0) Ma (0), Oṃ Yamadūtyai (0) Ya (0), Oṃ Karālinyāi (0) Ka (0). Then, for the seventh worship, those holding a skull-topped staff and an axe in their hands are to be meditated upon: Oṃ Keśinyai (0) Ke (0), Oṃ Mudryai (0) Mu (0), Oṃ Romajaṅghāyai (0) Ro Maḥ, Oṃ Nivāriṇyai (0) Ni (0), Oṃ Viśālyai (0) Vi (0), Oṃ Kāmukyāi (0) Ka (0), Oṃ Lokyai (0) Lo (0), Oṃ Adhomukhyai (0) Adho (0). Ta.

The eighth [deity] is Dhūmravarṇā, who is to be meditated upon as being adorned with a garland of spears, shields, and *bhiḍipāla* weapons. Oṃ muṃḍadhāriṇyai mu oṃ vyāghryai vyā oṃ kāṃkṣiṇyai kāṃ oṃ pretarūpiṇyai pre oṃ dhūrjaṭyai dhū oṃ ghoryai gho oṃ karālyai ka oṃ viṣalambinyai vi.
Having offered the desired [objects] as before, this is the seventh enclosure (*varaṇa*). Then, on the first line of the square, each respective [deity]:

Oṃ! The guardians of the directions (dikpālas), beginning from the east, are meditated upon as follows: they are red, white, black, smoke-colored, white, and both smoke-colored and black; Gaurī and Rūpā—these are proclaimed in order according to their colors. Oṃ Laṃ! To Indra, whose vehicle is Airāvata, who holds a thunderbolt (vajra) in his hand, the sovereign of the Asuras, the attendant of Śrī Caṇḍī, [I offer] Śrī Yāga.
Oṃ Raṃ! To Agni, whose vehicle is a ram, who holds a spear (śakti) in his hand, the sovereign of splendor, the attendant of Śrī Caṇḍī, [I offer] Agni.

*Śrī-yā*, to the one whose vehicle is a buffalo (*mahiṣa*), who holds a sword (*khaḍga*) in his hand, the Lord of the *Pretas*, the illustrious Caṇḍī (Yama-śrī): *Oṃ śvaṃ naiṛtye*. To the one whose vehicle is a man (*nara*), who holds a sword (*khaḍga*) in his hand, the Lord of the *Rakṣasas*, the illustrious Yaṃ (Niṛti-śrī): *Oṃ vaṃ vāruṇāya*. To the one whose vehicle is a sea-monster (*makara*), who holds a noose (*pāśa*) in his hand, the Lord of the Waters, the illustrious Caṃva (Varuṇa-śrī): *Oṃ vaṃ vāyavye*. To the one whose vehicle is a deer (*mṛga*), who holds a goad (*aṅkuśa*) in his hand, [the Lord] of Breath (*prāṇa*)...

Oṃ kuṃ kuberāya, to the Lord of Yakṣas, who has a horse as his vehicle and holds a mace in his hand, [namaskāra] to Śrī Caṇḍakubera. Oṃ haṃ īśānāya, to Īśāna, who has a bull as his vehicle and holds a trident in his hand, [namaskāra] to the Lord of Bhūtas, [namaskāra] to Śrī Caṇḍeśāna. Between Indra and Īśāna: Oṃ kaṃ brahmaṇe, to Brahmā, who has a swan as his vehicle and holds a lotus in his hand, [namaskāra] to the Lord of the World, [namaskāra] to Śrī Caṇḍabrahmā. Between Nirṛti and Varuṇa...

*Oṃ*, [salutation] to Ananta, who has the tortoise as his vehicle, holds a discus in his hand, and is the lord of the *nāgas*; [offerings are made] to Śrī Candra... as before. Having thus offered the preliminary worship, one should meditate upon the vajra and other [emblems] on the second line of the square [maṇḍala]. As for their forms: they are described as yellow, white, and dark; lightning-colored, red, and white; and white like a water-lily and pale-red (*pāṭala*). *Oṃ*, [salutation] to Vajra, whose crown is adorned with a vajra, who holds a vajra in his hand...

Oṃ, to Śakti, whose crown is marked by the Śakti, who holds the Śakti in his hand, Śrī Caṇḍa (0). Oṃ, to Daṇḍa, whose crown is marked by the Daṇḍa, who holds the Daṇḍa in his hand, Śrī Caṇḍa (0). Oṃ, to Khaḍga, whose crown is marked by the Khaḍga, who holds the Khaḍga in his hand, Śrī Caṇḍa Kha (0). Oṃ, to Pāśa, whose crown is marked by the Pāśa, who holds the Pāśa in his hand, Śrī Caṇḍa Pā (0). Oṃ, to Ākāśa, whose crown is marked by the Aṅkuśa, [who holds the] Aṅkuśa...

Oṃ, to the glorious Gadā (Mace), whose crown is marked with a mace, who holds a mace in his hand; Oṃ, to the glorious Caṇḍa-Gadā. Oṃ, to the Trिशूल (Trident), whose crown is marked with a trident, who holds a trident in his hand; Oṃ, to the glorious Tri-Indreśāna, between Indra and Īśāna. Oṃ, to the Padma (Lotus), whose crown is marked with a lotus, who holds a lotus in his hand; Oṃ, to the glorious Cakra, between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, whose crown is marked with a discus, [who holds] a discus...

Having performed the offering and libation as before for Hastāyaśrī, [he performs] the ninth enclosure (*navamāvaraṇa*). Again, [he offers] perfume (*gandha*) to Mahākātyai: "Obeisance to her who is with her limbs (*sāṅgāyai*) and with her retinue (*saparivārāyai*), [I offer] perfume. [He offers] perfume with the mantra "The door of fragrance" (*gandhadvārām*). [He offers] unbroken, pure, stainless *akṣata* grains, possessing a luster like a polished pearl:

"Accept these, O Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of the body's purity. Obeisance to Mahākātyai, with her limbs and her retinue. [I offer] these *akṣatas*. [He offers] betel-nut (*pūga*) with the mantra beginning "The door... (*mandāram*).
The Mistress of the Gods (Sureśvarī) was worshipped with *pārijāta*, *jāti*, *pāṭalaka*, *ketakī*, *campaka*, and other such flowers.

For each flower, she displayed the respective flower-mudrās. Then, having gazed upon the incense vessel, she recited the mantra: "Oṃ klīṃ, svāhā to the fragrant splendor," and cast into it incense such as *guggulu* and others.
She then worshipped the incense with the mantra: "To the incense whose deity is fragrance. [She worshipped] the root-mantra.

Having offered incense with the *lamahātyai sāṃyai* mantra, one should sprinkle water upon the bell to the left with the *astra-mantra*, saying "Oṃ, salutation to the Bell (*ghaṇṭā*)"; thus, having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, one should consecrate it three times with the mantra "Oṃ jadhvani mantre svāhā" and ring the bell with the left hand. Then: "Oṃ haṃ, accept this, svāhā! Born from the lord of trees (*vānaspati*), rich in fragrance, most excellent in scent—may this incense, which is to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted."

With the *ṛddhimūlamati* mantra, one should offer incense. Having filled the incense-offering vessel up to the navel with the incense mudrā and placed it within one's own portion, one should pour clarified butter or oil extracted from cow-products into it, place a wick containing camphor therein, and light it with the syllable *hrīṃ*.

Then, having worshipped it with "Obeisance to the lamp whose deity is Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇudevatyāya ghṛtadīpāya*) if it is a ghee lamp, or "Obeisance to the lamp whose deity is the Tree" (*anaspatidevatyāya tailadīpāya*) if it is an oil lamp, one should [offer] the nectar... always.

Having offered the ritual perfumes and flowers, one should offer the great lamp which is brilliantly radiant and dispels all darkness everywhere. Holding the lamp with the tips of the thumbs upon the middle joints of the middle and ring fingers, one should raise it and, as before, ring the bell. Having shown the lamp loudly from the feet to the head of the Goddess—if it is a ghee lamp, [it is held] on the right side of the Goddess; if it is an oil lamp, on the left.

Then, having prepared a four-cornered maṇḍala before the Goddess with ordinary *arghya* water, one should place there as an offering (*naivedya*) five kinds of food—consisting of edibles, chewables, lickables, and suckables—in a vessel made of gold or other materials, accompanied by various side dishes and endowed with the six flavors: pungent, sour, salty, bitter, astringent, and sweet.

Having established it there and worshipped it with the mantra "to Viṣṇu as the deity," one should gaze upon it with the root-mantra, sprinkle it with the *astra*-mantra, and [protect it] with the *astra*-mantra.

Having struck [the offering] with *kuśa* grass and sprinkled it with water while reciting the *Kavaca* mantra, one should place the left hand over the right hand, both palms facing downward. Reciting the mantra eight times, one should contemplate that this dries up the defects of touch in the food offering (*naivedya*). Then, placing the right hand over the left as before and covering it with the downward-facing left hand, one should mutter the mantra eight times. Contemplating that this burns away the defects of hatred, one should consecrate it with nectar (*amṛtīkṛta*) using the *Dhenu-mudrā*, and finally [protect it] with the *Astra-mantra*.

Having protected [the offering] with the *ṇa-cakra-mudrā* and consecrated it eight times with the root mantra, one should take water in the right hand and, having poured a handful of water over the food offering (*naivedya*), say: "O Supreme Goddess, accept this divine, supreme, well-prepared food contained in a golden vessel, endowed with the five types of flavors and sixty tastes. Having thus offered the water from the hollowed palm onto the food offering to Śrī Caṇḍikā, saying "Salutation to the food offering," and touching the thread with the left thumb, one should consecrate the water in another vessel as nectar (*amṛta*) for the Goddess. In the right...

Having offered a little water with the left hand while reciting "amṛtopastaraṇam asi," he should cause [the guest] to sip water (*ācamana*). Then, showing the *mudrā* resembling a blooming blue lotus with the left hand, he should touch [the guest's hands] with the right hand using the little finger, ring finger, and thumb for "oṃ prāṇāya";

the index finger, middle finger, and thumb for "apānāya"; the middle finger, ring finger, and thumb for "oṃ vyānāya"; again with the index finger, middle finger, and thumb for "oṃ udānāya"; and finally with all five fingers for "oṃ".

Having taken five mouthfuls with the five mudrās beginning with Samānāyāti-prāṇa, [he says]: "Salutations to You, O God of gods, supreme bestower of all satisfaction! Accept this excellent water—offered as food (anna), pure, in its natural state, very cool, and filled with supreme bliss. Having thus placed the water-vessel on the left side of the Goddess, he says: "O Goddess, along with Your attendants, I offer to You the true drink, the bliss of consciousness, for various and manifold moments."

Having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra *yaj juṣāṇa tat*, and performing the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the Astra-mantra while visualizing a pavilion (*jayanikā*) around the Goddess, one should offer this food-oblation (*naivedya*). [Offering] the Naivedya-mudrā for Mahādevī and meditating on her enjoyment, [one should visualize her] being respectfully fanned from all sides by those seated nearby— Brahmā and others— who are equally disposed and holding clusters of five kinds of side-dishes and condiments, and who are laughing and engaging in playful jests.

Having eaten with those who sit in rows and from a single vessel, one should meditate on the six limbs and the Goddess (Devī), reciting the root mantra ten times and offering the recitation as an oblation. Then one should perform the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*). According to the statement, "The rites beginning with the establishment of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) do not exist in the daily fire-sacrifice," [one should perform it] in the common (*laukika*) fire. Having thus meditated upon and worshipped [the deity], one should offer five oblations with the root mantra, six oblations with the mantras of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), six oblations for the planets, and one oblation each for the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*).

One should offer oblations (*huti*). If one is unable to perform the *āvaraṇa-homa* (the ritual of offering to the surrounding deities), one should offer six oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and the mantras of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-mantra*). This is the daily fire-sacrifice (*nitya-homa*).

Then, having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should draw mandalas consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square outside that [central area] in front of the Goddess, starting from the east and proceeding through the cardinal directions.
Having worshipped them with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the all-pervading mandala (*vyāpaka-maṇḍala*)," one should offer meat, fish, non-vegetarian food, *kūṣmāṇḍa* pumpkin, coconut, and so forth.

Having placed the vessels for the *kalala* and other stages into the vessel of the Goddess, one should offer the bali to the Goddess with the mantra: "O Great Mother, accept this bali; grant me the pacification of all calamities, svāhā! Having thus offered the bali to the Goddess, one should then first worship Gaṇeśa, who holds a noose (*pāśa*), a goad (*aṅkuśa*), a skull-bowl (*kapāla*), and a trident (*triśūla*) in his hands, and is adorned with various ornaments. Having meditated thus, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati! O you who are like a staff, bring all people under my control, svāhā!"
"O Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, bring all people under my control, svāhā! This offering (bali) is for Gaṇapati, obeisance!
Having thus offered [the bali], one should then meditate upon the Kṣetrapāla in the south, holding a sword, trident, skull-bowl, and hand-drum in his hands, naked, fierce, and dark-complexioned;
having meditated thus: "O Kṣetrapāla residing here, accept, accept this bali along with incense and lamps, svāhā! This bali is for Kṣetrapāla."

Having joined the thumbs and index fingers of both hands in the shape of a vulva (*yoni*), and having formed a fist with the left hand while keeping the index finger straight, one should offer [the oblation] there.

Then, one should worship in the west, having meditated thus: "One who holds a skull-bowl and a noose in two hands, possesses a trident, is adorned with ornaments, surrounded by his own host, fierce, and red in color.
With the mantra "To Vaṭuka," one should offer [the oblation] using the index finger together with the thumb, saying: "Come, come, O son of the Goddess, Vaṭukanātha, tawny-hued one!"

"O you whose face is the flame of the three eyes, radiant with the *ṭā-bhā-ra* [mantra], destroy all obstacles! Accept this *bali* offering accompanied by all ritual services; *svāhā*!"—with this mantra, [one should offer it] to the north. Having meditated thus: "One should worship the Yoginī here in the northeast, holding a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), a noose (*pāśa*), and a *liṅga* in her hands, wearing a red garment around her waist," one should say: "To the Yoginīs, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. To the Yoginīs, this *bali* is offered; *namaḥ*. [With this, one should offer it] with the right thumb...
One should offer [the oblation] by means of the *ṣṭhānāmāya*-yoga; one should satisfy the three with the nectar from the *bali* vessel—this applies everywhere.

Then, having drawn a square, circle, and triangle mandala in the northeast corner of the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*), and having placed the *bali* vessel there, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, saying: "Salutation to all beings (*sarvabhūtebhyo namaḥ*)".
[One should also honor those] who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, who dwell in the abode of Rudra, the yoginīs of terrible form, and the lords of the hosts of spirits and rākṣasas.
May all those who move upon the earth and likewise those who dwell in the intermediate space, becoming joyful in mind, accept this *bali* with the fingers of their left hands.

Having poured a stream of water from the *bali* vessel into another vessel using the fingers of the left hand, one should cast it into the *bali* vessel. Then, having offered the *bali*, one should take a handful of flowers and say: "Whatever beings exist here on the surface of the earth, having accepted this *bali* duly offered, may they depart satisfied; may they all forgive me."

Having offered a handful of flowers with the mantra "nyatranamaste bhyaḥ," one should sprinkle oneself with water while reciting the Astra-mantra. If that is not possible, having fashioned a maṇḍala on one's left side as before and meditated upon Gaṇeśa and the others, one should offer the bali-oblation in sequence using the five mantras; even if there is only one recipient, one may offer it using the plural form. This is the offering of the bali. Then, having meditated upon the Goddess as being satiated, one should give the subsequent water for rinsing (uttarāpośana) with the mantra: "amṛtakṛtyajalam amṛtāpipānam asi svāhā."

Having extracted the essence from the *naivedya* (food offering) and purified the site in the southwest (*nairṛtya*) with cow dung and other materials, one should take a small portion of the remainder and cast it toward the northeast (*aiśānya*) for the sake of feeding the *nirmālya-bhakṣaka* spirits. Then, having washed one's hands, one should offer fragrant powders and the like for the purpose of cleansing the Goddess’s hands, and water for rinsing the mouth.
Having caused her to rinse her teeth with fragrant water, one should then provide a tooth-cleansing stick (*dantadhāvana*) made of camphor pieces. Furthermore—

Having offered water for rinsing the mouth (*arghya*), having washed [his] feet and offered water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and having sprinkled [his] garments, hands, and feet, one should offer fragrant powders and the like into the hands.
Then, taking betel nut (*pūgīphala*) along with camphor, betel leaves, cardamom, and cloves—this root [of the ritual] should be accepted.
[Offer] fresh flowers, incense, lamps, fruit, and the *phala-mudrā*. O Mother, this [offering], adorned with a golden staff and possessing the luster of the full moon’s orb...

O Mother of the World, with joy I offer you this umbrella, fashioned by myself from the eight [directions], which shines with jewels and golden pitchers, gladdening the three worlds, and is encircled by a radiant net of pearls; O Mother of the Universe, I also offer you, amidst an abundance of bliss, wonderful whisks with handles of gold resplendent with gems and pearls, and colored like the rays of an autumnal moon.

I fan you with a chowrie as radiant as the orb of the rising sun; O Mother of the World, out of devotion, look upon your own face—beautiful as the full moon—in this jeweled mirror, and behold the tremulous play of your restless eyes.
Even Indra and the other gods constantly perform the *nīrājana* rite for your footstool with the lamps of their well-fashioned crowns; therefore, I now offer this body of mine to you.
"O Mother of the World, with a thousand lamps, I perform this *Nīrājana* for Śrī Caṇḍikā; [I offer] Durvā grass, unbroken rice, and water—this *Nīrājana*, obeisance!

Having thus cast the Durvā grass and other items upon the Goddess's crown, he performed the *Nīrājana*. [Then he said: "O Blessed One, this horse, which has a gait pleasing to the heart, is exceedingly swift, adorned with golden ornaments and a multitude of jewels, and possesses a smooth, deep sound; it is offered by me for the sake of your pleasure."

May that elephant, which possesses the speed of the wind accompanied by hundreds of trumpeting sounds, whose trunk is held high like a banner, whose neck is adorned with golden bells and small tinkling chimes, whose pair of ears are like chowries, who is equal to Indra, and who is fanned by horses as he moves upon his jeweled lotus-throne—may that elephant, the lord of beasts, bring joy to you.

I offer this chariot to the Blessed One—this chariot resplendent with horses, elephants, and charioteers, which makes the ten directions resound with the thunderous roar of kettledrums, and which is joined by an exceedingly skillful fourfold army; with a weight of devotion, I satisfy the Blessed One with this. I offer this powerful fortress named *Dharanītala*, surrounded by the seven oceans and accompanied by many armies, which has been maintained by me. Du...

May the Goddess—who possesses a flood of divine beauty arising from her lotus-face smiling amidst the mass of her hair loosely flowing over her Lakulī [shoulder], who is the supreme immortal *kalakaṇṭhī* (cuckoo/swan) dancing within the incomparable theater of her own attire, and who dwells upon the slopes of beautiful breasts—grant us steadfastness. In every house, there appeared daily the sound of lutes played by women whose breasts were not yet bound by time, accompanied by the rhythmic musical phrases: *dhimi kiti dhimi dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ dhiṃ gi*.
O Ambika, may the sound of the *ḍamaru* drum—uttering "ḍiṃḍim," "kṣarkṣa," "rakṣa," "kṣarīmṛdu," and "ravārdaghaṭārdrayakṣaṭhini"—be for your great compassion and mercy.

O Goddess, the Gandharva maidens, their minds fixed with momentary attention, sing this song as if striking the seven musical notes upon the ripples of the water; listen to it, for you have been entreated by me.

Having for a moment witnessed the dancing of the female dancers with their fresh and lovely gestures, and having himself performed the dance and played the instruments while singing songs dedicated to the Blessed One, he thought, "I remember Your dance, O Goddess. Having thus offered these royal services and worshipped with the *ārārtikā* (waving of lights), he performed the *nīrājana* (lustration) seven times over his head, accompanied by the ringing of the bell and the recitation of the root mantra.

[Having performed] the *damārārtika* [offering], with the mantra-flower (*mantrapuṣpa*) from the *Laghu-saptaśatī*: "Obeisance to you, the fierce one who wields the sword and the trident, the impure one, the pure one; obeisance to you, O Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), worshipped by the gods at the Śrī-pīṭha; obeisance to you, Mahālakṣmī, whose hands hold the conch, the discus, and the mace.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) at the root [of the mantra], and having recollected the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the meditation (*dhyāna*) and the ritual application (*nyāsa*) of the mantra, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).

Having sprinkled the rosary with water from the central vessel, having worshipped it with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having recited "Oṃ Ḍāṃ, O rosary, perform [this] without obstacle," one should place it near the heart upon the middle joint of the middle finger. Having uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times, at the completion of the count, one should utter the *praṇava* again and, saying "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Siddhi," place the rosary on the head. Then, one should assign the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other factors to its secret parts.

With the mantra, one should secretly place water and a serpent-garland in the left hand of the Goddess and cause her to swear an oath. Then, having praised her with the *Laghu-stava*, one should take the *arghya* water in a small vessel and circumambulate the Goddess three times. [Recite: "Whatever [sin] was previously committed by me through the authority of my vital breaths, in the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states, by mind, speech, body, or both..."

"Whatever has been performed by my two hands, my stomach, or my private parts—all that is offered as an oblation to Brahman; Svāhā! I offer myself, along with my lamp and my mental resolve, at the great feet of the Goddess;
*Tat Sat*. Thus, he should offer his own feet at the feet of the Goddess. Then, taking up the special *arghya* water and waving it three times over the Goddess:
"O Goddess, whatever action—whether good or bad—I have performed, please accept all of that out of compassion. My worship is complete, O Goddess; what more can I do for You?"

Having offered the *cijjala* (water for sipping) with the remainder, he should sprinkle himself and his attendants. Then, excluding those on the threshold (*dehalī*), he should unite them with Śiva through the *pūraka-yoga* by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.

Next, in the northeast, he should worship Caṇḍeśvarī with the mantra "Oṃ Caṇḍeśvaryai Namaḥ" using garlands, flowers, and water. He should then offer the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) along with water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*). [He should recite: "Obeisance!
By the command of Śrī Śiva, I give to you all that is to be licked, sucked, drunk, and so forth, as well as betel, unguents, and the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*). Thus, right there—

Having set down [the vessel], washed his hands, and filled a copper or other metal vessel with water containing fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), he stands facing [the sun] and recites: "Obeisance to Vivasvat, the Brahman; obeisance to the radiant one of showering splendor. Obeisance to Savitṛ, the pure, the impeller, the bestower of action. Having thus recited, he offers the *arghya* to the Sun with the mantra: "Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ śrī sūrya eṣa te arghyaḥ svāhā. Then, with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*), he says: "Whatever defect there is in the sacrifice, whatever defect in the teeth, whatever defect in the worship..."

"May all that [be] without flaw through the grace of the Sun. Having thus prayed, one should go to the place of worship, place the remaining fragrance from the worship upon one's left hand, pour a little water from the *arghya* vessel into it, stir it, consecrate it eight times with the root mantra, and apply it to the forehead.

Then, having removed the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) from one's body with the root mantra, and having consumed the water from the feet (*caraṇodaka*) with the root mantra and given some to others, one may proceed as one pleases.

Thus, because the worship of the Goddess is paramount, one should worship her at the three times of day. According to the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, one should daily offer a *bali* oblation of boiled rice mixed with black gram (*māṣa*). One should worship the Goddess at the three times of day, being devoted to the *Jaya-stotra*. From the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Having worshipped [her] in the month of Āśvina, one becomes free from sorrow in this world. And from the *Rudrayāmala*: "The Goddess Durgā is dear to me. And from the *Devī Purāṇa*: "One should worship the Goddess at night. This refers to the ritual of the Night-worship (*rātripūjā*).
The excellence of the fruit has been declared in the *Tārābhaktitaraṅgiṇī* composed by Vimūlānandanātha. Herein ends the procedure for the worship of Navacaṇḍī and others.

Now, the worship of the Kumārīs: For all undertakings, one should worship a Brahmin girl; for the sake of victory, one born of a royal lineage; for the sake of wealth, one born of a Vaiśya lineage; for the sake of sons, one born of a Śūdra lineage.

For fierce rites, one should worship according to the prescribed rule a girl of even lower castes. By means of nine [girls], one obtains land; by double that number, sovereignty; and by one hundred... [one obtains] a kingdom.

One should not accept even a single [girl] who lacks auspicious marks; however, one should avoid those who are one year old and those intended for worship. One should avoid a girl marked with a Brahmin’s [sacred thread], one who is born blind, one-eyed, deformed, or excessively hairy in any part of her body. Likewise, one should avoid a girl born of a slave-womb. Having had her anointed with fragrant oil and seated upon a prepared seat, [one should consider] the place and the time.

Having recollected [the purpose], for the sake of destroying suffering and poverty, for the destruction of enemies, and for the increase of longevity and strength, I shall perform the worship of one thousand maidens according to the portion of Caṇḍī.

Thus, up to Subhadrā, the fruit of that should be written down along with the auspicious rites. Having performed the *ṣaḍaṅga* (six-limbed ritual) with the root mantra, and having invoked [the deity] with the syllables of the root mantra:
"I invoke the maiden who is Lakṣmī herself, the Mātṛkā assuming form, who is manifest as the nine Durgās. Then [offer] the seat (*āsana*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*).

Having washed her feet with warm water and offered them worship, and having provided water for sipping (ācamana) and a bath, and having dressed her in fresh garments, a bodice, ornaments, collyrium, turmeric, and other such items, and having anointed her body with excellent fragrances such as saffron, red flower garlands, and the like, and having worshipped her with incense and lamps—O Mother of the World, O Goddess of the World, you whose very nature is all-powerful (sarva-śakti-svarūpiṇī), accept this worship; O Mother of the World, salutations to you! (0)

One should feed [the deity] with various offerings of worship, including milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cooked rice, and diverse edibles. At the time of feeding, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times and performed the ritual of protection (*rakṣā*), one should dismiss [the deity].
In this manner, one should worship others as well. Thus ends the first [section], which was declared by all as "the syllable of the mantra. Regarding the variation in the mantra for the prayer:

"I worship the Goddess Tripurā, the support of the three cities, whose form is the knowledge of the three aims of life, who is adored by the three worlds, and who is the triple-formed (*trimūrti*). This is the second [section].
"I worship here Śivā, whose heart is compassion, the auspicious Goddess, the mother of all that is auspicious, who is both of the nature of Time and beyond Time"—this is the third [verse].
"I worship here Kālikā, who is exalted by qualities such as *aṇimā*, whose essence is the imperishability of the letter 'A', the infinite power, the Fortune (Lakṣmī), and Rohiṇī"—this is the fourth.

"I worship here Kālikā, who acts according to her will, who is radiant, beautiful, whose nature is the Wheel of Time (*Kālacakra*), and who is exalted by compassion and grants desires"—this is the fifth.

"I worship Mīnā, Caṇḍavīrā, Caṇḍā, Māyā, Caṇḍamuṇḍaprabhajinī, and the Great Goddess Caṇḍīkā of fierce prowess"—thus [is] the sixth. "I worship the Goddess Śāmbhavī, who always brings joy, who is peaceful, who is saluted by all the gods, and whose self is all beings"—thus [is] the seventh. "I worship Durgā with constant devotion, she who is difficult to reach and difficult to traverse, the destroyer of fear and the arising of calamities, and the dweller in the fortress of those in distress"—thus [is] the eighth. "The beautiful one, the golden..."

I worship here the goddess Subhadrā, who bestows beauty, splendor, happiness, and good fortune, the auspicious mother-goddess; such is the fruit of this ninth day. In the Skanda Purāṇa: "By this rite, Indra quickly attains various desires as wished for by his mind; having ruled his kingdom, he thereafter goes to the world of the gods. In the Yāmala also: "The fruit of worshipping the Kumārī cannot be described by me; by whomsoever the Kumārī is worshipped..."

One shall become worshipped by the three worlds through their sequence; their names are stated in the Skanda-purāṇa: Kumārikā, Trimūrti, Kalyāṇī, Rohiṇī, Kālī, Caṇḍī, Śāmbhavī, Durgā, and Subhadrā—this is the order. A two-year-old girl is Kumārikā, a three-year-old is Trimūrtinī, a four-year-old is Kalyāṇī, a five-year-old is Rohiṇī, and a six-year-old is proclaimed by the name Subhadrā. Beyond this age, they are known as Bālā for all rites.

He states the fruits of these [deities] in sequence, excluding Śuvarjitā: for the destruction of service, suffering, and poverty; for the destruction of the power of Indra; for the increase of longevity and strength, a man should worship Kumārī. One desiring long life, for the attainment of the fruit of the three goals (trivarga), and for the non-occurrence of untimely death, the affliction of disease, and suffering, should worship Kalpā—always, O wise one—for the increase of happiness, grain, wealth, health, sons, and grandsons. Thus [one should worship] Kalpā.
A man desiring the increase of his progeny, as well as health, happiness, wealth, and fame, should always worship Rohiṇī.

Furthermore, one who seeks knowledge, victory, and especially sovereignty, and one who desires the destruction of enemies, should worship Kālī. One who desires victory in battle should worship Caṇḍikā. For the destruction of suffering and poverty, for the enchantment of kings, and for the eradication of great sins, one should worship the consort of Śambhu (Śāmbhavī).

In rites for fierce accomplishment (*ugrasādhana*), one should conquer those who are powerful, arrogant, and fierce; a wise person should worship with effort at difficult places (*durga*) to destroy those who dwell in difficulty.

For the attainment of fruits such as fortune, wealth, grain, and so forth, a mortal should worship Śivā; for the increase of female and male servants, one should worship Subhadrā. Thus ends the worship of the nine maidens (*navakumārī*) and its fruit. Then follows the worship of Brāhmaṇas and married women (*suvāsinī*). In this manner, during the Navarātra, the worship of the Goddess, the maidens, and so on, is to be known [to extend] from the Nine Caṇḍīs up to the Hundred Thousand Caṇḍīs (*lakṣacaṇḍī*).
Regarding the increase in the number of recitations for the *Cāmuṇḍī* rites: for the *Śatacaṇḍī* rite and others, the increase should be understood as doubling and so forth;

for the *Sahasracaṇḍī* rite, the increase is by ten; likewise, for the *Ayutacaṇḍī* rite, the increase is by one hundred; and for the *Lakṣacaṇḍī* rite, the increase is by one thousand. Then, it should be offered to the Goddess—this is the procedure for worship (*pūjā-vidhi*). Now, the procedure for recitation (*japa-vidhi*): after the worship, one should recite or listen to the *Mahātmya* (the Greatness) and other texts concerning the Blessed Lady, which are celebrated in the Purāṇas and other scriptures.
